title: Putting the Autonomous Car Before the Horse
author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman
content: Waymo has been testing its self-driving cars in D.C. for years. Bill Clark/AP Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: An inside look at Waymo, Tom Sietsema's favorite banh mi and new Commander Stefon Diggs. THE LATEST Self-driving cars aren’t yet legal in D.C., but that’s not stopping Waymo. The Google-owned autonomous car company is building out three new maintenance and charging facilities in D.C., and using them to lay the political and practical groundwork for what it hopes will be approval in the fall of a D.C. Council bill to legalize passenger service. “When you look at other ride-hailing companies, you don’t see this,” Matt Walsh, the company’s head of policy for the East Coast, said Wednesday during a tour of a 30, -square-foot maintenance center being built out just off Bladensburg Road Northeast. He said Waymo is investing tens of millions of dollars in its local infrastructure, and hiring D.C. residents as car testers and technicians. Waymo currently offers passenger service in 11 cities and has aggressive expansion plans. The company has been testing its self-driving white Jaguars in D.C. for upwards of two years, logging more than , miles of fully autonomous driving (with a human in the car as backup) and mapping every road in the city. Still, elected officials in D.C. have been slow to embrace full legalization, though a bill introduced by Ward 6 council member Charles Allen did have its first public hearing in July . The fight is still on, with some labor unions raising concerns about Uber and Lyft drivers losing jobs, and some disabled residents demanding requirements for wheelchair-accessible vehicles. Waymo has its own concerns with Allen’s bill, notably an initial cap on the number of cars that would be allowed to offer passenger service in D.C. Walsh said any cap could affect the type of service Waymo can offer, as well as the investments the company is making in the city. Allen tells NOTUS his bill’s initial -car cap is meant to phase in the service, in what he calls a “stepped and tiered” approach. Allen was also given a tour of the maintenance facility this week, where he was joined by D.C. Department of Transportation Director Sharon Kershbaum . “I’m going to read it as the company trying to show us they’re serious about making investments in D.C.,” Allen said. “It’s something both the council and mayor would want to see, that all the talk of investment and job creation gets backed up. I see it as a show of good faith.” IMG_8745.jpg ( , AR: 1.26) DEEP DIVE At-Large council member Robert White , likely D.C.’s next congressional delegate , told NOTUS the city’s housing committee will hold an “oversight roundtable” on the District’s housing authority next month. The committee, which White chairs, will convene Sept. 29 to discuss DCHA’s recent struggles, which include a scathing audit, a cyberattack and poor unit conditions. The announcement comes on the heels of a NOTUS report showing that the authority, which has one of the largest housing portfolios in the District, owes over $2.2 million in fines tied to more than 2, code violations. “Since it’s an independent authority of the District government, code enforcement is challenging, but residents deserve better,” White told NOTUS in a statement. “My priorities are making sure units are brought up to code, tenants and landlords are treated fairly, lease ups are efficient and DCHA’s finances are in order so we can deliver safe, stable housing.” FROM THE DISTRICT What’s on the menu will be on the ballot. Voters in D.C. will get to decide in November whether the city should ban the production and sale of foie gras , the fatty liver of ducks that the French consider a delicacy and many animal rights activists say is a disgrace. The D.C. Board of Elections ruled this week that proponents of what’s known as Initiative 86 collected enough signatures to put the measure on the general election ballot. FROM VIRGINIA The 9-year-old from Northern Virginia who died while riding an e-scooter last month was not an anomaly, The Washington Post reports . According to a March report, there were at least 2, pediatric e-scooter injuries between and . FROM MARYLAND Democrats are one step closer to picking up the only Republican seat in the state’s nine-member congressional delegation ahead of , after lawmakers passed a constitutional amendment on redistricting Tuesday, NOTUS’ Manuela Silva reports . TALK TO TOM Tom Sietsema is back answering your questions about the D.C. dining scene. Submit your questions here . What’s your favorite banh mi in the DMV? If forced to eat one sandwich for the rest of my life — and with apologies to France’s jambon-buerre, the Middle East’s shawarma and New Orleans’ muffuletta — I’d cast my fate with the Vietnamese wonder built with a crisp baguette and a combination of meat, tangy vegetables and a spread of butter or mayonnaise. And I’d eat them all at Bánh Mì Oi in Falls Church. (“Oi” is a call to attention in Vietnamese, similar to “hey.”) The signature banh mi packs ham, pâté, pork bologna and pork belly along with traditional enhancers of cucumber, cilantro, pickled carrots, daikon and aioli between slices of a roll that’s at once airy, crisp and fluffy. The monster bread, baked on site, is so good, people ask to buy just the base; requests are limited to five rolls per order, says owner Yeanie Bach , citing the business’s small kitchen. Other fillings include a delectable warm tofu seasoned with star anise, and Nashville (truly) hot chicken. In the full Q&A : how to support restaurants outside of dining, some tried-and-true spots in Montgomery County and the puzzling ubiquity of tuna crudo. SPORTS Stefon Diggs AP - ( , AR: 1.50) The Commanders signed Pro Bowl wide receiver Stefon Diggs on Wednesday afternoon in hopes of shoring up their shaky pass-catching corps. The 32-year-old Diggs, a DMV native, agreed to a one-year deal worth up to $12 million. NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson writes that the move transforms Washington’s pass-catching unit from merely average to dangerously deep. Training camp update: Martenzie reports that Wednesday’s session was messy in more ways than one: A rainy morning created plenty of mud, and there were multiple dust-ups between the offense and defense. Afterward, new safety Nick Cross said he likes the aggression — to an extent. “At the end of the day, all the chirping and stuff is cool,” he said. “But when it starts costing the team, costing the penalties, guys being kicked out of games and stuff like that, that's where it becomes an issue." What to Watch Today MLB: Nationals at Phillies, 6:05 p.m. ( MLB.TV ) Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com . The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson.

title: Talk to Tom: Restaurant Recs for D.C., Maryland ... and Germany!
author: Tom Sietsema
summary: Plus, ways to help the restaurant industry, and why tuna crudo is on every menu.
content: The pozole rojo at Cielo Rojo in Takoma Park. Kainaz Amaria/NOTUS Welcome to Talk to Tom , the dining advice column that aims to point you toward good meals, steer you from the dross and solve your pressing restaurant queries. Look for a fresh Q&A every Thursday in this space. Questions and comments can be submitted to TalkToTom@notus.com . Submissions may be edited for length and clarity. I don't have a ton of money, but I'd like to support the industry. What’s the best way to back those restaurants we love besides just dining there? Every restaurant operator I reached out to appreciated your question. These are tough times for the industry; even small gestures of appreciation help. “Restaurants need and love praise from guests,” says Amy Brandwein, the chef of Centrolina and Piccolina in CityCenter. “So share your love with news outlets, social media and review [sites]. That is a way to generate more business without spending a dime.” Word of mouth is crucial, says Anthony Jones , the chef at Marcus DC in NoMa, who makes a habit of frequenting area mom-and-pops, even if it’s just an ice cream shop. If you have some money to spare, restaurateurs say buying gift cards is a boon to a business. “It’s an immediate injection of revenue for us and a promise of future business,” says Bill Jensen, the vision behind Reveler’s Hour in Adams Morgan. Patrice Cleary of Purple Patch and Joia Burger in Mount Pleasant likes the idea of purchasing, say, four $25 gift certificates and passing them out to a kids program or other charity. Who knows, she says; “You may introduce somebody else to a [new] restaurant.” Remember that not every meal away from home has to be extravagant, says Matt Adler , the chef behind Caruso’s Grocery and Cucina Morini in the Capitol Hill East and Mount Vernon Square neighborhoods, respectively. “Even just grabbing a bowl of pasta and a glass of wine at the bar on a slower night makes a big difference for a restaurant,” he says, “especially during slower restaurant months.” Jones suggests forming a group or club to try a wider variety of dishes and spread out the cost of a meal. Since moving to Montgomery County 15 years ago, I’ve encountered few really good restaurants. Can you recommend anything, aside from strictly sushi spots, with price less of a concern than quality? (I’m really glad you’re doing this here, along with many other of my favorite writers from The Washington Post.) Thanks for the question and the welcome. When I think about Maryland’s most populous county — with more than a million people spread over about square miles — the restaurants I never tire of visiting suggest a U.N. buffet. DC0A7865 copyb.jpg ( , AR: 1.35)My tried-and-true spots are: The Salt Line for pleasing seafood, including an ace lobster roll, in Bethesda. Melina for polished Greek in North Bethesda. Beteseb for Ethiopian in Silver Spring, where my current fascination is dullet, or boiled, ground tripe spiked with jalapeño, mitmita and cardamom. Cielo Rojo for Mexican in Takoma Park, a fetching retreat that has me scraping the bottom of my brick-red bowl of pozole, thick with chicken and thrumming with dried chiles. Chennai Hoppers and Peter Chang for admirable Indian and Chinese, respectively, in Gaithersburg. Different as the restaurants are, they share consistency, comfort and choiceness. My biggest (pettiest) restaurant pet peeve is the ubiquity of tuna crudo. It's a delicious dish, but everyone has it and I'm ready to move on! Any day now, I expect Olive Garden to start selling the Italian appetizer — simply dressed raw fish, typically splashed with olive oil, salt and citrus — which I agree is seemingly everywhere these days. Behind the “Odyssey”-esque ubiquity swim several forces: a raw fish boom led long ago by sushi, the ongoing popularity of Italian coastal cuisine, the wide availability of sushi-grade tuna and the ease of preparation. Compared to a cooked dish, crudo involves minimal labor and saves on waste. Finally, tuna crudo gives even a mainstream menu a whiff of cachet. Tom, my last trip to Germany was when the country name started with “West.” My husband and I are nonetheless heading to Frankfurt for a week in early September with friends who recently moved there from Baltimore, and we would love your recommendations for restaurants. Cost doesn’t matter; value does. One person doesn’t eat red meat and another doesn’t eat seafood/shellfish. Ideally, at least one option would serve spaetzle and schnitzel. Some of the innovative places that should land on your list are Emma Metzler , set inside the Museum of Applied Arts and popular for its house-baked bread, nose-to-tail cooking and a terrace overlooking a park; Chairs, where the regionally focused menu changes monthly and the wines are natural; Rausch , which serves a tasting menu featuring modern German fare (and where I’m told Friday lunch is the prime time to go); and Main Tower Restaurant & Lounge , whose menu combines Asian and Austrian influences and whose dining room sits high in the sky in the banking district. For more traditional German cooking, one option is the lively, cash-only Ebbelwoi Unser, dressed with communal tables and home to Hessian classics like schnitzel with green sauce and fresh apple wine. Help! I need a “nice-ish” D.C. restaurant that can accommodate a range of appetites and won’t cost a fortune. (I’m paying.) You want Unconventional Diner, the spirited American restaurant near the convention center (get it?) that never fails to please. No issue if one of you wants meat, one wants plants, another diner hopes for something adventurous. Chef-owner David Deshaies offers something for everyone on his menu: a meatloaf fueled with Sriracha for heat and Gruyere cheese for succulence; a refreshing and beautiful Thai salad; crackling duck confit with steaming bao buns in a circle of accessories. (The idea with the last dish is to create your own duck sandwiches with cilantro, hoisin sauce, chiles and more.) Your question prompted a reunion with the restaurant over the weekend, when it was packed with Otakon attendees, many dressed as their favorite characters from Japanese video games and comics. A companion and I split a heaping helping of “nachos” coaxed from kale and striped with electric sauces, and a stellar chicken parm escorted with a bundle of spaghetti tossed in butter, Parmesan and chicken stock for flavor. Busy as the place was, the staff took time to charm. As I debated between miso salmon and that duck confit, a server asked, “What’s your aim tonight?” before describing each dish in detail. All this, at a price that will make you as happy as the food: The generous entrees — buttermilk pancakes for dinner, if you’re so inclined! — average an agreeable $24. Direct me to your preferred banh mi in the DMV, please. If forced to eat one sandwich for the rest of my life — and with apologies to France’s jambon-buerre, the Middle East’s shawarma and New Orleans’ muffuletta — I’d cast my fate with the Vietnamese wonder built with a crisp baguette and a combination of meat, tangy vegetables and a spread of butter or mayonnaise. And I’d eat them all at Bánh Mì Oi in Falls Church. (“Oi” is a call to attention in Vietnamese, similar to “hey.”) The signature banh mi packs ham, pâté, pork bologna and pork belly along with traditional enhancers of cucumber, cilantro, pickled carrots, daikon and aioli between slices of a roll that’s at once airy, crisp and fluffy. The monster bread, baked on site, is so good, people ask to buy just the base; requests are limited to five rolls per order, says owner Yeanie Bach , citing the business’s small kitchen. Other fillings include a delectable warm tofu seasoned with star anise, and Nashville (truly) hot chicken. Know before going in that there are fewer than 40 small stools spread across two small floors and outside. Expect a line. Know, too, Bánh Mì Oi delivers. Clearly, I’m not the only fanboy. Bach says she sells an average of 1, to 1, of her hits — per day.

title: Commanders to Sign Stefon Diggs, Shoring Up a Shaky Receivers Room
author: Martenzie Johnson
summary: The former Patriot is expected to slot in as Washington’s No. 2 receiver, answering one of the offseason’s biggest questions.
content: Former Patriots wide receiver Stefon Diggs is joining the Commanders on a one-year deal. Adrian Kraus/AP Commanders fans' long nightmare is over. After a spring and summer full of rumors, opinions, guesses and many, many social media posts, Washington got its No. 2 receiver on Wednesday as the team is set to sign veteran free agent Stefon Diggs. The former Patriot has agreed to a one-year, $12 million contract, according to ESPN . The signing of Diggs, who totaled 85 receptions for 1, yards and four touchdowns for the AFC champion Patriots last season, transforms Washington’s receiving corps from an average group to a position of strength. A source close to Diggs said the 32-year-old DMV native chose Washington because he was impressed by the entire organization, from the front office to the coaches to the players. Diggs, a four-time Pro Bowler, wanted a “chance to play with one of best young [quarterbacks] and opposite one of [the] best receivers — and to do it all at home,” the source said. The fifth-round pick out of Maryland has been one of the most decorated and consistent receivers in the league for nearly a . His 9, receiving yards since is the third-most in that time period behind only Davante Adams (9, ) and Tyreek Hill (9, ). His primary strengths are his route-running and catch radius, skills best highlighted by his famous “Minneapolis Miracle” catch with the Vikings during the playoffs. According to Next Gen Stats , Diggs had the highest catch percentage (83.3%) in the league last season. Putting a player with career receptions, 11, yards and 74 touchdowns alongside Terry McLaurin ( receptions, 6, yards and 41 touchdowns) makes the receiving unit deep and dangerous. The two veterans will be grouped with promising rookie Antonio Williams, who has had breakout moments during training camp; former first-rounder Treylon Burks; veteran Van Jefferson and a host of other young receivers. Diggs spent the first five seasons of his career with the Vikings before being traded to the Bills in . After four years in Buffalo, Diggs played in Houston before joining the Patriots and reaching last year’s Super Bowl. Diggs has also garnered headlines away from the field. In May, he was found not guilty of assaulting his private chef. He is currently suing a social media influencer who has accused him of sexual assault and facing a civil lawsuit for accusing a former concierge of stealing his Ferrari.

title: On the Right Track
author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman
content: People board a Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority (WMATA) train while others wait on the opposite platform at the Metro Center station in Washington, D.C. on March 11, . Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: A drop in Metro crime, $1.4 billion for the National Guard and a confusing Nats trade deadline. THE LATEST Crime on Metro has hit a “new historic low.” New crime data released by WMATA shows that Part I crimes — more serious offenses like assaults, robberies and thefts — are down 12% since last year and 61% since . The consistent decreases in crime come from cops, cameras and compassion , says WMATA general manager Randy Clarke . There are more police officers and security guards patrolling stations and buses; 30, cameras are monitoring the system; and low-income riders are offered discounts to help prevent fare evasion. Clarke said Tuesday the drop in crime and increase in ridership have created something of a virtuous cycle for Metro, with safer trains and buses encouraging ridership, and more riders putting more eyes to work. “Not only is [Metro] much safer, it’s much safer for a lot more people,” he said. (Even still, ridership numbers remain below where they were pre-pandemic.) Fare evasion enforcement has been a particular focus for Metro in recent years. Clarke said enforcement on trains increased % from to . Ramped-up enforcement on buses that was launched this year has led to a 1, % spike in citations. Clarke himself has even gotten in on enforcing the rules. He said he recently stopped an older man who tried to get into a Metro station using one of the Kids Ride Free cards that are handed out to schoolchildren in the city. (Note to self: Don’t use your kids’ cards.) Still, there have been snags. NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle recently reported that a bureaucratic snafu has led to most fare-evasion citations issued in D.C. being dismissed. Clarke says he wants a regional solution to ensure that fare evasion is prosecuted consistently across the Metro system. President Donald Trump plans to spend $1.4 billion in taxpayer funds keeping the National Guard in D.C. until January , NOTUS’ Angie Orellana Hernandez reports . The eye-popping estimate, provided to Sen. Elizabeth Warren ’s office and shared with NOTUS, includes a recently announced $ million contract to keep troops housed through the end of Trump’s term. For context: The D.C. police department’s annual budget for its 3, officers is roughly $ million. National Guard DC AP - ( , AR: 1.50) FROM THE DISTRICT The left-leaning Free D.C. Slate swept up 75% of the seats up for grabs on the D.C. Democratic State Committee, ousting the committee’s more moderate members, The Washington Post reports . JBG Smith — a real estate investment trust with a massive footprint in the DMV — delayed its earnings report after a D.C. Superior Court judge ordered last week that the company pay $ million to a condo association, the Washington Business Journal reports . The condo owners sued in , alleging defects in their building’s elevators, roof, HVAC system, electrical system, exterior walls, parking garage elevators and foundation. JBG Smith has about $2.6 billion in debt and has reported 12 straight quarterly losses. NOTUS previously reported on abysmal conditions at another property it co-owns: The Gale Eckington . FROM MARYLAND Montgomery County’s gun laws are in the Trump administration’s crosshairs. This week, the Justice Department sued the county over a law it says makes it “practically impossible for individuals in the county to go about their daily business while lawfully carrying a firearm.” Late last year, the DOJ similarly filed suit against D.C. over the city’s ban on AR-15 assault rifles. FROM VIRGINIA Virginia’s health department is investigating the state’s first documented case of locally acquired dengue virus. The disease is spread through infected mosquitoes, but officials said the public’s risk of acquiring it is low. PLAN YOUR WEEKEND For Mac, Charlie, Frank, Dennis and Dee: “ SUNNY RAVE ” at Howard Theatre, Friday. For the crafter : Crochet Community Social at Museum of Contemporary Art Arlington, Saturday. For the sneakerhead: SneakerCon at the Washington Convention Center, Saturday and Sunday. For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here . SPORTS Training camp update: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson breaks down the Commanders’ options at center, as a group of converted guards aims to fill one of the offense’s most important positions. The Nationals took a hybrid approach to the trade deadline , which meant selling key players to add a bunch of new pitchers — a few of whom could help the team this season. But since there was still more selling for the future than buying for the present, the deadline felt familiar to fans who are tired of rooting for a team that keeps trading away some of its best talent every summer, NOTUS' Jesse Dougherty writes . The Freedom IndyCar race taking place in the District this month will be longer than anticipated: Officials announced this week that the race will be extended from laps to so it can hit the -mile mark. What to Watch Today MLB: Nationals at Phillies, 6:40 p.m. ( MLB.TV ) WNBA: Mystics vs. Wings, 7:30 p.m. ( Monumental ) Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com . The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photo by Samuel Corum/Sipa USA. One last thing: That $ , home we showed you yesterday is located in D.C.

title: Do the Commanders have a problem at center?
author: Martenzie Johnson
summary: With presumed starter Nick Allegretti sidelined, the position has drawn attention early in camp.
content: Washington's Nick Allegretti, a converted guard, is the presumed starter at center heading into the season. Chris Szagola/AP Things are looking a little dicey at the center of the Commanders’ offensive line. The team’s presumed starter at the center position is actually a converted guard. His backup is also a converted guard. The rookie they drafted in the sixth round of April’s draft — a converted guard. The center they signed earlier this week to fill in due to injuries? You guessed it. As the Commanders make their way through the second week of training camp, the centers have drawn a fair amount of attention. With the offense seeking to rebound from a bottom-10 performance last season, it's unclear what one of the unit’s most important positions will look like next week, let alone next month. Coach Dan Quinn isn’t in panic mode. Despite the absence of starter Nick Allegretti due to a calf strain, Quinn said the offensive line has held up. “Both sides of the line I thought had, you know, advantage here, advantage there, and that's what I'm hoping to see,” he said ahead of practice Tuesday. “If one gets tilted too much to the other, then I'd be more concerned. So I like the back-and-forth, honestly, to say good run here, good blitz there.” Despite Quinn’s optimistic take, there are still plenty of question marks. Allegretti has not practiced since July 29. His backup, Julian Good-Jones, has had an up-and-down run as fill-in with the first team, including one snap that went over Jayden Daniels’ head during team drills on Tuesday. Rookie Matt Gulbin has rolled almost exclusively with the second team, but depth is clearly a concern. The team worked out centers Gus Hartwig, Joe Michalski and Trey Hill on Saturday. Hill, a sixth-round pick by the Bengals in who played guard early in college, was signed the following day. Following Saturday’s and Monday’s practices, guards Timothy McKay and Brandon Coleman and tackle Trent Scott stayed to take snaps with Marcus Mariota. Quinn said all the maneuvering has been aimed at building depth (before Hill’s arrival Gulbin was the only player on the team roster listed as a center), but is also an experiment to see who is capable of handling center responsibilities. “If you can play inside, you want somebody that can play both [center and guard],” Quinn said. “And that's basically kind of the rhythm behind it.” The center position is pivotal to the offense. The job isn’t solely about successfully snapping the ball to the quarterback. Centers are responsible for calling out defensive alignments, coordinating blocking assignments and, of course, handling the defender in front of them. And yet Washington has not had consistency at the position for years. Since , at least 10 players have taken snaps at center for Washington. Last season, the offensive line was just about average in ESPN’s pass- and run-block metrics, and that was before starting center Tyler Biadasz was released in February. Quinn has commended Gulbin for his command of the second unit line. “I think it's just kind of a next-man-up mentality,” Gulbin said. “I have to step up to the plate and make sure the O line's functioning, and I'm getting out calls.” Allegretti has helped coach up Good-Jones and Gulbin from the sideline. Those three, and now Hill, can be seen bouncing ideas and techniques off one another. After practice they often put in extra work with assistant offensive line coach Shane Toub. “I come off the sideline, he's [Allegretti’s] helping me out with ‘Oh, what was this? What was this look?’ We break it down together,” Good-Jones said. “So it's a brotherhood, man. It's a collaborative unit.” Quinn has said he doesn’t expect Allegretti to be out much longer. And even though the seven-year veteran started just one game at center for Washington last season, his teammates, the coaching staff and front office have raved about him. “What stands out to me with Nick is just his leadership, his command, his confidence, the way the guys gravitate to and listen to him,” general manager Adam Peters said at a press conference before camp. “And so that's a big part of it. Knowing what to do, knowing where to go, knowing where to direct the guys, just the calling up in the huddle — it's a big deal.”

title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (Aug. 7)
author: Rebecca Ritzel
summary: The grand opening of Olney Theatre’s expansion, a sitcom-inspired dance party, and a canine competition at the Wharf.
content: Olney Theatre. Photo by Kiati Plooks Photography Thursday “ Woody Guthrie’s American Song ,” Theatre Alliance at Wharf Park Water St. SW, 7:15 p.m., pay what you can One of D.C.’s buzziest theater companies opens a three-month, citywide festival of performances and exhibits celebrating “America's most enduring folk poet and social agitator.” Expect more than a “This Land Is Your Land” sing-along at this outdoor musical revue that addresses America’s turbulent social climate through the lens of Guthrie’s writings and songs. Recommended for fans of Bob Dylan, Pete Seeger and Rhiannon Giddens. Rip! Tear! Collage Exhibit at Eye Street Gallery I St. SE, 6 p.m. free The D.C. Commission on the Arts and Humanities picked “Collage as Critique” as the theme for its annual juried show, which awards grants to artists whose work is chosen for display. More than 20 local artists have work in the exhibit, and three of them will be on hand to lead a workshop on shredding, tearing and ripping up paper, then turning the scraps into art. More to explore: “Apollo 13” blasts off at the Library of Congress’ Movies on the Lawn. Friday “Tosca” at Wolf Trap Trap Road, Vienna, Va., 8 p.m., $39 to $ The Washington National Opera Orchestra — a beleaguered group of veteran musicians who were recently kicked out of the Kennedy Center — will accompany up-and-coming singers on the Wolf Trap stage. The summer company produces one major opera each year, and this season it’s Puccini’s classic about an artist, his muse and the religious zealot police chief out to thwart their star-crossed romance. Husband-and-wife team Ryan and Tonya McKinny, who have vocally opposed President Trump’s Kennedy Center takeover, will direct the production and provide subtext, while José Luis Gómez conducts. “SUNNY RAVE” at the Howard Theatre T St., 10 p.m., $30 New York and Toronto may have “Heated Rivalry” parody musicals, but D.C. has [ checks notes ] a late-night “Always Sunny in Philadelphia” dance party? Yep. That’s a thing. The Philadelphia-based “dj pressed” will spin tunes accompanied by clips from the long-running FX comedy at the Howard Theatre. Come dressed as Mac, Dee or Danny DeVito. More to explore: Country singer Jordan Davis performs a free show for ticketholders after the Nationals game. Saturday Chesapeake DogDocks at The Wharf District Square SW, 10:30 a.m. to 6 p.m., free Come watch Prince, Banana and their canine frenemies play fetch in a 40-foot pool installed outside The Anthem. Billed as the mid-Atlantic’s premiere “aquatic dog performance” club, the Chesapeake DockDogs are hosting their first District competition surrounded by bougie people drinking beer. (Cerveza Pacifico and Tito’s “Vodka for Dog People” are the event sponsors.) Think your pooch might have what it takes to take the big leap next year? The club is organizing a “Youth Day” introductory session in Marriottsville, Md., on Aug. 15, minus the pool and booze. Crochet Community Social at Museum of Contemporary Art Arlington 14th St. S, Arlington, Va., 2:30 to 4 p.m., free Bring your own needles or pick up a free pair at this informal gathering hosted by the Crochet Cart Project. Participants will each contribute a square for a community blanket. That may sound more wholesome than trad-wife Instagram, but the group also aims to spread the joy of crocheting to all communities and help people express “creativity through fibre art.” More to explore: Swing Fling dance convention at the Dulles Hyatt Regency; Sneaker Con at the Walter E. Washington Convention Center. Sunday Summerfest Open House at Olney Theatre Olney-Sandy Spring Road, Olney, Md., 11:30 a.m. to 5:15 p.m., free Families in the Northern suburbs (and anyone else who loves theater and has a car) are likely to love the grand opening of Olney Theatre Center’s multimillion-dollar expansion project. After two years of construction, the 88-year-old Montgomery County theater has a new lobby, studios and education spaces. More than two-dozen free shows, tours and workshops are on the schedule, while food trucks and a used costume shop are open all day. A gala performance featuring “Younger” star and Tony-winner Sutton Foster caps off the celebration, but tickets have long been sold out. Mandoleers at Lyon Park Community Center N. Fillmore Street, Arlington, Va., 5 p.m., free Since , the Mandoleers have been making music together on instruments that resemble miniature guitars. The ensemble holds a three-day intensive each summer, open to anyone who plays the mandolin, mandola, mandocello, classical guitar or upright bass. It’s unclear how exactly this merry band of musicians will celebrate the Declaration of Independence, but the event culminates with a free community concert called, “America at : We the People, All of Us.” Ernesto Parets conducts. More to explore: Final weekend to see the critically hailed “American Aspirations” exhibit at the Smithsonian Institution Building.

title: The Nationals’ Confusing Trade Deadline
author: Jesse Dougherty
summary: Monday’s trade of pitcher Foster Griffin capped a busy deadline for the Nats, and left fans wondering where the team is headed.
content: The Nationals traded all-star pitcher Foster Griffin as part of their deadline dealing. Nick Wass/AP “Isn’t this trade deadline kind of a mindfuck?” That's how a member of the Nationals’ front office put it to me in late July, a week before Monday’s deadline passed. The Nats weren’t supposed to be so competitive this season — if competitive at all — meaning the decision to buy or sell was expected to be fairly easy, at least up to the tough choice of whether to deal shortstop CJ Abrams. But then they kept winning a tad more than they lost, mostly because of their league-best offense (and very much in spite of their abysmal bullpen). And so somewhere along the line, as a reaction to the team’s surprising record, explosive lineup and obvious lack of pitching, the decision to buy or sell morphed into figuring out the best way to do some of both, which seemed like a shift from what was once a stubborn plan to just use to prepare for the future, not to actually invest any more in … . “Yeah,” I replied, “mindfuck feels right.” Now, on the other side of the deadline, the hybrid approach certainly brought more selling for the future than buying for the present. That was expected, too, especially after the Nats lost five in a row to end last week, which dropped them to 4 ½ back for the National League’s final wild-card spot, now 5 ½ after they lost their sixth straight Monday night. There was, then, a well-reasoned baseball case for most of what the Nationals did in the last 10 days, if not all of it. We’ll get to that in a minute here. But there’s also well-earned frustration for fans who are tired of rooting for a team that believes the best path forward is to trade some of its best players, even when it’s on the outer edge of the playoff race. Paul Toboni, the team’s first-year president of baseball operations, kept saying Monday evening that he still believes in this club, that it still has an “it factor,” that it could still “go on a heater here soon and put us right back in the mix,” which is why he felt a responsibility to improve the current bullpen while also subtracting from the lineup and a paper-thin starting rotation. Which begged the question of how, if he truly believes in the Nats’ chances of making a run, he justifies trading their most reliable starter, Foster Griffin, for four unproven pitchers. Which, once again, comes down to the heavy tension between now and later while trying to build a sustainable winner. Which gets even more complicated with an ownership group that hasn’t spent anywhere close to real money in free agency — or with pre-free-agency extensions — since . “It's one of the hardest things about my job, balancing the here and now with the future,” Toboni said. “I think every baseball fan that's really, really into it understands it. I think if they're asked, in practice, how do you do that … it becomes a lot more challenging, you know what I mean?” Here are some snippets of how he explained it from there: “ … And so what I try to do is just be real with everyone. Like: ‘Hey, if the goal here is to be good for a long period of time, you only have so many opportunities to make this foundation really strong.’ … “ … but if we pass up those opportunities to create this really strong foundation — live with me for a second on this metaphor — basically we'll be moving into the house without the foundation being totally strong. And it might turn out that two, three years down the line, we might have to move out of the house because the foundation is cracking …” “ … but at the same time, yeah, just speaking from the heart, I believe in the guys in the locker room and I believe in what they can do. And I can see how it would be received as: ‘Hey, you're telling me you believe in this team but then you just shipped out, you know, one of our better pitchers.’ I get that. What I would say is basically it's probably my brain and heart at odds, too. …” “ … we want to make sure this is really stable while at the same time, yeah, when I say that, I hope when Woody hears it or CJ hears it or whoever hears it — Blake — they sense that it's genuine.” Toboni is aware that the fan base is not his only audience, that he has to sell the clubhouse on the long view, too. Woody is James Wood, a 23-year-old who is already one of the best hitters in the sport. CJ is CJ Abrams, the star shortstop who the Nats held onto through the deadline, maintaining an extremely high bar to move him. Blake is Blake Butera, the team’s first-year manager. Over the last week and a half, they’ve said goodbye to Curtis Mead, who had an . on-base-plus-slugging percentage, Luis García Jr., who led the National League in slugging percentage, and Griffin, who made the NL’s All-Star team with a 2.77 ERA at the break. On Monday night, the Nats lost because — wait for it — their pen couldn’t hold a late lead. Wood left after feeling discomfort in his left oblique. The vibes are turning fast. Soon, then, there could be more time to look ahead and analyze what the Nats received for Mead, García and Griffin. The total haul, factoring in a minor league trade that sent outfielder Christian Franklin to the Orioles, included 10 players, nine of them pitchers. The deals included … Mead to the Red Sox for left-handed starter Connelly Early García to the Yankees for four right-handed pitchers: Jack Cebert, a starter, plus Ben Grable, Yovanny Cruz and Jake Bird Griffin to the Guardians for left-handed pitchers Will Dion and Josh Hartle; right-handed pitcher Kendeglys Virguez; and outfielder Nick Mitchell And Franklin to the Orioles for right-handed pitcher Joe Glassey As for immediate help, Toboni listed Early, Cruz and Dion as pitchers who could contribute in August and September. Early is working his way back from the injured list, where he landed in July because of elbow pain. Cruz, a flamethrower, is already in the majors. Dion, a soft thrower who gets a lot of chase, appeared in 12 games for the Guardians this year. Bird, 30, has career relief appearances between the Rockies and Yankees. He could also chip in soon as a marginal improvement over one of the Nats’ low-leverage arms. The Mead-Early trade was probably the best example of dealing for now and later, as the Nationals traded from a clear strength (hitting) for five-and-a-half years of a big league starter that Toboni drafted while working in Boston. The García and Griffin trades, while including major league-ready relievers, seemed more focused on stockpiling minor league arms to mold, which should give the Nats a shot at better pitching depth in upcoming years. For Griffin, who is a two-month rental for Cleveland, the Nationals only received one player (Hartle) in the Guardians’ top 25 prospects, at least according to MLB Pipeline. Virguez is already a reliever at 22. With any trade of this nature, the Nats are betting on their player development system. Notably, none of Mead, Griffin or García were penciled in as major contributors to start the year. They signed Griffin to a one-year deal out of Japan, which also means he will be a free agent this fall. Mead was adrift before the season, just released by the White Sox, then had a breakout season under the Nats’ new coaching staff. Much like Mead, García unlocked much more power by improving his pitch selection and pulling the ball in the air more. Through the dispassionate lens of logical roster building, flipping each of them now, at what could be the height of their value, made perfect sense. But for the past four summers, Nats fans have been told to turn away from a shoddy product because there’s a new reliever in the minors with an intriguing fastball. Then, it was Jarlin Susana. Now, it’s Ben Grable, plugged right into an all-too-familiar mind trick of ignoring what you can see to believe in what you can’t just yet. Two things can be true, as Toboni said Monday when describing the conflict between his head and heart: His front office, new to the job, deserves the opportunity to build a foundation without the burden of what happened before they arrived. And yet, after four months of competitive baseball, after what felt like the first warm days of a long overdue spring, it’s fair for D.C. to wonder when this kind of deadline selling will stop. Maybe next July.

title: Won't You Be My Neighborhood Commissioner?
author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman
content: A voter casts a ballot at Calvary Episcopal Church in Northeast on primary election day in Washington, D.C., on Tuesday, June 16, . Tom Williams/AP Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Advisory neighborhood commissioners, Montgomery County schools and a NYC-DC crossover. THE LATEST No one is on the ballot for a good chunk of the District’s advisory neighborhood commissioner positions ahead of tomorrow’s nomination deadline . Of ANC positions, 58 had no listed candidates as of Saturday . Though the unpaid position isn’t the flashiest in D.C. politics, ANC commissioners are vital neighborhood voices, advising the government on community issues like local zoning decisions. Some, including Mayor Muriel Bowser , go on to higher office. “I'm not concerned about the vacancies that are on the nominating list, and I probably wouldn't be concerned until after the deadline,” Kent Boese , head of D.C.’s ANC office, told NOTUS. There are fewer vacancies this cycle than there were two years ago , Boese said, and many candidates file right before the deadline or launch write-in campaigns closer to November. The vacancies are an opportunity for advocacy groups like the Washington Area Bicyclist Association. The nonpartisan nonprofit circulated an email this week urging members in empty districts to apply. “We do want to encourage the District to create safe transportation infrastructure, including bike lanes, bus priority projects, and working with the ANCs is a great way to do it,” Seth Grimes , an organizer with WABA, told NOTUS. “Many times vacancies are hard to fill. There are no candidates, and so we thought, well, why not use our database and reach out to people?” WABA has filled nine vacant ANC spots with its members since March , Grimes said. FROM THE DISTRICT President Donald Trump is considering removing U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro from her post, CNN reports . Pirro, a longtime Trump ally, recently angered the president when her office dismissed all charges against David Hearn , the Olympic canoeist who was arrested on suspicion of vandalizing the Reflecting Pool. Pirro’s office said the damage was more likely due to a botched job by the contractor, not widespread vandalism as Trump has repeatedly claimed. On Monday, Trump said Pirro “ folded like an umbrella. ” FROM VIRGINIA Amazon wants to build four data centers on George Washington University’s Ashburn campus, which the company bought this year for $ million, the Loudoun Times-Mirror reports . Amazon got its application in ahead of a fall meeting in which Loudoun County officials will weigh a data center moratorium as they consider how to regulate the industry. FROM MARYLAND Montgomery County redrew its public school boundaries this spring, but the debate didn’t end there. Some parents are suing, saying the plan illegally closes one of the county’s most prestigious high schools, Jeff Barker writes for NOTUS . FROM YOUR FEED tweet attempting to map New York City boroughs onto the DMV made the rounds over the weekend. Our team has some thoughts: “It is genuinely hard to think of a single thing College Park, Maryland, has in common with the Upper West Side. And I say that as a proud Maryland alum.” — Michael Errigo, deputy editor “Comparing Capitol Hill to New Jersey is a choice.” — Shamira Muhammad, D.C. reporter "This is pretty perfect social media content: It plays on D.C.'s occasional insecurities of not being NYC, it makes sweeping generalizations about D.C.'s neighborhoods that miss loads of local nuance, and, despite my best efforts not to, I end up arguing with people about it." — Martin Austermuhle, D.C. reporter WHAT YOU GET FOR $ , Kenyon St Real Estate 2 ( , AR: 1.50) Listed for $ , , this two-bedroom, two-bathroom home features solid oak hardwood floors, modern finishes and an open-concept living space. Guess where this listing is sold: Maryland Virginia D.C. We’ll let you know tomorrow how many of you got it right. SPORTS The MLB trade deadline has officially passed, and the Nats turned out to be both buyers and sellers. After adding an arm last week, Washington made three trades in the 24 hours before Monday’s 6 p.m. deadline. They sent out infielder Luis García Jr., pitcher Foster Griffin and outfielder Christian Franklin. In return they got back eight more pitchers, some of whom are expected to contribute right away. NOTUS’ Jesse Dougherty broke down the Garcia deal, calling it both strategically sound and emotionally fraught for fans. Training camp update: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson reports that the Commanders’ offensive struggles may have been greatly exaggerated. On Monday in Ashburn, Jayden Daniels got the unit rolling. He completed multiple impressive touchdown passes, and the offensive line held up much better than it did last week. What to Watch Today MLB: Nationals at Phillies, 6:40 p.m. ( MLB.TV ) Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com . The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Real estate photo by Derek & Vee. Finally, yesterday’s trivia answer was A) D.C. A special shout-out to Carolynn Race, who answered first.

title: Montgomery County Approved New School Boundaries. Parents Won’t Let It End There.
author: Jeff Barker
summary: Some residents are pursuing a legal challenge to the planned closure of the highly rated Wootton High School.
content: Rockville Council member Adam Van Grack. Kainaz Amaria/NOTUS A smattering of “Save Wootton” and “It’s Not Over!” yard signs dot neighborhoods surrounding the Rockville, Maryland, high school whose name and student body are due to be transferred in -28 to a new building several miles away. With the Montgomery County Board of Education having approved the shift last spring, the red, white and blue signs — matching the colors of Thomas S. Wootton High School — remain as a defiant statement by residents, some of whom are pursuing a legal challenge to plans they say would illegally close the highly rated, half-century-old school in the Washington suburbs. “It’s such a necessity,” said Rockville Council member Adam Van Grack, whose son attends Wootton. “It’s not a question of if it’s going to be a permanent school again, the only question is when.” A dozen miles away, similar yard signs remain in the neighborhood around the sprawling Silver Spring International Middle School, which area residents fear isn’t in the county’s future plans. “The school gives us an opportunity to greet one another. It gives us a sense of community," said Angie Kronenberg, an attorney who, during the campaign's busiest periods, devoted as many as 30 to 40 hours a week organizing efforts to preserve the school, which is adjacent to Silver Spring’s downtown and home to sought-after Spanish and French immersion programs. Montgomery County, home to Maryland’s largest public school system, completed sweeping boundary studies in March that upended the futures of Wootton and Silver Spring International, and redrew boundaries for other schools to account for enrollment shifts, school building conditions and other factors. But the school assignment debates never quite seem over, and in the case of Wootton, parents and community members have lodged complaints over everything from deteriorating building conditions to property values. Boundary shifts stir powerful protective instincts, said Sarah Asson, a senior researcher at the nonprofit research group Education Northwest, often turning parents into activists fighting for what they view as their children's best interests. “These rezonings touch two of the most important things for parents -– their kids’ education and their communities,” Asson said. While parents typically frame their objections around their children's education and their communities, issues regarding image and status are often at play as well, said Genevieve Siegel-Hawley, a professor in Virginia Commonwealth University’s School of Education. “There is a lot of anxiety — status anxiety — about securing their kids’ futures through education,” Siegel-Hawley said. DC0A5520 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)Real estate values can also be an important, if less openly acknowledged, subtext. Homes assigned to highly regarded schools often command a premium, and some residents worry boundary changes will diminish their property values. Wootton, which has about 1, students, is one of the county’s prestigious, so-called “W” schools along with high-achieving Walt Whitman, Walter Johnson and Winston Churchill. It is not uncommon for families in the more diverse eastern portion of the county, including Silver Spring and Wheaton, to move to the western part so their kids can attend a “W” or the highly rated Bethesda-Chevy Chase High School. “For 20-some years if I had a property in the Wootton school district, I hardly had to say anything about the house. I just said ‘Wootton,’ and it had this magnetic attraction for buyers,” said Kevin Grolig, a real estate agent in the county. If plans to move Wootton remain intact, Grolig estimates that values of homes within walking distance of the school’s current location could drop 15% or more. Wootton remains open for now. An oversized “Wootton Strong” banner hangs from the back of the football field bleachers. But the school, whose former students include actor Thomas Jane, NFL player Trevon Diggs and several members of the rock band O.A.R., was built in and has issues with leaking ceilings, heating and cooling units and mice. On March 26, the county Board of Education voted 7-1 to approve moving Wootton to a new school in Gaithersburg for the -28 school year. Thomas Taylor, the superintendent of Montgomery County Public schools, said a single school could efficiently handle current enrollment and that the old Wootton would be employed as a “holding school” for when other schools are undergoing construction. At the meeting, parents held signs reading “Don’t Close Wootton” and “Vote No,” and some parents chanted “shame” when the vote was complete. “This is not a closure of Thomas S. Wootton High School — this is a move of the school to a new building,” said a Montgomery County Public Schools announcement in February explaining the plan. It said Wootton students “will transition to a state-of-the-art facility” and that the system was responding “to updated enrollment data showing needs can be met more efficiently with the current number of schools.” But critics said importing the school’s name, colors and “Patriots” mascot to a new building won’t make it the real Wootton, but rather a weird facsimile. DC0A5489 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50) In April, a nonprofit group composed of Wootton parents, alumni and others filed an administrative appeal with the Maryland State Board of Education challenging the March decision. “At the heart of the appeal is a straightforward question: Can a school board avoid Maryland’s statutory school closure requirements by characterizing a school closure as a ‘relocation?’” the group said in a prepared statement. The case is pending. Montgomery County Public Schools said it could not comment on any litigation. The school system declined to make Taylor available for an interview or answer NOTUS’ questions about possible scenarios for the futures of Wootton and Silver Spring International. Rather, Montgomery County Public Schools emailed a statement about the new two-year, elementary and middle school boundary study. The statement said the study will address “system-wide facility capacity, optimize building utilization and evaluate potential school closures or consolidations" with community input. Last year, the county Board of Education declined to pursue Taylor’s recommendation to convert Silver Spring International, whose buildings are in deteriorating condition, into a holding school. While the school wasn’t targeted for closure in the March vote, many parents say the board’s decision to reduce its number of feeder elementary schools has placed the school on an uncertain path because its enrollment will decline. Proponents of maintaining Silver Spring International and Wootton often raise concerns that are difficult to quantify. Some speak nostalgically of the quiet ritual of children being close enough to walk to their neighborhood schools. “That was the number one thing parents were saying to me: ‘Our kids can still walk to school, right?’” said Kronenberg, who helps lead a Silver Spring group called “Save Our Schools.” “We believe our school is still at risk,” Kronenberg said. "We have to keep at it."

title: What $800K Gets You in D.C., Maryland and Virginia
author: Torrie Herrington
summary: Our weekly column compares home listings across the metro area.
content: Derek & Vee A penthouse condo in Columbia Heights. A spacious townhouse in North Bethesda. A cozy and convenient house in Arlington. Here’s what $ , gets you in the District, Maryland and Virginia. (Which one would you choose? Or, have a comparison you’d like to see in an upcoming column? Let us know at metro@notus.com .) D.C. Untitled The Listing: Kenyon St. NW #3 The Price: $ , The Specifics: This two-bedroom, two-bathroom penthouse condo comes in at just over 1, square feet, and features a private rooftop deck in addition to parking spaces for two cars. The home also includes a spacious primary bedroom with a spa-like bath, walk-in shower and dual vanities, according to the listing. The real estate agent also highlights the home’s solid oak hardwood floors, modern finishes and open-concept living. The Neighborhood: This home is in the heart of Columbia Heights, within a short walk to the neighborhood’s Metro station with access to the Green and Yellow lines. Also nearby are a number of fitness studios and grocery stores, in addition to popular bars and restaurants like Wonderland Ballroom and St. Vincent Wine. The neighborhood itself is densely populated and known for its historic row houses and cultural diversity. Maryland Untitled The Listing: Gloxinia Drive, Rockville The Price: $ , The Specifics: This spacious townhome comes in around 2, square feet, with the real estate agent describing it as “a rare blend of timeless character, effortless open-concept living, and modern peace of mind.” The three-bedroom, five-bathroom home has only had two previous owners, and features a secluded private courtyard. Recent updates in the home include a new roof, new HVAC and new doors, according to the listing. The Neighborhood: The home is in North Bethesda, and is 10-minute drive from the Bethesda Trolley Trail and just five minutes from Pike & Rose, a shopping and entertainment area featuring restaurants, a movie theater and live music venues. It’s also a short drive from the North Bethesda Metro station, with access to D.C. via the Red Line. Virginia Untitled The Listing: 6th St. S., Arlington The Price: $ , The Specifics: This home offers just over 1, square feet of room with three bedrooms and two full bathrooms. The lower level features hardwood floors, while the upper level is carpeted. The basement is unfinished, making it the perfect spot for storage or a workshop. The shaded and spacious backyard features raised gardening beds and a storage shed. The Neighborhood: This Arlington home is located in the Alcova Heights neighborhood, which is known for its proximity to Columbia Pike, connecting Northern Virginia to D.C for a commute the real estate agent describes as “effortless.” The home is also conveniently close to Alcova Heights Park, shopping centers and restaurants.

title: So Long, Luis García Jr. (And Hello to Four New Arms.)
author: Jesse Dougherty
summary: On Sunday, the Nats traded García, their longest-tenured player, to the Yankees for four right-handed pitchers.
content: The Nationals have traded first baseman Luis Garcia Jr. to the Yankees. David Zalubowski/AP Photo If every trade is a peek inside a front office’s collective brain, the Nationals’ latest deal — sending Luis García Jr. to the Yankees for four right-handed pitchers on Sunday — only furthers what we’d already learned about the new group running the team: They view pitching as a real organizational weakness and are willing to trade controllable bats to change that. And rather than always hunting one or two high-upside prospects in trades, they’re up for swapping established talent for a handful players, which reads as having high confidence in their development process. In this case, the big haul included Jack Cebert, Ben Grable, Yovanny Cruz and Jake Bird. None of them ranked in the Yankees’ top 10 prospects on Baseball America, which slotted Cebert at No. 11, Grable at No. 19 and Cruz at No. 24. Of the four, Cebert is the only starter, a 24-year-old who’s dominated AA in recent weeks. Grable, also 24 and in AA, has an intriguing fastball that’s generated a lot of in-zone whiffs in the minors. Cruz, a 26-year-old with four big league appearances, can run his four-seamer into the triple digits. Bird, 30, has made relief appearances between the Yankees and Rockies and never finished a season with an ERA better than 4.33. Unlike the others, he is no longer a prospect. Each has their flaws, of course, which is why they were part of a four-player package for a high-end platoon player. But the head says this is a definite win for the Nats, especially given their need for pitching — and especially given that García, 26, was treading water before this season and then turned into a valuable trading chip. Instead of cutting him loose, Paul Toboni, the club’s first-year president of baseball operations, made him a full-time first baseman who mostly played against righties. The Yankees, first in the American League wild-card standings, will almost certainly use him in a platoon, too. In plate appearances, García has already set a career high with 23 homers, all but three of them against righties. He also has the best slugging percentage (. ) in the National League. And he’s under team control for another season beyond . So if you’re a Nationals fan, it may feel a bit more complicated for the heart. Signed out of the Dominican Republic in , García was the team’s longest-tenured player, the last on-field link to the best era in the franchise’s short history. Trading him now, as the team is finally on a jagged upswing, can be both strategically sound and emotionally fraught. For five summers, the team has often traded away its most recognizable players, leaving the city starved for reliable connection points. At some point, in theory, the Nats’ short-term ambitions might outweigh the benefits of selling high on a player like García to improve future rosters. That point just isn’t this week. The trade deadline is 6 p.m. Monday. For the last couple months, ever since the Nats’ strong start proved more than a statistical oddity, Toboni has been saying that team performance could affect his deadline approach. Or put another way: If the Nationals kept winning, Toboni seemed willing to bend his long view to the present. At the start of last week, with five games to the deadline, the Nats were 55-53, smack in the middle of the wild-card race. Then they lost five in a row, dropping to 4½ games out of the final wild-card spot with four teams in front of them. Still, despite a crowded, fragile path to the playoffs, Toboni has seemingly sold and bought at the same time. For the Nationals’ first trade of the deadline season, they sent infielder Curtis Mead to the Red Sox for left-handed pitcher Connelly Early, who is on the injured list but could return this month. With the package for García, both Cruz and Bird could immediately contribute to a bullpen that has blown 27 saves. That doesn’t mean the present was the main focus for either of those deals. It does, however, show the front office is interested in addressing short- and long-term needs this summer (and capable of trying both within the same transaction, results pending). Bird was optioned to AAA after the deal was completed Sunday, as was right-handed reliever Riley Cornelio. That indicates that Cruz could join the team ahead of a series opener in Philadelphia on Monday night. The Nats will have to fill García’s and Cornelio’s spots, at a minimum, since they could also make more trades. Abimelec Ortiz, acquired in the five-player return for MacKenzie Gore last winter, is the logical replacement for García, a left-handed first baseman with a compelling offensive profile. If the Nats use him just like García, he’ll pair with Andrés Chaparro in a platoon at first. The offense, still ranked first in runs scored by a good margin, will need some new energy after losing two players (García and Mead) with an OPS over . . And as for what the Nats could do before the deadline, Foster Griffin, their all-star starting pitcher, has attracted a lot of interest. So has shortstop CJ Abrams, though the chances of him moving are far, far lower than the Nationals flipping Griffin for future parts, according to multiple people familiar with the team’s thinking. The market for starting pitchers has thinned in recent days, with Tarik Skubal (Tigers to Dodgers), Luis Castillo (Mariners to White Sox), Freddy Peralta (Mets to Rays) and Kevin Gausman (Blue Jays to Cubs) all off the board. Broadly, those deals have favored the buyers, though a scarcity of front-line arms could now work in the Nationals’ favor. Then D.C. will make a full assessment of Toboni’s first deadline after 6 p.m.

title: A Big, Beautiful Parking Garage
author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman
content: A sign of Washington Dulles International Airport station is seen during the opening of new Silver Line Extension at Washington Dulles International Airport, in Chantilly, Va., Nov. 15, . Jose Luis Magana/AP Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Dulles’ new parking deck, Trump’s golden horses and fans at Commanders training camp. Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region . THE LATEST One of the D.C. area’s biggest attractions may soon be a parking garage. As part of his sweeping $22.5 billion overhaul of Dulles International Airport, President Donald Trump says a new parking deck will be built in front of the historic main terminal with enough space for 32, cars. “It’ll be the largest garage in the world,” he said last week. “It will be beautiful.” What’s unclear is whether Dulles even needs that much parking. NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle reports that a master plan for the airport drawn up by the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority, which manages Dulles, found that the existing 22, parking spots would suffice until at least . But just to be on the safe side, the authority had drawn up plans for a new parking deck — with one-fifth the capacity of what Trump is pledging. There are also unanswered questions about the sheer physical scale of Trump’s garage. As proposed, it could stand some 15 stories tall, towering over the iconic terminal designed by Finnish architect Eero Saarinen. With a garage that big, there’s likely to be “all kinds of issues with throughput of vehicles, wayfinding, ventilation and fire safety,” said local parking expert Bill Boyle . “There’s no precedent for building a parking deck this big.” FROM THE DISTRICT GoldHorses_Grid.jpg ( , AR: 2.05) Trump’s golden horses have (finally) arrived. In May, NOTUS’ Anna Kramer reported that the National Park Service was re-gilding the four massive horse statues near the Lincoln Memorial with an unusually thick layer of 23.75-karat gold, to the tune of 5 million taxpayer dollars. The Park Service wanted the horses (known as the Arts of War and Arts of Peace) finished in time for the July Fourth festivities, calling it an “immovable deadline” in their justification for handing out a rushed, no-bid contract this spring. But the rush was for naught: Two of the horses were just unveiled last week, and two more are still covered up. The city’s July Fourth crowds got nothing more than some scaffolding and drapes. A high-level aide to D.C. Mayor Muriel Bowser is parting ways with the city, marking the first big departure in the waning months of the mayor’s time in office. Lindsey Parker , who joined Bowser’s administration more than a ago and rose to chief of staff, will next take the reins of the Maryland Stadium Authority. It’s a logical move: Parker’s last role in D.C. government was as senior adviser for the Commanders stadium project. A Republican senator wants more patriotism in D.C. schools. Sen. Ashley Moody (R-Florida) has introduced a bill that would require that the U.S. flag be displayed in every classroom in D.C. schools, and mandate that students recite the Pledge of Allegiance at the start of every day. (Parents would be allowed to opt their children out.) Moody said the bill would help “restore pride in our nation” and fight an “outrageous curriculum” that includes lessons on LGBTQ+ history. Critics say this is another unnecessary intrusion into the city’s affairs. Organizers of the popular Cherry Blossom 10-Miler recently warned runners that, starting next year, the race’s “most memorable sections” could be affected or even eliminated by Trump’s planned construction in Memorial Circle and around East Potomac Park. Preservationists are mounting their latest campaign to stop a Trump-led remake of a D.C. building, seeking an injunction to stop the administration from painting the Eisenhower Executive Office Building white, NBC4 reports . TRIVIA In which jurisdiction can you get married without an officiant? D.C. Maryland Virginia Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout-out. The answer will be at the end of tomorrow’s newsletter. SPORTS Training camp update: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson was in Ashburn on Saturday for the first of 11 Commanders practices open to fans. Thousands showed up, with some arriving hours ahead of the 8:30 a.m. start time. The session featured a lot of fan service, including a fun segment where the offensive linemen ran pass routes. But the biggest reaction of the day came during the appearances of Hall of Famers Darrell Green and John Riggins, who will have new roles with the franchise this season. The WNBA trade deadline has come and gone , with the Mystics standing pat. Washington will be leaning on the second-youngest roster in league history as it makes a playoff push.
