title: Let’s Talk About the Massive Parking Garage Trump Wants to Build at Dulles
author: Martin Austermuhle
summary: The 32, -spot deck would surpass both existing parking capacity and what airport officials have said is needed.
content: President Donald Trump unveiled plans to build a parking garage with space for 32, cars at Dulles International Airport. Francis Chung/POLITICO/AP It won’t exactly be the eighth wonder of the world, but it will be big — like, Guinness World Records big. That’s what President Donald Trump promised last week when he unveiled plans to build a parking garage with space for 32, cars as part of his sweeping $22.5 billion renovation of Dulles International Airport. “We’re building a massive … parking garage that will be right next to the terminal,” he said as he sat in front of a model of the new airport splayed across the top of the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office. “It’ll be the largest garage in the world. Thirty-two thousand is big. It will be beautiful.” The new parking deck got less attention than Trump’s announcement that the long-maligned mobile lounges that have shuttled passengers around Dulles since it opened in will be retired. But the detail does speak to many travelers’ annoyances with parking at Dulles, most of which is in satellite lots that require a shuttle to get to and from the main terminal. Still, the big, beautiful deck-to-be stands as one of the Dulles renovation’s most surprising elements, since it would increase the airport’s parking capacity beyond what existing plans say is necessary, would add significant construction and airport operation challenges and would likely tower over the iconic terminal designed by Finnish architect Eero Saarinen. Dulles currently has just over 22, parking spots for travelers, half of them in the distant economy lots. (This reporter almost lost track of their car in one of those lots.) While parking capacity fluctuates during the year (and can be viewed on a daily basis here ), the Dulles Master Plan finalized by the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority in July predicted that the existing number of parking spots available at the airport would suffice until at least . The plan noted that parking demand can fluctuate based on a number of factors, including “rises in gasoline prices could result in the reduced use of private vehicles.” (Gas prices have risen in the U.S. due in part to the ongoing conflict in Iran.) Still, the authority has already started planning to increase capacity to more than 28, spots, most of which would come through the construction of a new parking deck in front of the main terminal building where a surface lot now exists. That three-story deck — to be built between and — would fit 6, cars. During his presentation, Trump seemed to be unaware of those plans. “We have an empty site right directly across the street that nobody wanted to tinker with, which is crazy,” he said. His proposed parking deck — which would go in that same location — would accommodate five times as many cars. But few details exist: The deck wasn’t included in any of the renderings of the new airport that were put out by MWAA and the U.S. Department of Transportation (in fact, the main rendering kept the existing surface lot), and neither agency responded to specific questions about it from NOTUS. The proposal has drawn skeptical reactions from some parking experts, including Bill Boyle, who owns a parking company in D.C. and runs the Washington Parking Association, a trade group. “I looked up the biggest terminal garages in the U.S.,” he told NOTUS. “One is in Seattle and has 13, spots, and the other is in Detroit and has 11, . This would be two-and-half times bigger than those two. That creates all kinds of issues with throughput of vehicles, wayfinding, ventilation and fire safety. There’s no precedent for building a parking deck this big.” The world’s biggest parking lot is outside the West Edmonston Mall in Canada; it fits 20, cars in surface lots. Without specifics, it’s impossible to know the actual physical scale of the proposed parking deck. But if MWAA kept to Trump’s pledge that most of it would be above-ground — “People don’t like down underneath,” he said — it could reach up to 15 stories. That would make the parking deck taller than the main terminal, which tops out at 65 feet. It would also likely block most views of the historic terminal itself for passengers arriving by Metro or car, a concern that MWAA was already aware of with its plan for a three-story parking deck in front of the terminal. The master plan says it would address viewshed concerns by raising Saarinen Circle — a traffic circle in front of the terminal — “approximately 11 to 15 feet” above where it is now. Boyle also said that building a record-breaking parking deck while the airport remains in operation would be challenging. “When you build it you’ll have to have cranes, materials and hauling routes,” he said. “You’re building an enormous garage in a constrained space and doing it while everything is functioning around it, and I don’t see anyone addressing that problem.” It’s also unclear what such a parking deck would cost. A February report from the UCLA Institute of Transportation Studies estimated that each above-ground spot in a parking deck in and around Washington, D.C. can cost $29, to build. While that’s below the national average of $52, , it would also mean that Trump’s proposed 32, parking spots could cost more than $ million. (And that price tag would go up if any levels were underground; the UCLA report says that underground spots can cost $40, a piece to construct.) Since November , there has been an alternative for getting to and from Dulles: Metro. The Silver Line station Dulles sees anywhere from 1, to 4, entries per day, depending on the time of year. “Why should we build the world's largest parking garage in the world on an airport we just invested $6B to connect to Metro?” tweeted Virginia Democratic Senate Majority Leader Scott Surovell. But Trump has touted the proximity and convenience of his new parking deck. “People will literally be able to park their car and walk 15 yards and be in the terminal,” he said. “It will be a parking garage the likes of which no one has even seen before!” offered one commenter on Reddit, in what could be seen as either a high compliment or a sarcastic criticism.

title: Past Due
author: Martin Austermuhle, Michael Brice-Saddler, Zara Norman
content: Quarterback Jayden Daniels works out on Day 2 of the Washington Commanders' training camp Thursday. John McDonnell/AP Photo Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: D.C.’s worst landlord, a $ million Metro expansion and the legendary Venus Williams. Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region . THE LATEST D.C.’s worst landlord is its housing authority. Of all city landlords with unabated violations, DCHA is far and away the biggest offender, with more than 2, violations and more than $2.2 million in associated fines, NOTUS’ Zara Norman reports . “It does not surprise me,” said Megan Browder , a director with Legal Aid D.C. “I think it is partially the size of the portfolio and also a systematic disregard for their mission.” D.C.’s Department of Buildings cannot collect fines from DCHA like it can from other landlords. The agency is responsible for policing its own payments. The housing authority is not the only proprietor with a long list of unresolved violations: More than local landlords owe the city more than $ , each. To better resolve cases, the DOB is shifting its strategy: It’s starting to settle with landlords before heading to adjudication, allowing them to avoid fines if they make immediate fixes. “For me it’s really concerning,” Browder told NOTUS. “I think it just lessens the accountability for landlords to say, ‘Hey, you can kind of just limp along and settle with DOB without any meaningful corrective action.’” DEEP DIVE Fort Myer Construction — a D.C. road-paving titan since — has agreed to settle a lawsuit with Attorney General Brian Schwalb that alleged nearly a of illegal water pollution at the company’s Ward 5 facility. On paper, the $ , penalty might seem like a slap on the wrist. City records show that D.C. has paid Fort Myer more than $1 billion through infrastructure and paving contracts over the past , including more than $ million since the lawsuit was filed in October . But Schwalb’s office says the real victory is the settlement’s operational requirements. Under a three-year consent order announced today, Fort Myer must overhaul its equipment, fix drainage infrastructure and submit to monthly water-quality testing to stop the alleged petroleum and industrial runoff from reaching city waterways. In a statement, Schwalb said the agreement ensures that Fort Myer will make “much-needed and long overdue changes to its equipment and business practices to protect the District, our environment and our residents moving forward.” FROM THE DISTRICT All aboard for the Commanders stadium. Metro has signed a pair of agreements with D.C. to start working on two projects that will be critical for getting fans to and from the new stadium when it opens in . The first is a $ million expansion of the Stadium-Armory station. The second is a new bus rapid transit line — dubbed the Gold Line — that will run from Union Station to the stadium along H Street and Benning Road Northeast. There are only about 8, parking spots planned for the new stadium, so city and team officials are pressing to increase mass transit options. D.C. Public Schools officials told parents Wednesday that sensitive student information, such as names and home addresses, may have been exposed in a data breach, NBC4 reports . A major D.C. law firm’s political action committee told federal regulators that a thief stole multiple political contribution checks from mailboxes in Cleveland Park last year, NOTUS’ Jenna Monnin reports . The embattled chairman of the D.C. Public Service Commission , which regulates utilities including Pepco and Washington Gas, says he is resigning in August . Emile Thompson ’s decision comes ahead of what could have been a contentious fall, especially as the commission has felt the heat over rising electric and gas bills. “Rising energy prices are not attributable to any one agency, group or thing,” Thompson emphasized in his resignation statement. METRO MOMENTS Leyla Adali’s tweet asking locals to share their “worst day in D.C.” caught fire this week. NOTUS asked her why. (Responses have been lightly edited for length and clarity.) What inspired you to start that thread? I was hanging out with my husband and two of our friends — a couple getting married. The groom was not interested in having a bachelor party. We started joking around that he could pick the worst day in D.C. ever. I said we should crowdsource. Were you surprised by some of the responses? There were some frequent offenders. Some answers I hadn’t thought of that I quite liked: David’s Tent (religious tunes on the Mall), the Scientology museum. A lot of people captured the spirit of a bad day in D.C.: It’s hot, humid, you’ve been going to museums for hours, you start to feel ill and run to the nearest food truck. Why do you think this got so much engagement? One thing about Twitter is people love to complain. This summer in D.C., we have the National Guard around, it’s very hot, a lot of locals felt frustrated by [Freedom ]. I also think a lot of the worst things in D.C. have been the worst things for a while. … I think it was that Tom Sietsema reviewed Founding Farmers. I will say, I love D.C. and this was all in the spirit of fun. There are a million ways to have the best day in D.C. Have an image from around D.C. you want to share? A question for our reporters? An “only in D.C.” moment? Tell us about it . SPORTS “How would you like to play doubles with Venus Williams?” That was the question posed to 22-year-old Russian pro Diana Shnaider on the eve of this week’s D.C. Open. In a last-minute reshuffling, Shnaider was paired with the 46-year-old tennis legend, and the duo played two matches together. As NOTUS’ Dave Sheinin writes , the two players — meeting at opposite ends of their careers — both learned plenty from the experience. Training camp update: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson reports that the Commanders’ revamped defense has made a strong first impression through two days of camp. title: D.C.’s Worst Landlord Is Its Housing Authority
author: Zara Norman
summary: The Department of Buildings fines the city’s bad landlords. None owe more than the DCHA.
content: The District’s housing authority owes the Department of Buildings more than $2.2 million for over 2, unresolved violations across its properties. Alex Brandon/AP D.C.’s beleaguered housing authority — which has leadership turnover , a cyberattack and a scathing audit this year — is the city’s worst offender when it comes to unresolved housing violations. The District’s housing authority (DCHA) owes D.C.’s Department of Buildings (DOB) more than $2.2 million for over 2, unresolved violations across its properties, per a public DOB dashboard . Some violations date back to . The issue stems in part from the fact that the agency, which owns more than 8, public housing units, polices itself. Unlike private landlords who answer to DOB, by law, DOB cannot do more than issue fines to the housing authority. “If someone calls us up, we’ll go out, we’ll inspect, we will see what’s broken, we’ll create a [notice of infraction], and we will provide it to DCHA. They are supposed to then fix it and tell us,” Keith Parsons, DOB’s director of strategic enforcement, told NOTUS. “There is really no ‘stick,’ by law.” That the housing authority is the District’s worst offender doesn’t surprise Megan Browder, Legal Aid DC’s director for systemic advocacy and law reform. “I think it is partially the size of the portfolio and also a systematic disregard for their mission,” Browder told NOTUS. In , the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development found that DCHA was out of compliance with its annual inspection requirements, inspection outcomes weren’t monitored, and emergency work orders went uncompleted at night due to safety concerns. In , D.C.’s attorney general sued the DCHA for endangering thousands of tenants across 10 of its properties. D.C. has the country’s highest rates of rent nonpayment for low-income tax credit buildings, a fact landlords often point to as an explanation for their inability to make repairs. But DCHA doesn’t have that excuse, Browder said, as their properties are subsidized by the government. “DCHA takes steps to fully abate any infraction within the abatement timeframe listed on the notice and provide proof of abatement to the DOB,” Alison Burdo, a DCHA spokesperson, told NOTUS in a statement. “There may be a delay in updates to DOB’s public database if further clarification between DCHA and DOB is needed.” Some of the violations on the public dashboard are “associated with vacant units currently undergoing modernization or awaiting modernization pending sufficient funding,” Burdo said, and others are for properties DCHA doesn’t own or control but where the agency may have a long-term ground lease for redevelopment. The housing authority is in the middle of a three-year “ recovery plan ” meant to improve the quality of its housing stock and improve work order systems, among other goals. The agency meets monthly with DOB to review any notices of infraction, Burdo said. DHCA is far from the only landlord with an extensive list of outstanding violations. Per DOB’s dashboard , more than 84, housing violations, dating back to , are currently unresolved, with more than $83 million in associated fines. More than landlords owe at least $ , each. Some of the violations — particularly those dating back years — are in active litigation, Parsons said. Others may have already been fixed, but either DOB is waiting for evidence of that abatement or associated fines are tied up in the department’s adjudication process. That adjudication process is why it’s so hard to collect. It starts when DOB issues a notice of infraction after a property inspection, which may also carry a fine. There, the department runs into its first problem: the D.C. Council found in that over half of those infraction notices were sent to the incorrect address. Once a landlord receives a notice, the department must take them through a monthslong appeal and adjudication process administered by the city’s Office of Administrative Hearings (OAH) in order to collect any money. “A landlord is entitled to due process,” Browder said. “That does take time, largely because there’s a big backlog at OAH.” Because of that system, each year DOB receives just a fraction of the fines it assessed and abates less than half of violations. In the fiscal year, the department collected $2.6 million in fines, but referred $25 million more to the city’s collections unit. Even as D.C. navigates a tight fiscal era , the DOB argues that the best outcome for the city is not necessarily collecting that $83 million. “Success is making sure the problems are fixed, and the fines are a way to motivate the landlord to do it,” Parsons told NOTUS. “So, if we can get things fixed, that is our goal.” In that spirit, and in line with the council’s recommendations from , the department is shifting its approach. Instead of chasing down every penny owed, the department is trying to settle with landlords for less or no money in order to fix violations sooner. It has set a “very ambitious” goal of resolving 80% of emergency violations within 30 days, and 90 days for non-emergencies, Parsons said. “There’s work to do here, but because we’re timing ourselves now, we are actually orienting operations around trying to move those things more quickly,” he said. The strategy seems to be paying off: DOB’s collection rate for fines increased by 10% from fiscal years to . Last year, fines collected before final order exceeded $1 million for the first time. “We’re doing more outreach. We're doing more talking to people. These options have usually been here, but we’re emphasizing them more,” Parsons said. “If you fix [violations] soon enough, we will just resolve it without fines at all.” Not everyone thinks that’s a win. Browder worries that landlords, some of whom already don’t take the abatement process seriously, won’t be incentivized to make fixes. “For me it’s really concerning,” she told NOTUS. “I think it just lessens the accountability for landlords to say ‘Hey, you can kind of just limp along and settle with DOB without any meaningful corrective action.’” Browder thinks informal settlements could be beneficial for smaller landlords, but that bigger housing providers — especially corporate landlords who own multiple properties under LLCs — should be forced to go through the fine collection process. She is hoping for a more transparent violations dashboard, and a public list of the owners of properties held under LLCs. “DOB enforcement should be the last step before litigation. The landlord should just fix the issue; it shouldn’t get to the point where you have to request DOB,” she said. “If we could figure out who the repeat violators [are], DOB could focus on those folks.”

title: The Commanders’ Defense Has Made a Strong First Impression at Camp
author: Martenzie Johnson
summary: The offense? Not so much.
content: Commanders rookie Sonny Styles has been one of the early standouts at training camp. John McDonnell/AP Commanders defensive coordinator Daronte Jones had a simple message for his unit ahead of Thursday's training camp practice: “They don’t get in the fucking end zone.” Two days into camp, it’s clear Jones’ players have taken heed. The defense has mostly smothered the offense so far, both starters and reserves. Facing a relentless pass rush and suffocating coverage, Washington’s offense has struggled to move the ball, let alone reach the end zone. This defensive unit was slow and aged just a year ago, so the front office went out and signed eight players in free agency, hoping the group could become faster and more versatile. Based on first impressions in Ashburn, that effort appears to be paying off already. “When you look at this roster … the firepower we got, guys coming off the edge, guys all the way on the front seven, guys we got flying around in the back end — the sky's the limit,” veteran safety Will Harris said. It’s hard to decide who or what has stood out most for the defense since training camp kicked off Wednesday. The line and edge rushers, particularly free agent signee Odafe Oweh, have practically moved into the offensive backfield and declared squatter’s rights. Oweh stuffed multiple plays on Day 1 and swatted down a pass from quarterback Jayden Daniels, while fellow linebackers Jordan Magee and K’Lavon Chaisson (another new ) have made their way into the backfield on multiple run plays. Safety Nick Cross (also new) blitzed Daniels at one point to blow up a pass play. “When we put it all together, it’s going to be a masterpiece,” linebacker Frankie Luvu said. “I'm excited for the guys up front — we got some dogs. We holding them back right now because we ain't got the pads on, but when it’s time to let them loose we’ll have a lot of splash plays in the backfield.” In coverage, new cornerbacks Ahkello Witherspoon and Amik Robertson have looked solid. Rookie linebacker Sonny Styles — picked seventh overall in large part because of his elite athleticism — has stayed hip-to-hip, stride-for-stride with his assignments like he’s their ballroom dance partner. The defense nabbed two interceptions Thursday, one by undrafted free agent Malik Spencer early in the session and a would-be pick-6 by newly signed corner Rasul Douglas on the final play of the day. During two-minute drills, the defense forced three field goals after stuffing the offense on third down. “We bring in those guys that come in and get after the quarterback,” Daniels said Wednesday about the new defensive linemen. “It's good work on both sides that at the end of the day, that's all camp really is. Building our identity, making sure guys get good work, make each other better.” On the other side of the ball, the offense is going through the growing pains expected of a unit run by a first-time playcaller implementing a new system . The group has looked out of sorts at times. The receivers have been a source of much debate this offseason and that uncertainty hasn’t been quelled in these early days. They have consistently struggled to gain separation. The defense “had a really good day. I'm not afraid to say that,” veteran receiver Terry McLaurin said Thursday. “But, that's camp. There's gonna be back and forth.” You can see the vision that coordinator David Blough has for his unit: lots of pre-snap motion and shifts; quarterbacks alternating from shotgun to under center; plenty of play action to hold the defense. It just hasn’t led to immediate success. Ahead of Wednesday’s practice, coach Dan Quinn said he expected early mistakes from the offense, but hoped to see less and less as camp progresses. “I just wanna see the execution, guys functioning at a high level together,” Quinn said. On Wednesday, there were highlight throws to receivers Antonio Williams, Jaden Bradley and Treylon Burks, who hauled in multiple difficult touchdown catches. (Burks missed Thursday’s practice due to foot soreness.) Tight end Chig Okonkwo found success on back-to-back out routes Thursday while receiver Luke McCaffrey shook free from cornerback Mike Sainristil for an impressive toe-tapping touchdown grab in the back of the end zone. When Daniels or his backups have had time, they’ve made quick and accurate throws. It’s just that those moments have come few and far between. But, as most players have emphasized, it’s only been two practices and the sky has not fallen. “It's just Day 2,” McLaurin said Thursday. “It's good to have guys out there flying around. The juice is what I'm super excited about, the competitiveness. We shake [hands] with guys after practice. I didn't really wanna shake up with anybody because we got beat. That's how I am. But at the end of the day, we're still brothers. We're going back and forth, but we still have ‘Commanders’ across our chest, so that's the main thing.”

title: JLG Holds Court
author: Martin Austermuhle, Jenny Gathright, Zara Norman
content: DC Council member and Mayoral candidate Janeese Lewis George, 37, campaigns at the Wah Luck House Senior Day Center in Chinatown on May 29. Kainaz Amaria/NOTUS Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Janeese Lewis George meets with campaign foes, a veteran sues the National Guard and Dulles Airport gets a makeover. Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region . THE LATEST Oh, to be a fly on the wall in that meeting. Janeese Lewis George , winner of last month’s Democratic mayoral primary, recently met with the leadership of the D.C. Police Union, which was highly critical of her during the hotly contested campaign. The meeting — brokered by the firefighters union, which endorsed her — was part of what Lewis George’s aides do not yet want to call a mayoral transition, but is an effort to lay the groundwork for the significant shift in priorities and policies that will take place if and when she takes office in January. “There is a sense of urgency here,” said Ward 6 council member Charles Allen, who has been advising Lewis George’s post-primary efforts. “We have a lot of work ahead of us, and any candidate who won with a massive mandate would be champing at the bit to be engaged.” That includes meetings with friends and foes alike to try to find common ground — or at least open channels of communication, NOTUS’ Martin Austermuhle reports . Other than the D.C. Police Union, Lewis George recently sat down with a small group from the Greater Washington Partnership, which represents large employers in the region. The business community has been especially concerned about what Lewis George will do in office, though some leaders think it’s best to keep an open mind. “We can’t walk in saying, ‘We don’t like this,’ without saying, ‘This is what success looks like,’” said one local business leader. Lewis George’s aides say they believe winning the primary with 54% of the vote gave her a broad mandate, and they are still focusing on her plans to try to bring down prices of child care and utilities, build more housing and end police cooperation with ICE. DEEP DIVE A veteran alleges that National Guard troops assaulted her outside her D.C. home, and she’s asking for $3 million in damages. Anna King said she was sitting on her front patio, scrolling on her phone, when National Guard troops walked onto the property and violently detained her, restraining her with handcuffs so tight that she tore at least one ligament in her wrist and required surgery. The ACLU of D.C. posted a video of the interaction , which happened in May. King filed a tort claim with the Idaho National Guard and the Defense Department on Wednesday. She has been a vocal critic of the Guard’s presence in the District, and was detained in May over an accusation of assaulting Guard members two days earlier. She was never charged in that case, but has been charged with assault over the incident on her patio. A spokesperson for the Idaho National Guard declined to comment on the specific allegations in King’s tort claim, citing the pending litigation, but said the Guard takes “all allegations of misconduct seriously.” The Defense Department did not provide comment. Michael Perloff , a senior staff attorney at the ACLU of D.C., which is helping to represent King, told NOTUS the incident shows that National Guard troops have been acting like police. “Military members are trained for war,” he said. “There shouldn't be people who are trained for war policing the streets in American cities.” FROM THE DISTRICT Revving up: Mayor Muriel Bowser hopes next month’s Freedom Grand Prix will be the first in a series of IndyCar races in D.C., she said at a press conference Wednesday. “Let’s see how it goes this year,” responded Penske president Bud Denker, who is chairing the race. Denker estimated the event, scheduled for Aug. 22 and 23, will see “about , people a day come through the gates.” FROM VIRGINIA President Donald Trump announced a $22 billion renovation of the “really horribly thought of” Dulles International Airport in a Wednesday press conference , promising to add more than 5 million square feet of new or renovated space, NOTUS’ Jenna Monnin reports . The airport will also get a new 32, -space parking garage and do away with its famous “people movers.” United Airlines will help fund the project. FROM MARYLAND The Education Department threatened this week to yank federal funds from Anne Arundel County Public Schools after parents complained a high school helped “their daughter pretend to be male,” The Washington Post reports . TALK TO TOM Rooster and Owl ( , AR: 1.50) Tom Sietsema is back answering your questions about the D.C. dining scene. Submit your questions here . Question: Is it just me, or are tasting menus getting longer? Ah, you must have heard me grouse about the time I sat for over three hours at a D.C. hotspot and ended up taking home 99% of the pastry chef’s multiple desserts because I simply couldn’t eat ONE. MORE. THING. While much of the food was very good, the flurry of dishes felt like a forced march, as though the chef wanted to pack all his ideas into one epic seating. By the end of the night, I felt as if I had dispatched a Thanksgiving’s worth of food and drink (and wished I had stretch pants on). My one-word review would have read, “Uncomfortable.” But I digress. The opposite of that night occurred just last week, at Rooster & Owl on 14th Street Northwest, where chef Yuan Tang offers what might be my favorite tasting menu in D.C. One, it’s four courses, with multiple choices. Two, the cost is $ , a value given the quality, creativity and competition around town. Three, the meal is paced perfectly, so there never seems to be a rush or a lag. Two of us were in and out in about 90 minutes. We left sated but not stuffed, and eager to return. In the full Q&A : Why slow restaurants sometimes provide worse service, how to tip on a comped item and the gradual disappearance of free bread. SPORTS Training camp update: NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson was out at Day 1 of Commanders training camp Wednesday, and he reports it was a great opening session for the defense. Linebacker Odafe Oweh, the team’s biggest offseason addition, was disruptive whenever he was on the field, and there were near interceptions by Mike Sainristil and Jordan Magee. Daronte Jones , the team’s new defensive coordinator, is a football nomad with roots in rural Maryland. The Athletic’s Barry Svrluga profiles the 47-year-old tasked with getting Washington’s defense back into shape. What to Watch Today Nationals at Braves, 7:15 p.m. (ESPN) Thank you for reading!
