title: Want to Play Doubles With Venus Williams? The Correct Answer Is Yes.
author: Dave Sheinin
summary: In a last-minute pairing, the 46-year-old tennis legend played alongside 22-year-old Diana Shnaider at this week’s D.C. Open.
content: Venus Williams played two doubles matches with 22-year-old Diana Shnaider this week at the D.C. Open. Kyle Gustafson/AP The most impressive athletic feat anyone has pulled off so far at the Mubadala D.C. Open didn’t occur on a tennis court, but on the leafy walkways and concourses connecting the tournament’s corporate offices to the players’ area. It was performed not by a tennis player but by the tournament’s longtime chair, Mark Ein, who covered those several hundred yards — in dress shoes and sport coat, his cell phone pressed to his ear — well, faster than anyone could have reasonably expected from a 61-year-old. Ein, at that instant, was on a desperate mission to salvage a sizable chunk of the tournament’s star factor. It was 1:10 p.m. Saturday and Ein had just gotten a call from Andrea Preti, the husband of tennis legend Venus Williams, informing him that Williams’ intended doubles partner, Alexandra Eala, had scratched at the eleventh hour. With the 2 p.m. deadline for doubles entries looming, they had 50 minutes and ticking to find Williams a replacement. Ein didn’t wait to finish the call before rushing out his office door and down the walkways. Upon bursting into the players’ dining area, the first person he saw was Diana Shnaider, a 22-year-old Russian and the 18th-ranked women’s tennis player in the world, having lunch with her support team. “Diana,” Ein said, catching his breath, “how would you like to play doubles this week with Venus Williams?” For the roughly 3, fans who crammed into the outlying John Harris Court at the Rock Creek Park Tennis Center on Monday for an up-close glimpse of tennis royalty — the 46-year-old Williams owns seven Grand Slam singles titles and another 14 in doubles — then crammed in again Wednesday evening for their quarterfinal match, they have Ein’s resourcefulness and Shnaider’s intrepidness to thank for the experience. And Williams, on a miserable run of bad luck with her choice of doubles partners of late, may have just accidentally hit upon a solution to her problem. Despite having never played together before, Williams and Shnaider demonstrated an uncanny degree of chemistry in winning Monday’s first-round match, 6-3, 6-4, over American Quinn Gleason and Norway’s Ulrikke Eikeri, before falling in Wednesday night’s quarterfinals to Chinese duo Qianhui Tang and Yifan Xu, 6-4, 6-2. Venus Williams AP - ( , AR: 1.50) If one thing has defined the first half of this year’s D.C. Open, it is the slow bleed-off of A-list American stars, both male and female, from the tournament draw. Among those joining Williams in departing well short of the weekend are hometown legend and sixth seed Frances Tiafoe; fifth-seeded Learner Tien, the 16th-ranked men’s player in the world; and Madison Keys, the Australian Open champ and sixth seed in the women’s draw. All lost their first-round matches. For Williams, as with many American players, the D.C. stop on the North American hard-court circuit holds a special place in her heart. It’s no coincidence she chose this tournament as the site of her own return to the game last summer following a 16-month absence. (Her singles victory here a year ago over Peyton Stearns at age 45 made her the second-oldest player in history to win a singles match, but she is 0-12 since in singles, including a loss Tuesday night to Austria’s Anastasia Potapova. Williams entered Wednesday ranked 664th in the world in singles, 124th in doubles.) “You can just feel it from the fans,” Williams said. “They’re ride or die.” To the extent that Williams’ radiance permitted anyone to pay attention to Shnaider, they would have noticed, above all else, the incredulous smile that seemed to be plastered across the young Russian’s between points and during changeovers. It was the same smile that Ein encountered on Saturday — “Absolutely giddy,” he described her — when he presented the offer of being Williams’ partner. “It was definitely the right choice,” Shnaider said of her decision to accept. “I feel like it was definitely a great partnership.” Paradoxically, playing doubles these days with Williams — among the most decorated players of her generation and, along with sister Serena, half of the second-most-prolific doubles team in history — is both an intimidating notion for a young player and an egalitarian rite of passage, open to just about any current WTA player with a racket and a halfway decent world ranking. In the four-plus years since Serena famously stepped away from the sport — a decision she would eventually reverse , also famously, this summer — Venus has found it almost impossible to find a full-time doubles partner. Her last seven tournaments have seen her paired with seven different partners, and she only found herself scrambling at the last minute to find a new partner this week because Eala, with whom Williams partnered last month at a tournament in Germany, pulled out in order to focus on her singles matches. (Williams’s eleventh-hour switch from Eala to Shnaider was described by tournament officials as a “repairing,” which is the sort of beautiful euphemism that would seem to have enormous potential for divorce lawyers.) Diana Shnaider AP - ( , AR: 1.50) Eala’s late scratch extended a brutal streak of rotten luck for Williams in recent doubles competition. In May, American up-and-comer Hailey Baptiste scratched out of their planned French Open pairing with a knee injury. Then, at last month’s Wimbledon, where Serena launched her comeback and where the Williams sisters secured a wild-card entry in doubles, Serena injured her knee during her first-round singles loss to Maya Joint and was forced to withdraw from doubles. Then came Eala’s last-minute decision to withdraw in D.C. “It’s just unlucky. Time and unforeseen circumstances befall us all,” Williams said. “I would like to hopefully get lucky.” It’s not as if Williams is an undesirable or unsavory doubles partner. Shnaider’s eagerness to pair with her this week speaks to Williams’ magnetic pull on younger players. So do the words offered this week by Leylah Fernandez, who has played doubles with Williams twice, including at the U.S. Open. “It's tough [playing with Williams], because I knew how competitive she was and how much she loves winning and hates losing. I was stressed, I was nervous,” Fernandez said. “What I didn't know was [her ability] to calm me down. … Venus definitely has a welcoming aura where she always wants to support and help as much as possible. It motivates me. It encourages me, and it brings me back to why I play tennis.” On Wednesday evening, at the instant their loss was sealed, Williams and Shnaider met on their side of the net and shared a good, long hug. The adoring crowd, by this point well thinned out, stood and cheered and snapped photos, just in case it might be the last time they see Williams in these parts. But she doesn’t sound like someone who is ready to bow out. She spoke of her hopes for a delayed reunion with Serena in U.S. Open doubles later this summer, provided Serena is healthy. And despite the chaos of this week — a “repairing,” an unfamiliar partner, a riveting win, a gutting loss — she sounded like someone who wouldn’t want it any other way. “In tennis, you're learning something about yourself every day. It just doesn't end,” Williams said. “It's such a beautiful and sometimes painful discovery, and I look forward to every day of it.”

title: Janeese Lewis George Has Been Meeting With Her Critics
author: Martin Austermuhle
summary: In recent days, the Democratic nominee for D.C. mayor met with a business organization and the D.C. Police Union.
content: Janeese Lewis George is in line to become D.C.'s next mayor. Kainaz Amaria/NOTUS You could call it fence-mending, extending an olive branch, opening lines of communication, or simply municipal diplomacy. Whatever it is, it’s happening. Over the last week, Democratic D.C. mayoral nominee Janeese Lewis George has met with a prominent business organization as well as the leadership of the D.C. Police Union, engaging in conversations with two groups that have expressed unease with — if not outright hostility toward — her progressive proposals. The outreach marks the very early days of what campaign aides don’t yet want to call a mayoral transition; Lewis George still has the November general election ahead of her, after all. But after her decisive victory in the District’s June 16 primary, in which she won with 54% of the vote and all but ensured she’ll be the next mayor of the overwhelmingly Democratic city, there is consensus that Lewis George has to start laying the groundwork now for what will be a significant shift in priorities and policies if and when she takes office in January. “There is a sense of urgency here,” says Ward 6 Council member Charles Allen, who has been advising Lewis George’s post-primary efforts. “We have a lot of work ahead of us, and any candidate who won with a massive mandate would be champing at the bit to be engaged. She has been incredibly busy since the election.” Campaign aides say Lewis George has been “meeting with tons of groups,” including those that were part of her winning coalition: teachers, environmentalists, tenants and immigrant rights organizations. But the aides — who spoke on the condition of anonymity so they could comment on internal campaign matters — say say she also has spoken with housing providers, developers and CEOs. “It was a tough primary, and she’s reaching out to people on all sides, including people not in her camp,” one aide said. One of those meetings happened this week with a small group of executives who are part of the Greater Washington Partnership, which represents large employers from Baltimore down to Richmond. The meeting is notable because the business community more broadly backed Kenyan McDuffie in the primary, seeing him as a more reliable quantity — a continuation of Bowser, to a certain degree. Some business leaders are concerned that Lewis George’s policies won’t help revive and diversify D.C.’s economy, and that proposals for possible tax increases could instead drive employers to Maryland and Virginia. There is particular worry around a Business Activity Tax , which would target law firms, lobbyists and consulting firms whose owners live outside the city. Some have said they need to impress upon Lewis George how challenging D.C.’s business climate has gotten. “I couldn’t raise a dime now if I tried,” said one real estate developer, who, like others, spoke on the condition of anonymity. Others, though, are more encouraged by Lewis George’s promise to work with universities and other institutions to help revitalize downtown D.C. , as well as her pledge to cut red tape and bureaucracy that can complicate housing construction and running a business in the city. One person in the world of finance and investment said approaching Lewis George openly is better than simply assuming the worst of her. “We can’t walk in saying, ‘We don’t like this,’ without saying, ‘This is what success looks like,’” the person said. Kathy Hollinger, the CEO of the partnership, tells NOTUS that the meeting with Lewis George was intended to open lines of communication and press the argument that D.C. is a vital component of the region’s economy — but that companies, like residents, have choices in where they locate. “The conversation was an encouraging first step in establishing what we expect will be a needed relationship,” Hollinger said. “These were CEOs from the region’s most significant private sector industries together with leading universities, health systems and nonprofit institutions. We shared with her very directly that just those who were around the table employ more than 70, people in the District. Many of the priorities discussed included housing, affordability, permitting and downtown revitalization.” At-Large Council member Elissa Silverman, a fellow progressive who during her career has clashed and worked with the business community, said the outreach is necessary — and can be mutually beneficial. “I think there’s a lot of room to make the rules less bureaucratic, more understandable, better both for business and the economy,” she said. “The change in administration is an opportunity to reimagine programs that haven’t had scrutiny or a good look taken in a while.” Lewis George also met last week with the leadership of the D.C. Police Union, which represents more than 3, police officers. The union has been highly critical of Lewis George and the D.C. Council in the past; union leaders have aggressively pushed Republicans in Congress to intervene in the city’s local affairs and broadly supported President Donald Trump’s move last year to deploy the National Guard in the city. Lewis George and other lawmakers have been critical of both stances. Lewis George has promised to end any cooperation between MPD and ICE on her first day in office. She has also endorsed non-police approaches to fighting crime, but has generally backed away from her support in and for defunding the police. The tension between the two camps was evident in how the meeting was set up: Lewis George asked that the D.C. firefighters union, which endorsed her during the primary, make the initial outreach on her behalf. (Dozens of unions backed Lewis George; the police union did not make an endorsement.) Police union President Gregg Pemberton did not respond to requests for comment on the meeting with Lewis George, and her campaign aides said little about what was discussed. “It was a positive meeting,” one offered. “It was introductory. There will be more to come.” The next D.C. mayor will immediately be with a big decision for MPD: who to appoint as chief. Current Police Chief Jeffery Carroll remains in an interim capacity, and Bowser is unlikely to nominate him for the permanent post considering the upcoming change in administrations. The next mayor will also have to handle what has been a persistent issue with the department: staffing. As of this month, there are some 3, sworn officers in MPD , down from roughly 3, a ago. The lower number of officers and increased demands on their time has led to record overtime budgets. In the fiscal year, for example, the department spent $ million on overtime pay. Ultimately, though, Lewis George’s campaign aides say they’re entering the meetings they have with the election’s results in mind — and trying to find ways to bring critics on board. “There are mandates for universal access to affordable child care, to build tens of thousands of homes, to lower utility prices, and to end cooperation with ICE,” said one aide who spoke to NOTUS. “How do we deliver on them on day 1 or year 1? That starts by bringing in as many players while also continuing the conversations and relationships with our base.”

title: Talk to Tom: What Is the Best Tasting Menu in D.C.?
author: Tom Sietsema
summary: Tom Sietsema answers reader questions on restaurant bread baskets, tipping etiquette and a go-to Baltimore steakhouse.
content: The steamed bass from Rooster & Owl's new tasting menu by chef Yuan Tang. Kainaz Amaria/NOTUS Welcome to Talk to Tom , the dining advice column that aims to point you toward good meals, steer you from the dross and solve your pressing restaurant queries. Look for a fresh Q&A every Thursday in this space. Questions and comments can be submitted to TalkToTom@notus.com . Submissions may be edited for length and clarity. If I get comped for something, like a drink or appetizer, and it wasn’t because something was wrong, how should that be reflected in my tip? There are a couple of schools of thought on the matter, and my answer depends in part on a diner’s relationship with a restaurant. One response is to tip as if you ordered the item. What server won’t appreciate that? More often than not, however, something gratis is going out to a guest who is celebrating a special occasion or who makes regular appearances. In those situations, industry pros tell me, the gift should be considered what it is: a gesture of hospitality that requires no more reciprocation than a “thank you very much.” Restaurants deal with leftovers differently. Do you prefer to box unfinished food yourself or have staff take care of the task? Some places want diners to do the job, because diners know exactly what leftovers they want. (I’ve heard stories about customers getting upset because, for instance, cleaned steak bones and tiny garnishes weren’t included in their bags of leftovers.) Personally, I appreciate places that handle the matter behind the scenes; that’s part of hospitality. Have you ever tried to transfer a big piece of unfinished meat or slippery noodles from plate or bowl to take-out container, sometimes without proper serving utensils? Not so easy, or neat. I also like it when a server instructs you to retrieve your leftovers at the host stand, on the way out, versus plopping a bag on your table or the floor while you’re still there. At the fun new steakhouse Ox & Olive in Georgetown, servers give you a playing card to remember food to go. Guests pick up the bags that match their cards from a cute wooden “tree” at the entrance. It feels like tasting menus are getting long again. Ah, you must have heard me grouse about the time I sat for over three hours at a D.C. hotspot and ended up taking home 99 percent of the pastry chef’s multiple desserts because I simply couldn’t eat ONE. MORE. THING. While much of the food was very good, the flurry of dishes felt like a forced march, as though the chef wanted to pack all his ideas into one epic seating. By the end of the night, I felt as if I had dispatched a Thanksgiving’s worth of food and drink (and wished I had stretch pants on). My one-word review would have read, “Uncomfortable.” But I digress. The opposite of that night occurred just last week, at Rooster & Owl on 14th Street Northwest, where chef Yuan Tang offers what might be my favorite tasting menu in D.C. One, it’s four courses, with multiple choices. Two, the cost is $ , a value given the quality, creativity and competition around town. Three, the meal is paced perfectly, so there never seems to be a rush or a lag. Two of us were in and out in about 90 minutes. We left sated but not stuffed, and eager to return. DC0A6147 copy 2.jpg ( , AR: 1.34)Tang’s new menu speaks to the season and makes me wonder how, for instance, cantaloupe might be rethought as dan dan noodles, crab fritters would taste with spiced honey, pork skewers could be embellished with fish sauce gastrique, and mango sticky rice gets fused with a pavlova. My long history with the upscale mom-and-pop forecasts that everything will be on point — and my recent reunion proved as much. My pet peeve continues to be loud restaurants. Why do so many of them sound like boom boxes? In many restaurants, the culprit is in the design: lots of glass, metal and exposed brick, sometimes in combination with bare concrete floors and high ceilings. Hard surfaces reflect sound, rather than absorb it. A packed dining room increases the noise, too, as customers raise their voices to be heard, a phenomenon known as the Lombard effect. The problem is exacerbated when restaurants crank up their playlists, thinking loud music creates a sought-after buzz. Open bars and kitchens, with their distinct sound effects — espresso machines, clanging pots, ice bins — also contribute to the noise pollution. Restaurants can lower the volume by installing acoustic panels, curtains, rugs or even artwork designed to sponge noise; adding more space between tables; selecting softer finishes; and measuring sound levels rather than relying on instinct. (There are apps for that, don’t you know.) An average of between 65 to 70 decibels should be the aim. For their part, diners ISO peace with their meals should consider eating on the early side, asking for tables on the perimeter of dining rooms — and letting their voices be heard by management. Wouldn’t it be great if more restaurants offered something along the lines of a designated music- and phone-free time period for people who don’t want to read lips or shout throughout dinner? Research has shown that excessive noise can shorten restaurant visits and increase stress — not exactly agreeable outcomes for anyone. My grandson is about to turn 18. We’re in Baltimore and steak is on his wish list. A big birthday (your progeny can vote now!) calls for something special. The place that leaps to mind is the family-owned Prime Rib , launched in and as popular for its ambience — tuxedoed servers, live piano, retro supper club look — as for its succulent, signature cut, which diners should order cooked medium-rare and eat with grated horseradish. It seems service is inevitably worse in a restaurant that’s slow. Your take? You’d think a slow dining room would translate to more customer attention, but that’s not necessarily the case. A busy restaurant creates momentum and buzz; in a nearly empty one, staff can become less focused because there’s no rhythm to the service. To control labor costs, during slow periods restaurants might schedule fewer workers — servers who might then take on multiple tasks, including answering the phone, greeting and seating guests, busing tables and maybe bar tending. Management might also ask them to help with duties like stocking, napkin-folding or food preparation, which can distract them from their primary job of looking after customers. Morale also takes a hit in a slow restaurant, with servers worried about tips and schedules. Places that struggle to attract business might have a hard time hiring and keeping good workers. To be clear, good restaurants can be slow for reasons unrelated to quality. Bad weather and traffic jams, for instance, can wreak havoc on reservations and walk-in customers. Given high prices, my rant is restaurants that charge for bread service. It immediately turns me off. I long for the bread baskets at Le Diplomate or Obelisk. The reality is, the complimentary gestures at those establishments cost a lot, in terms of labor and/or money, and this in an industry with particularly thin margins. At Le Diplomate , the beloved French brasserie on 14th Street Northwest, chef Greg Lloyd tells me the amenity — a basket brimming with slices of baguette, rye wheat boule and cranberry-walnut loaf, served with lightly salted whipped butter — costs the restaurant $ , a year. As for the fixed-price Obelisk , Esther Lee , the chef-owner of the intimate Italian townhouse in Dupont Circle, says her grissini and other breads aren’t so much about the expense of ingredients, but the time it takes the small business to produce them in-house. A bread basket is more than a way to stave off hunger before the first course. It’s a way to signal care and craftsmanship — a welcome handshake, if you will. Gratis bread baskets haven’t exactly gone the way of pay phones. I’ve been offered them at restaurants as diverse as Ristorante i Ricchi and Joe’s Seafood, Prime Steak & Stone Crab downtown, Filomena Ristorante in Georgetown and Et Voila! in the Palisades. (Readers, help me grow this list, which I can share in a future column.) To cut waste, the owner of I Ricchi, Chris Ricchi , says her gratis schiacciata, baked in the restaurant and adding to the Tuscan experience, is preceded by a question: Would you like bread? At Et Voila!, the Belgian restaurant offers the first basket free and charges $3.50 for a second.

title: Chris Murphy Demands Answers From Education Department Over Disputed Civics Competition
author: Sam Fortier
summary: The contest’s results left the family of Aangad Singh “reeling,” Murphy wrote to Secretary Linda McMahon, calling for a detailed explanation of the scoring.
content: Murphy wrote on behalf of Aangad Singh and his family, who are seeking to understand why Singh did not advance to the civics competition finals. (Graeme Sloan/Sipa USA)(Sipa via AP Images) Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy demanded “transparency” from the Department of Education Wednesday regarding the disputed results of a national civics contest for high school students. “This competition was supposed to be a celebration of this nation’s founding, uplifting principles of equality and justice,” Murphy wrote in the letter addressed to Education Secretary Linda McMahon, exclusively obtained by NOTUS. “Instead, the Presidential Award’s opaque rules and scoring have cast serious doubts about basic standards of fairness and left a family reeling.” The Connecticut senator wrote on behalf of Aangad Singh, the 15-year-old Connecticut boy who competed, and his family, who are seeking to understand why Singh did not advance to the finals. The controversy, first reported by NOTUS, has drawn national scrutiny over whether the results were rigged or biased against a boy of Indian descent in favor of three finalists who fit President Donald Trump’s education agenda. One was home-schooled, another attended a private, Catholic school, and the third, who went to public school, told CNN that she supported Trump and believed the most important thing was “everyone walking away from the competition knowing this is the greatest country of the world.” “The students who won the competition were undeniably impressive,” Murphy wrote. “However, it is easy to understand why groups like the Congressional Asian Pacific American Caucus have suggested the competition was biased since the Trump Administration has made clear it believes anyone who is not a white male is inferior. Through hateful rhetoric, sweeping executive orders, and devastating funding cuts, Trump has turned discrimination into a governing agenda.” Murphy, who sits on two Senate committees that oversee the Department of Education, requested “a full review of the results,” including detailed explanations for disputed answers and any scoring documents. He set a Sept. 1 deadline for the department to respond. “We are very grateful to Senator Murphy and his team for raising these questions, and we hope this will help us finally receive clear answers,” Bhalindar Singh, Aangad’s father, said. The Department of Education did not respond to a request for comment. CBS broadcast the Presidential Award competition on June 30, and immediately, Singh and his family questioned the results. According to their analysis, two of Aangad’s answers were incorrectly scored as wrong, and if either had been scored correctly, he would have advanced to the final three. The finalists received a share of $ , in scholarships and a trip to the Oval Office to meet the president. The first disputed answer was about the finer points of Article 3 of the U.S. Constitution. The second was about which amendment ended slavery. To the latter question, Singh said “13th,” according to auto-generated subtitles, which was correct. But on the broadcast, it was marked as wrong. “His answer to question two is undeniably correct,” Murphy wrote. “As has been publicly reported, there is some debate about how to score his answer to question one, but his answer is clearly at least partially correct.” On July 14, Aangad’s father asked the Education Department to review his son’s scores. A week later, an aide to McMahon wrote back that the “judges exercised independent good faith judgment in selecting finalists and winners.” “The graphics shown in the broadcast accurately reflected the points awarded by the judges’ interpretation of answers and scoring,” the aide said. The response did not engage with the substance of their questions, Aangad’s father said, and Murphy echoed the sentiments in his letter. In an initial statement to NOTUS before the story was published, an Education Department spokesperson said any questions about the integrity of the competition should be directed to the James Madison Memorial Fellowship Foundation, the federal organization that it said independently developed, judged and scored the questions. As Education secretary, McMahon holds one of the foundation’s two active board seats. None of the five judges responded to multiple requests for comment. The panel scholar, Abbylin Sellers, initially agreed to an interview but then canceled, saying, “I have informed the Department of Ed press team of your request and will let them handle it.” Roger Jones III, the principal at a Tennessee high school where one of the judges teaches social studies, said in an email that he was not aware of the controversy and referred questions to the foundation. “While the James Madison Memorial Fellowship Foundation may have provided the judges,” Murphy wrote to McMahon, “it is incumbent upon the Department to clarify the results as the host of this official competition put on by the federal government.” Murphy’s letter is the latest twist in a relationship that can seem like a storyline straight out of the wrestling organization McMahon once helped run. In , Murphy and McMahon, a former WWE executive, battled for the Senate seat Murphy now occupies, a race that Murphy won by 15 percentage points. McMahon spent a record $ million in personal funds on two unsuccessful Senate bids — she also lost in to Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal. Five years later, Trump nominated McMahon to lead the Small Business Administration. During her confirmation process, Murphy struck a more conciliatory tone. He voted for her confirmation and said in a statement that, “while Linda and I haven’t always seen eye-to-eye, I look forward to working with her to help small businesses in Connecticut." In , when Trump returned to office, they went back to battling. During McMahon’s confirmation hearing to lead the Education Department, Murphy, who sits on the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee, pressed her about how an executive order restricting federal funding for DEI programs would impact schools. “It is good to see you again outside of the state of Connecticut, where we run into each other,” she replied . This time, he voted against her nomination. The committee advanced her on a 12-11, party-line vote, and she was ultimately confirmed.

title: Trump Announces $22 Billion Renovation for ‘Impossible’ Dulles Airport
author: Jenna Monnin
summary: “Basic disasters” is how the president described two of the terminals that would be replaced.
content: President Donald Trump looks over a scale model of Washington Dulles International Airport after a proposed $22 billion renovation to replace terminals, add a horseshoe-shaped train and thousands of new parking spaces. Julia Demaree Nikhinson/AP President Donald Trump shared plans on Wednesday for a massive, $22 billion construction and renovation project at Washington Dulles International Airport. The president, who’s pushing forward on projects to revamp iconic sites around Washington, D.C., showcased a scale model and pictures of the proposed new hub that would do away with the infamous “people movers,” add thousands of parking stalls and replace entire terminals. “We are announcing plans to add more than 5 million square feet of new or renovated space,” Trump said in the Oval Office. “We'll replace the current C and D concourses, which are basic disasters, all the while preserving the iconic original terminal.” The architect Eero Saarinen completed the original terminal in , the same year the airport, about 25 miles west of Washington, opened. The terminal’s iconic mid-century modern architecture features concrete columns and a concave cable roof. Trump described Saarinen as “one of the great architects of the world,” but said the original terminal was both an “asset and a liability” because “nobody wanted to build anything near it.” The airport could also get a new 32, -space parking garage, which Trump said will be the largest in the world. The current largest parking complex is in Edmonton, Canada, with parking for about 20, vehicles. United Airlines, which has a major hub at Dulles, described the timeline for the project as being completed “over the next .” Construction could start in the spring. The project proposes do away with the fleet of people movers, which function like buses, transporting flyers between terminals. “It's an impossible airport. You get off a bus, you go into a train, you get from a train, you get onto another bus,” Trump said. Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy said a “horseshoe train system” would replace the people movers and provide travelers with “easy access to all of your gates.” The administration reviewed designs from more than 30 architects, and the president described the project as a “bipartisan” effort. “Whether you're a Republican or Democrat, you don't want to go and be subjected to this airport because this airport, it's a terrible place to be,” Trump said. United Airlines will help pay for the project, which is set to include the largest United Polaris lounge in the world, according to Trump. “This is not requiring federal dollars,” Jack Potter, president and CEO of the Metropolitan Washington Airports Authority, told reporters. “This is going to be airport-generated dollars, airline contributions — which is phenomenal.” Trump said doing the airport construction “all at one time” would allow the project to be completed in a few years, far less than the original 60-year estimate if it was broken up into stages. “It's time to ensure that the United States has the greatest airports anywhere in the world, and we're starting right here with the capital city,” Trump said.

title: As Training Camp Begins, Commanders Say They Are ‘Happy’ With Receivers
author: Martenzie Johnson
summary: Despite months of speculation about Brandon Aiyuk and others, GM Adam Peters said the team is satisfied with its weapons.
content: General manager Adam Peters said the Commanders are feeling good about their receiving options as camp gets underway. Mark Schiefelbein/AP Despite months of online chatter and media speculation, the Commanders believe they are set at the wide receiver position as the team begins training camp Wednesday. At a Tuesday evening press conference with head coach Dan Quinn, general manager Adam Peters said he feels comfortable with the 11 receivers Washington has on the roster, emphasizing classroom learning, the competitiveness within the group and the leadership of Pro Bowl veteran Terry McLaurin. “[We’re] really happy with who's in that room, really happy with how the guys progressed in the offseason and stepped up,” Peters said. “I think they're going to take another step in this training camp.” Despite the confidence, the GM that those beliefs could change over the course of camp. Of the receivers on the roster, only McLaurin had more than receiving yards last season. “If we have ways to get better, we're always going to look into that and assess the decision if it's the right move for our team or not,” Peters said. “And if we do think it is, we're not afraid to do that.” San Francisco 49ers receiver Brandon Aiyuk has been at the center of most offseason chatter, as the former All-Pro has publicly angled to join his college quarterback, Jayden Daniels, in Washington. Even as Aiyuk has increasingly posted to social media about the possibility of a move, Washington has declined to publicly discuss the 28-year-old. San Francisco has yet to officially release Aiyuk, although it is widely believed he will not play another snap for the 49ers. At Tuesday’s press conference, Peters was asked if a prospective player's social media activity is taken into account when considering an acquisition. The question got a laugh out of Peters and Quinn. “We do look at everything, and we want to make sure it's the right player to be in our locker room, in our bloodstream, in our culture,” Peters said. While Washington hasn’t made a splashy acquisition at receiver, Peters believes the team has taken the requisite steps to make Daniels’ job easier. The general manager noted the signing of tight end Chig Okonkwo, the offseason overhaul of the team’s defense and the scheming by new offensive coordinator David Blough . “There's a great energy in the building on both sides, so I think when you bring all those things together … the staff has done a really good job of surrounding him with opportunity to win,” Peters said. On the other side of the football, cornerback Trey Amos should be practicing “soon” after missing all of spring practice rehabbing the fractured fibula he sustained in Week 10 last year. Peters said Amos dealt with soft tissue soreness earlier in the offseason and the team is taking a cautionary approach to his return. To shore up the defensive backfield, Washington signed veteran Rasul Douglas on July 9. The 10-year veteran started 13 games for the Dolphins last season, totaling 13 pass deflections and a 54% completion percentage allowed in coverage. “He's played at a high level,” Peters said. “He started a lot of games recently, and he always performs.” Neither Quinn nor Peters provided further detail on the team’s decision to fire tight ends coach Ben Steele on Monday. Steele, who was hired in February, was arrested on June 7 and charged with driving while intoxicated. “A lot of thought was put into that decision, and it's just unfortunate,” Quinn said. Offensive assistant Wes Welker, a former All-Pro wide receiver, will fill the role, though no official title change has happened yet. Welker coached the unit during spring practices after Steele’s arrest.

title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (July 31)
author: Rebecca Ritzel
summary: Canadian invasion at the Anthem, Latin jazz at Glen Echo Park, and “Sleeping Beauty” in the woods at Wolf Trap.
content: The Canadian band Stars is coming to the Anthem. Courtesy photo/Robbie Freeman Thursday Passport to Patriotism at the Art Museum of the Americas 18th Street NW, D.C., 9:30 a.m. to 5 p.m., free (through Oct. 18) If the wife of a Trump golf club manager curated a contemporary museum exhibition, what art would she hang on the walls? This is not a theoretical question. The Organization of American States tapped Erin Scavino, the wife of Dan Scavino, Trump’s longtime aide now serving as the White House director of the Presidential Personnel Office, to helm Passport to Patriotism . The exhibit, celebrating America’s 250th birthday, opens Thursday and runs through Oct. 18. Erin Scavino has no background in art curation or art history, but she does run the State Department’s Art in Embassies program and chose a mix of American flag photography and mixed-media pop-art paintings for her first big curation project. “ The President’s Own” Latin Jazz Ensemble at Glen Echo Park MacArthur Blvd., Glen Echo, Md., 7:30 p.m., free Lose the lottery for Jazz in the Garden again? Sorry. But if you have a car, try jazz at Glen Echo instead. Tonight "The President's Own" Latin Jazz Ensemble, featuring musicians from D.C.’s top U.S. Marine Corps band, makes its annual appearance at the historic Glen Echo Park. The setlist includes tunes by Chick Corea, Tito Puente’s “Cha Cha Cha,” and for the Disney demographic, Alan Menken’s “Under the Sea” calypso. More to explore: Faction of Fools’ “Leftover Lazzi: A Commedia Cabaret” at Capitol Hill Arts Workshop Friday The Funset at Woolly Mammoth Theatre Company D Street NW, D.C., 6 p.m., free The Penn Quarter theater and Downtown DC BID team up to offer this free indoor dance party with tunes spun by DJ Jahsonic and Harry Hotter. Guzzle gratis Topo Chico while supplies last, and watch local artist Urshula Dunn create a live installation in the theater lobby. Otakon at the Washington Convention Center 8 a.m. to 10 p.m., $70 adults, children 8 and under free Cosplay the day away at this 30th annual gathering for fans of all things Asian sci-fi, including anime, music and video games. Festivities include a live-art action (Ballroom C), 30 custom-painted cars (Hall D) plus a K-Pop concert, dance parties and Lyra’s Formal Ball. Dress code: Whatever the character you’re portraying would wear to prom. More to explore: A live taping of the Broadway musical “Hadestown” screens at local cinemas Saturday All the Feelings Tour with Metric, Broken Social Scene and Stars At the Anthem, Wharf St. NW, D.C., 7 p.m., $74 Tariffs, bans on American booze and the 51st State blues. Canadians have lots of feelings about Washington at the moment. For more positive vibes, head to the Anthem to catch Canadian supergroup Broken Social Scene, plus Metric and Stars, on the All the Feelings tour. The three bands have long shared personnel but rarely share a tour bus. This is your chance to see Stars and Metric form a brass section for their pals, as well as play their own up-tempo, angst-fueled sets. Washington Sculptors Group: Sculpture NOW at Harmony Hall Arts Center Livingston Rd., Fort Washington, Md., opening reception 2 to 4 p.m., free. Men on horseback may be the most common monuments in the District, but more than local artists belong to this society promoting three-dimensional artwork. The Washington Sculptors Group kicks off its annual juried group show this weekend and keeps the doors open through Sept. 5. More to explore: Celebrate Dark Star Park Day in Rosslyn Sunday Maryland Youth Ballet performs “Sleeping Beauty” at Wolf Trap Trap Road, Vienna, Va., 10:30 a.m., $14 For the youngest dance fans, there’s no better way to experience ballet for the first time than at Wolf Trap’s Children’s Theatre-in-the-Woods. Gasp at the beauty of Princess Aurora, giggle with the fairies, or yell when Maleficent casts a spell. All’s fair at this outdoor, abridged staging of the classic story ballet. Imagining Shakespeare: Mythmaking and Storytelling in the Regency Era At the Folger Shakespeare Library, E. Capitol St. SE, D.C., 11 a.m. to 6 p.m., suggested donation $15 When the Folger Shakespeare Library opened its new exhibition space in , the entrances were designed to accommodate the largest painting in the library’s vault: James Northcote’s massive depiction of the final scene in “Romeo and Juliet.” It’s the last day (for now) to see the painting yourself, plus 13 other Regency-era works featuring familiar characters from Shakespeare’s plays. More to explore: Live at the Lyceum Summer Sundays Chamber Music Series in Alexandria

title: Max Scherzer Is Still in the Fight. These Nats Are, Too.
author: Jesse Dougherty
summary: Five years after his trade kicked off the Nationals' rebuild, the World Series hero returned to his former home.
content: Max Scherzer returned to Nationals Park on Monday as a member of the Toronto Blue Jays. John McDonnell/AP A man spent his 42nd birthday pitching at Nationals Park on Monday night. And then everyone clapped for him. And then Max Scherzer waved. And then … OK, wait. Look. There’s a lot going on with the Nationals this week, important baseball things that, practically speaking, matter way more than looking back. When the present’s good, when life suddenly goes from bleh to exciting again, you don’t have to grip so tight to the past any longer, which is maybe just a winding description of happiness. And after losing, 3-2, to open a series against the struggling Blue Jays, the Nats keep hanging at 54-53, explosive on offense but still too imbalanced to pull much further from . . With six days until the trade deadline, they’re right on the edge of the wild-card race, meaning the reasons to buy or sell — or to do some combination of the two — feel like one of those DIY detective boards, the colored strings connecting a bunch of little clues. Depending, of course, on the player and the offers, could a couple of wins or losses really make a difference? Could, in theory, a single series determine whether the team trades Foster Griffin? Luis García Jr.? What about, gulp, CJ Abrams? That’s how Blake Butera, the team’s first-year manager, is talking. That’s how Paul Toboni, the team’s first-year president of baseball operations, has talked in recent interviews, too. The Nats are still exploring all options, which wouldn’t be news around here if not for the last five Julys, when there was no strategic gray area, just different forms of dread. “The last thing we want to do here is play games where it doesn’t really matter, right?” Butera said before Monday’s game. “We want to avoid that as long as possible. I know I haven’t been at this level, but in the minor leagues I never coached a game in August or September that was like: ‘Oh we’re out of it and we’re just trying to get to the end of the season and we have to get into the offseason.’ I don’t want to know what that feels like. What’s going on right now …” And that’s when Butera started tapping the table in front of him. Quick taps, like he was testing a microphone. “How these games feel and how important each one seems to be, is what I want to feel and I think what we all want to feel for as long as possible.” Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region . Which sounds a lot like when Max Scherzer was on the team. Which is why, no matter how much is happening right now, trade deadline or otherwise, Monday might have made you feel something else, something raw, something about how it once was and how fast it all goes. Was it the way he kept throwing his arms out, just like he used to, as if they’ll fall off if he stops moving them? The solo walk — no, stalk — from the bullpen before the top of the first? Those waves before he exited to a standing ovation, quite possibly for the last time in this stadium, right as he stepped on the P in an on-field advertisement for AARP? I bet it was the waves . “The great moments that we had with my time here in D.C., those are just things you never forget,” Scherzer said after the game. “So coming back here is a good trip down memory lane.” Scherzer, more than any active player, is a reminder of very good days in Washington, of moments and seasons that will stretch into forever. There used to be his blue and brown eyes above right field and now it’s a Toyota ad. But if you, like me, are into connecting narrative dots, he’s also a reminder of how long it’s been since this city could feel what it’s feeling this month. That each game can mean something. That it’s not pointless to care. Five years ago this week, the dread began. That was when, after a team with Scherzer, Trea Turner, Juan Soto and a hobbled Kyle Schwarber wasn’t good enough, the Nats completed a full teardown by trading Scherzer and Turner to the Dodgers. For Nationals fans, the half since had brought little joy until this season. And for Scherzer, it’s included stops in L.A., New York, Texas and Toronto, which has all aged him a good bit, which is what happens in baseball when you’re 42 and not ready to quit the only adult job you’ve ever had. Forearm and back issues have limited him to 24 ⅔ innings this year. On Monday, in his first start back from the injured list, he needed 75 pitches to record eight outs, which meant his night ended before the third inning did. He labored right away, loading the bases in the first before stranding the three runners. In the second, García, the only current Nat who played with Scherzer, tagged him for an RBI double. Then to finish his outing, Scherzer struck out Daylen Lile, who was 4 when the Diamondbacks drafted Scherzer in the first round in . “We’re all getting old,” Scherzer said of himself and Justin Verlander (and also everyone, in theory). “All of our bodies are not quite the same.”But the stadium wasn’t dotted with Scherzer jerseys because anyone expected him to dominate. No, it was dotted with his name, with his No. 31 in white and red, because of what he meant to you, you and yes, you, too, because your heart wasn’t always so cold. Because for six and a half years, Scherzer did what so few athletes can, which was make almost everything he did must-watch, all the way down to how he vibrated in the dugout. Because he once pitched a day after breaking his nose, when his right eye — the blue one — looked as if it had been jabbed by Mike Tyson. Because when he did dominate, it looked like two Cy Young Awards, two no-hitters and a World Series ring. Twice in his postgame interview Monday, he threw out buzz phrases from the title run, which are apparently burned into his vocabulary. He said the Blue Jays just have to go 1-0 every day. He said, when asked about striking out Lyle, that it’s just a matter of staying in the fight, especially with how hard it’s been for him to stick on the mound. Five years is long enough to change a lot of things. But it’s also, in this small corner of the universe, long enough for things to start changing back.

title: Pipe Dream
author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman
content: Hector Martinez, a contractor working for District of Columbia Water and Sewer Authority, bends an older lead water service pipe after removal form a residential home and replaces it with a new copper water pipe, Friday, July 17, in the Columbia Heights neighborhood of Washington. Pablo Martinez Monsivais/AP Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: sky-high utility bills, development delays and the Commanders’ new offensive coordinator. Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region . THE LATEST Gas is now fueling the ongoing debate over high utility bills in D.C. The D.C. Public Service Commission is holding a pair of hearings this week on Washington Gas’ ongoing plans to replace its aging pipes across the city. Over the last , some 50 miles of pipes — some dating back to the 1940s — have been swapped out; the utility company told NOTUS that continuing the effort is “essential to maintaining a safe, reliable, and resilient energy system for the more than , customers we serve in the District.” But opponents worry about the impact on residential bills and the environment. The next three-year pipe replacement plan is expected to cost $ million, and D.C. consumers will see those costs factored into their monthly bills. That would come on top of rising Pepco bills, which the Public Service Commission is similarly getting heat for. D.C. Attorney General Brian Schwalb is opposed to Washington Gas’ plan. He says the pipe replacements thus far have been too expensive and have failed to contain some leaks. Environmental groups like the Sierra Club would rather see D.C. fully phase out natural gas and turn toward building electrification and renewable energy. Some experts say replacing aging pipes in D.C. is critical. Speaking to the D.C. Council last month, former federal regulator Cynthia Quarterman said the city has more 1940s-vintage cast-iron gas pipes than almost anywhere else. “A jurisdiction with the nation’s highest concentration of the nation’s most dangerous pipe material is the last jurisdiction that should slow down,” she said. The Public Service Commission will use the two hearings to craft the specifics of the next portion of Washington Gas’ pipe replacement plans. The utility says it is focused on “completing this work efficiently and responsibly, while keeping customer affordability top of mind.” But Schwalb wants any approved plan to “keep the community safe from dangerous gas leaks … and protect ratepayers from excessive and unwarranted rate increases.” Utility prices will be back on the commission’s docket in October, when regulators will again take up a controversial multiyear rate increase requested by Pepco. FROM THE DISTRICT Start your engines. Construction is underway at the National Mall, where the Freedom Grand Prix will take place next month, ABC7 reports . There are delays on Metro’s Red Line — just not the ones you’re used to. A plan for a -unit residential development on the Takoma Metro station’s parking lot is facing setbacks due to high construction costs, challenges securing financing and complications delivering promised affordable units, reports UrbanTurf . Delays are nothing new for the project, which has been floating around for at least 15 years and hit just about every bureaucratic, political and civic snag possible. FROM VIRGINIA The son of Eric Bieniemy , the Commanders’ former offensive coordinator, has been arrested and charged with shooting his mother in their Ashburn home, The Associated Press reports . FROM MARYLAND A Montgomery County Council member said last week that firefighters violated a county law prohibiting voluntary ICE cooperation, The Banner reports . GUESS THE LISTING -uncropped_scaled_within_1536_1152 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)Listed for $1, , , this four-bedroom, five-bathroom home totaling more than 4, square feet features cathedral ceilings and two large garages. Guess where this listing is sold: Maryland Virginia D.C. We’ll let you know tomorrow how many of you got it right. SPORTS The Commanders’ new offensive coordinator is young — very young. At 30 years old, David Blough is not far removed from his NFL playing days. Now, as training camp gets underway this week, the former quarterback is tasked with bringing Washington’s offense back to life. In a deep-dive profile , NOTUS’ Martenzie Johnson talked to Blough’s friends, family and former teammates about what makes him the man for the job. In soccer news , the Spirit are now two points clear at the top of the NWSL table after a win against Denver Summit FC over the weekend. What to Watch Today MLB: Nationals vs. Blue Jays, 6:45 p.m. ( MLB.TV ) WNBA: Mystics vs. Sun, 7:30 p.m. ( Monumental ) Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com . The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Andrew Burton. Photo courtesy of HomeVisit Photography. Finally, yesterday’s trivia answer was B) wine. A special shout-out to David Shaw, who answered first.

title: Commanders’ David Blough Has Been Preparing for This Moment His Whole Life
author: Martenzie Johnson
summary: Friends and former teammates say Washington’s new, 30-year-old coordinator is just the man to lead an offense.
content: After two years as an assistant, David Blough will be calling plays for the first time this season as Washington's offensive coordinator. Nick Wass/AP Facing nearly insurmountable odds, David Blough was not fazed. It was , his senior season at Creekview High School in Carrollton, Texas, and the Mustangs were playing for a spot in the Class 4A playoffs. Entering the fourth quarter, Creekview trailed North Forney, 26-13. Where some other teenage quarterbacks might succumb to defeat, Blough remained stoic. He walked the sideline, assuring his teammates everything was fine and they still had a whole quarter to play. “He’s just walking around telling everybody,” said Creekview offensive coordinator Robert Paschall, a longtime high school coach in Texas. “It wasn't fake bullshit. I've seen fake bullshit, like people running around being hype. … This was ‘By God, we're gonna win.’” At some point, Blough and Paschall noticed North Forney had difficulty covering flood routes, where multiple receivers go to one side of the field. They started spamming the playcall the rest of the way, and within a few possessions, they had erased the deficit — clinching a 33-29 win and earning Creekview’s first playoff berth in five years. The moxie Blough displayed that night was an early indicator of the player and coach he would become — one who knows how to remain calm, lean on what works and take the lead. He showed it then as a three-star quarterback prospect with just one college offer, from Purdue. He showed it with the Boilermakers, once throwing for over yards and three touchdowns in a rout of No. 2 Ohio State. And he showed it as an NFL backup, working his way from undrafted free agent to a five-year career in which he made seven starts. Now, he’ll need those traits as the Commanders’ offensive coordinator, a role he inherits after just two years as an assistant coach. Starting this week at training camp, he will be tasked with cooking up a new offense that takes full advantage of Jayden Daniels, Washington's young franchise quarterback, and helps the team bounce back from a disastrous season. The hardest part of this task? Blough is just 30 years old. And he’s never called plays before. “He was always somebody we knew would develop into this role as a play caller,” Commanders coach Dan Quinn said of his young coordinator. “He came in as a coach ahead of the curve, so he had a bigger vision and perspective [than] maybe a coach just coming out of school or something in that space wouldn't.” Save for his father, the most important and impactful men in Blough’s life have been his coaches. Because of them, he’s always had a strong passion for mentoring young people and giving back to his community. Those who’ve known Blough the longest say he was born to do this job. “I've always wanted to build men,” Blough said. “And I've learned this is the closest thing I could ever do to calling a play in a huddle again is building it, creating it.” David Blough Purdue 1 AP - ( , AR: 1.50) Leading from the front Ask anyone from Blough’s childhood and they’ll tell you he has always been a leader. In elementary school, Blough got the lead in the school musical despite not knowing how to really sing. A few years later his mother, LuAnn, signed him up for soccer even though Blough had never played before. "He went out and scored four goals," she said. When Blough was in middle school, he walked up to the coach of the football team and told him, "Hi, Coach, I'm your quarterback." Andres Ruiz was Blough’s 7-on-7 coach in those early years. The ex-Marine said he used to push his young athletes hard, implementing some military tactics. No matter how tired Blough seemed, he never stopped trying to lift up his teammates. “Even though he may not have been the most talented kid on the field, he was always front of the line, encouraging guys, keeping their heads up when they get tired, leading from the front,” Ruiz said. Blough was always the one looking for extra reps, both on the field and in the weight room. By the time he got to high school, Blough — who started on varsity as a sophomore — would wake up teammates at the crack of dawn and wrangle them into throwing sessions. “He would send me [a text message], ‘Well, our competition isn't sleeping in.’ And then it's like, ‘OK, you just rage-baited me into going to work out, and of course I want to work out,'” said Raul Bustillos, Creekview’s starting running back. Blough’s known since high school that he wanted to be a coach. It might sound like an odd dream, but this was in Texas, home of Friday Night Lights . He once dressed up as legendary Cowboys coach Tom Landry, complete with the trademark fedora and blazer. “It was like 95 degrees, so I don't think he wore it that long,” said Dylan Kittrell, the team’s receiver. On the bus to games, Paschall would hand his teenage quarterback the playsheet and tell him to pick what he wanted to run. When Blough was asked why he picked a particular play, he’d explain his rationale in detail, saying he knew the safety would react a certain way or his receiver could get to a certain spot. “He was very precise and exacting,” Paschall said. David Blough Purdue 2 - AP - ( , AR: 1.50) ‘A designer, not a dictator’ John Shoop, Purdue’s offensive coordinator, came to Carrollton for a recruiting visit during Blough’s junior season. But there was a mix-up with the school, and no showcase on the schedule. Instead, Blough organized his own throwing session on the fly with about 10 of his teammates. That day, Shoop said he witnessed someone who showed command of an offense and clearly garnered so much respect from his teammates that they’d drop everything to shine a brighter light on him. Shoop, who was an assistant coach with the Carolina Panthers from to , said he hadn’t seen anything like that since evaluating future MVP quarterback Steve McNair out of Alcorn State in the mid 1990s. “It was really revealing to me,” Shoop said of Blough’s showcase. Blough committed to Purdue in . After his second season, the school hired former Louisville quarterback Jeff Brohm as its new head coach. Early on, Brohm asked his players to bring him ideas for plays if they ever had any, assuming no one would actually take him up on the offer. Blough did. The coach allowed his quarterback to script his own plays at times, and away from the field Blough designed his own playbook in his free time. “He was not shy about that, which was outstanding, because a lot of people don't fully get invested that much,” said Brohm, who had planned to hire his former quarterback as a graduate assistant in before Blough signed as an undrafted free agent with Lions. “And I think when he did that you knew at some point down the road, ‘OK, this guy's gonna be a good coach, because he really, really is into this.’” In addition to passion, Blough always had composure. While his former coaches admit to losing their cool sometimes, they say Blough has never been the type. He is never frantic. He has an empathy that doesn’t allow mistakes or a lack of discipline to turn into anger. When he does raise his voice, it's more encouraging than demeaning. “Some quarterbacks are kind of a-holes,” said Kittrell. “And others are able to teach it to everyone.” “I truly believe that I am a designer, not a dictator,” Blough said, referring to a philosophy he learned from author Martin E. P. Seligman’s book “Flourish: A Visionary New Understanding of Happiness and Well-being.” When Blough found out that his college teammate, running back Markell Jones, was in Purdue’s aviation school, the competitor in him came out: If Markell can do it, I can do it too . So he began studying to earn his private pilot license, work you can still find on his LinkedIn page . Jones, now a pilot for United Airlines, said the studies speak to Blough’s competitive nature, which can be infectious to those around him. “When David was speaking to our team, everyone locked in,” Jones said. “You could look on his and see that David's going to go down dying. David will die to get the job done to execute the play to the best of his ability.” David Blough Stafford - AP - ( , AR: 1.50) No surprise No matter how much of a whiz kid Blough may be or how good a high school and college quarterback he was, he has never been an offensive coordinator. Teams hiring first-time play callers have had uneven results over the years: In the NFC East alone, the Cowboys’ Kellen Moore led a top-10 offense in his first season as a play caller in while the Eagles’ Brian Johnson and Kevin Patullo were each fired following single seasons in and , respectively. But that’s the paradox of experience: You can only gain it from doing the job, but oftentimes you can’t get the job without it. Blough, who will be making a rare and sizable leap from assistant quarterbacks coach to coordinator, said that imposter syndrome is almost unavoidable. “I think everybody at some point who's made it to this level, whether it's our quarterback or head coach or head chef down there probably feels imposter syndrome in some way,” Blough said. “And then you prepare really hard and you believe in what you're doing, and there's a trust established between who you're doing it with, and it helps ease all that.” One of Blough’s best traits, former teammates and coaches say, is understanding both the tendencies of the defense and the characteristics of his own roster. It’s something he picked up from Paschall, whose offensive system at Creekview was simple: maximize what each individual player was good at and avoid what they were bad at. Rumors have swirled for months about the Commanders signing another starting receiver to pair with veteran Terry McLaurin, but for someone with Blough’s mentality, it’s less about who you can add and more about making the most of the players available. “We put Terry and Antonio [Williams] and Treylon [Burks] and Dyami [Brown] … in the best position possible to go be successful, and that gives me confidence, knowing that they're the best in the world at what they do. I just get to help facilitate that,” Blough said. But his transition to coordinator, like all major transitions, will not be without hiccups. Throughout last month’s team activities, there were mishaps on offense: fumbled snaps, overthrows, interceptions, false starts and bobbled handoffs. But that’s just part of the process, according to Blough. It’s better to make those mistakes now, he says, and learn from them rather than commit a false start in the playoffs when the game is on the line. “We know that if we're worth our salt as coaches and able to correct and teach, that you know when it's fourth and 4 in the biggest stage, we'll be able to make the play, because we've communicated and committed to excellence,” Blough said. Blough is still cagey about what the offense will actually look like this season, other than acknowledging that Daniels will take more snaps under center, McLaurin will line up all over the formation, and he plans to change up tempo and personnel groupings more to make the offense unpredictable. But in the small glimpses of his play-calling, Blough has shown the ability to take advantage of a defense. During a matchup with the Eagles, Blough, still the team’s assistant quarterbacks coach, was behind what became the game-winning play: a 9-yard touchdown pass from Daniels to receiver Jamison Crowder . Blough had helped design the red-zone play — empty backfield, trips left, mirrored post routes toward the back of the end zone — years earlier for a different team. The Commanders practiced it earlier that week during two-minute drills. In the moment, with the game on the line, Blough delivered. Quinn is betting big that Blough will help Washington return to the playoffs following last season’s catastrophic 5-12 finish. But for every bit of confidence the head coach has in his new coordinator, those that have been on this journey with Blough the longest are twice as certain he will succeed. “In that league, people don't care if you're 20, people don't care if you're 60,” said Shoop, who has known Blough since college. “If you can help them get good, they listen to you, and Dave can help people get good. He really can. He's clearly done it.” “All of this, to someone looking at it from the outside in, it probably looks like a surprise,” said Kittrell, who has known Blough even longer. “But for us, people that know him and are close with him, it's not a surprise whatsoever.”

title: What $1.2 Million Gets You in D.C., Maryland and Virginia
author: Torrie Herrington
summary: Our weekly column compares home listings across the metro area.
content: Orchard Way in Silver Spring, Md. (Courtesy of HomeVisit Photography) What does $1.2 million get you in the D.C. area? Old Town Alexandria is 15 minutes away.

title: On the Docket
author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman
content: 16 October , USA, Washington Dc: US National Guard soldiers walk up the steps to the Lincoln Memorial in the early morning. Photo by: Kay Nietfeld/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Images Kay Nietfeld/picture-alliance/dpa/AP Images Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Judicial nominations, Waymo and a new pitcher for the Nats. Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region . THE LATEST Judging by the facts, it looks like the Senate is about to help D.C. The upper chamber is soon expected to approve the nominations of six judges for D.C. Superior Court and two for the D.C. Court of Appeals. The nominations moved out of committee last week, and are expected to be voted on before the Senate heads to recess at the end of next week. Judicial nominations — or the lack thereof — have long been a point of contention between Congress and the District. While Superior Court and the Court of Appeals function as the city’s judiciary, their judges are nominated by the president and confirmed by the Senate. The process has been historically sluggish, often sparking complaints from city and court officials about judicial vacancies. That’s even more of a problem now, as Superior Court saw a 38.5% spike in criminal cases from to , due in part to the surge of federal agents . The Senate action will go a long way to addressing existing vacancies , says courts spokesman Doug Buchanan. He tells NOTUS that two of the nine seats on the Court of Appeals are vacant, while there are 13 vacancies — out of 62 total judgeships — in Superior Court. “But adding judges without providing the operational workforce and infrastructure that supports them limits the effectiveness of that investment,” adds Buchanan, noting that D.C.’s courts are funded by Congress. “Justice depends on an entire system working together.” DEEP DIVE D.C.’s disabled residents say they don’t have a reliable form of on-demand transportation. Would Waymo help? Opinion is split, NOTUS' Zara Norman reports . At a hearing this month, some blind and residents testified that they’re excited by the possibility of autonomous vehicles in the District. But the bill that would legalize Waymo and other driverless cars in the city has no requirement that those vehicles be wheelchair accessible, sparking concerns in the community. Waymo told NOTUS that it’s “actively assessing how we will provide an additional fleet of wheelchair accessible vehicles alongside our fully autonomous fleet,” should the company be allowed to operate in the city. But advocates want a mandate , highlighting the fact that taxi companies in D.C. are required to make 20% of their fleet accessible. FROM THE DISTRICT The National Guard is moving in. The federal government will spend $ million to house thousands of troops in apartments in D.C. over the next year, NOTUS’ Raymond Fernández reports . The contract for 2, “apartment-style lodging units” provided by extended-stay company Placemakr is yet another indication that Donald Trump ’s deployment of the Guard is a long-term commitment — this month, its stay was officially extended through . A change to property taxes? Any D.C. homeowner knows that you pay your property taxes twice a year — in March and September. But a new bill from Ward 1 council member Brianne Nadeau would move D.C. to quarterly payments in an attempt to smooth out the city’s cash flow over the year. Her legislation would also allow the city to explore taxing only the value of the land that a house or building is on, or taxing the land and building at different rates. That approach, she says, could make buying and building in D.C. more attractive. FROM MARYLAND Montgomery County has acquired White’s Ferry in a $1.5 million deal, WTOP reports . But restarting the service , which ferried people and their vehicles across the Potomac from Poolesville to Leesburg until it shuttered in , would require Virginia officials to strike a similar deal. The answer will be at the end of the newsletter tomorrow. SPORTS The Nationals' first deadline trade sent infielder Curtis Mead to Boston for left-handed pitcher Connelly Early. The move felt like a clear self-assessment for the new front office and coaching staff, NOTUS' Jesse Dougherty reports . For more analysis from Jesse, check out his AMA on r/Nationals from Friday.
