title: A Player-Led Labor Effort Could Be a Sign of College Football’s Future
author: Jesse Dougherty
summary: Stanford players have formed a chapter with the College Football Players Association. They hope more teams follow soon.
content: Linebacker Ernest Cooper was elected by his Stanford teammates as one of the leaders for their chapter with the College Football Players Association. Adrian Kraus/AP Football players at Stanford have organized a chapter with the College Football Players Association, which could be a significant first step toward athletes in the NCAA’s most lucrative sport unionizing in the future. Others have tried, of course, and the CFBPA is not attempting to form a union at Stanford at the moment. But five years after the labor group launched, this is its first chapter led by active players, and it described the infrastructure as providing the “firm foundation for unionization and collective bargaining.” The CFBPA is hopeful the announcement Monday leads to similar organizing at other Division I football programs. That could happen in the near future, according to Jason Stahl, the CFBPA’s executive director. The broader goal here is to give football players a real say in the decisions shaping the name, image and likeness (NIL) era of college sports. And the timing is certainly interesting, too, as a handful of U.S. senators keep pushing the Protect College Sports Act , a bill supported by the NCAA and many conferences but generally loathed by labor groups. It’s impossible to separate any athlete organizing from what’s going on on Capitol Hill , especially with how the possibility of employment and unions plays into most — if not all — of these policy discussions. Just take it from Ernest Cooper, a redshirt senior linebacker at Stanford who was elected by his teammates as one of the leaders for their chapter with the CFBPA. “You see what’s going on in Congress; I think it’s hard when people who can’t relate, or try to say they understand the space, are trying to govern and put rules over you when you don’t have an ambassador at that table to advocate on your behalf,” Cooper said in a phone interview. “They’re trying to determine what’s right for us without talking to us.” Late last week, Senate Majority Leader John Thune told reporters he doesn’t expect a floor vote on the Protect College Sports Act before this session ends Aug. 7. And while that doesn’t mean a vote couldn’t happen post-recess, it does raise doubts about its chances of passing through the Senate — let alone the House — despite the legislation being driven by two powerful senators on opposite sides of the aisle: Maria Cantwell (D-Washington) and Ted Cruz (R-Texas). In June, the bill made it out of the Senate’s commerce committee with a 19-9 vote. To that point, Cruz and Cantwell had a lot of control over its fate, seeing that Cruz is the committee’s chair and Cantwell its ranking member. But now the midterms are closing in. Soon, as Sen. Eric Schmitt (R-Missouri), one of the bill’s co-sponsors, explained recently, focus will shift to campaigning, then to budget negotiations —- at which point the PCSA could run out of time. A major hangup has been opposition from the SEC and Big Ten — the two biggest, richest conferences in college sports — which has led to ongoing negotiations with Cruz and Cantwell, along with Schmitt and Chris Coons (D-Delaware), the last original co-sponsor. Employment is not among the issues they are going back and forth on. But ever since the bill was introduced, including a line about how it is “neutral on, and does nothing to alter, employee or non-employee status for student athletes,” employment has been a complicating factor for Democrats and Republicans, though largely for different reasons. Many Republicans, in the Senate and House, want any sweeping college sports bill to bar athletes from becoming employees. That includes Sen. Tommy Tuberville (R-Alabama), a former D-I football coach who’s been pushing against the PCSA, according to multiple people familiar with his messaging to fellow Republicans. This is also a long-running goal for the NCAA and its schools. On the other side, many pro-labor Democrats believe the bill could stunt future attempts to organize college athletes. Their argument: By giving the NCAA and conferences the antitrust protection needed to regulate compensation, player movement and eligibility without the threat of lawsuits, the PCSA would set rules that should be subject to collective bargaining, like in the NFL, NBA and other pro leagues. Then to take that argument a step further: If the PCSA instituted those rules along with antitrust immunity, labor groups would lose key leverage points. Why would college athletes unionize if they couldn’t negotiate over these issues? Which brings us back to Stanford’s new chapter with the CFBPA. On Capitol Hill, its existence should only strengthen those sentiments on both sides. Again, it’s not an immediate attempt to unionize. But a number of factors will determine whether that’s eventually possible. One, of course, is what happens with the PCSA. Another is the outcome of Johnson vs. NCAA, a federal lawsuit that is seeking employment status for college athletes under the National Labor Relations Act. And another is whether a Democrat wins the White House in , which would almost certainly lead to a more union-friendly National Labor Relations Board. The Dartmouth men’s basketball team began its attempt to unionize when Joe Biden was president. It then withdrew its petition with the NLRB a few weeks before Donald Trump’s second inauguration. “Collective is what you eventually want to get to, one hundred percent,” Cooper, the Stanford linebacker, said of the long-term plan for his team’s chapter and the CFBPA. “You see the NFL and how they have their players association. All I want is for college athletes to not just get what they deserve, but to be protected while playing, too.” The CFBPA is one of a few prominent college athlete labor groups. Others include Athletes.org and the National College Players Association, whose executive director, Ramogi Huma, led the attempt to unionize Northwestern’s football team more than a ago. But the CFBPA, founded by Stahl, is the only group that is solely focused on football players. While Stahl’s ultimate vision is to scale this across the country, a more specific goal is to leverage Stanford’s chapter to get more ACC teams on board. Down the line, he hopes, ACC football players would collectively bargain with the conference over compensation, player safety and so on. If that were to happen, chapter leaders from each program would participate in negotiations. The ACC, meanwhile, has been lobbying hard for the PCSA. The conference’s Student-Athlete Advisory Committee recently sent a letter to a handful of senators stumping for the bill. When the NCAA and conferences select athletes to testify for their interests on Capitol Hill, they are usually involved with the advisory committee, which is an NCAA-sponsored program. And this letter, a full-throated endorsement of the PCSA, further illustrates the divide between the big-money sports and everyone else. Of the 28 athletes who signed the letter, none was a football or men’s basketball player. It’s only reason one million why it’s difficult to govern D-I sports with one set of rules — and, to that end, one federal bill. “If there is collective bargaining down the line, it would make sense for football to be the focus,” Cooper said. “It’s just where the most money is.”

title: D.C.’s Disabled Residents Have Dismal Transit Options. Would Waymo Help?
author: Zara Norman
summary: Advocates fear that autonomous vehicles will be allowed to operate in the District without accessibility requirements.
content: The possibility of Waymos in D.C. has already divided the city's disability advocates. Phelan M. Ebenhack/AP When Kelly Mack orders a wheelchair-accessible Uber or Lyft, she does so knowing that most rides will cancel on her. Even when Claire Stanley’s rideshare is accepted, some drivers pull up to the curb, see her guide dog and tell her they don’t want her in their car. As members of D.C.’s disability community, both Mack and Stanley are accustomed to “abysmal” experiences getting a ride. But there is a potentially powerful newcomer in the market, one that has already divided disability advocates: Waymo. A bill before the D.C. Council would allow companies to operate a fleet of up to autonomous vehicles in the District. The bill, which received a hearing this month but won’t get a vote until the fall, has its supporters, including some disabled Washingtonians who are excited by the prospect. “There is just something very cool, as an adult who’s never been able to drive, that when you take an AV, you feel that freedom and that autonomy,” Stanley, an advocacy director at the American Council Of The Blind, told NOTUS. But the bill doesn’t require operators to make their vehicles wheelchair-accessible, and that troubles wheelchair users, who say they have no reliable on-demand transportation service in the city. “We support the wider disability community getting their needs met, we just want to widen the scope of what [AV operators are] required to do to meet the needs of all of our community members,” said Heidi Case, a wheelchair user and disability advocate. In theory, D.C. residents with disabilities can use the Metro system, for-hire vehicles or the city’s paratransit service to get around. But the bus and rail aren’t door-to-door services. Rideshare is only reliable in the heart of the city and sometimes refers riders out to taxi services, which struggle with driver shortages and have limited operating hours. City paratransit has to be booked at least a day in advance, and often has multiple stops. “They either pick you up super early, or they get you there super late, or there’s multiple people on paratransit at the same time,” Stanley said. “So, what should be a 20-minute ride suddenly is an hourlong ride.” Mack said she and her husband once had to show up at the airport a full day before their early-morning flight because paratransit couldn’t guarantee they’d have an accessible vehicle available for her to use. WMATA did not respond to a request for comment on how it plans to improve or expand its paratransit service. The limited options are, in part, a product of policy. D.C. green-lit Uber and Lyft’s operations over a ago without mandating those companies provide accessible rides. That was a “big flaw” in that legislation, Jonathan Rogers, executive director of D.C.’s Department of For-Hire Vehicles, told NOTUS. He believes District leaders have an opportunity to do something different this time around. “Instead of just hoping that they will prioritize those issues more than [companies] did when Uber and Lyft came here over a ago, let’s require it,” said Rogers. At a hearing last week, Waymo contended it can’t mandate what the automotive industry doesn’t manufacture. A Tesla spokesperson testified the company is trying to develop a “purpose-built wheelchair-accessible autonomous vehicle.” “We are a technology company. We do not develop our own and manufacture our own vehicles,” testified Waymo spokesperson Matthew Walsh. “We have not been able to identify an electric vehicle platform that is fully wheelchair-accessible while also meeting the very unique specifications that we need to retrofit that vehicle with our technology.” But D.C. requires taxi companies to make 20% of their fleet wheelchair-accessible. Those companies don’t employ drivers directly, and they also don’t own most of the fleet, Rogers said. “It’s a little ironic,” he said. “It’s challenging to provide that service, but taxis are these tiny little small businesses, and they’re in the exact same position as these multinational corporations.” Taxi companies complete about 96% of the city’s wheelchair[accessible rides, Rogers said. In , taxis completed more than , wheelchair-accessible rides. A spokesperson for Waymo told NOTUS the company is “actively assessing how we will provide an additional fleet of wheelchair accessible vehicles alongside our fully autonomous fleet,” should Waymo be allowed to operate here. The company could do what it has done in some of the 11 cities where it operates: partner with local organizations to provide wheelchair-accessible vehicles — though with a human behind the wheel. Private companies aren’t required by law to provide wheelchair-accessible cars, but they cannot discriminate against people with disabilities. A settlement in an ongoing disability discrimination lawsuit between the Equality Rights Center and Uber required the platform to incentivize drivers to provide wheelchair-accessible rides. But D.C. advocates hope they will be given access to autonomous vehicles without getting tied up in court. “I ask you to please require [Waymo] to do it,” Mack testified at the council hearing. “Otherwise, it’s putting the onus on my community to litigate.”

title: What the Nationals' First Deadline Deal Really Means
author: Jesse Dougherty
summary: The Nats traded infielder Curtis Mead to the Red Sox on Saturday in exchange for pitcher Connelly Early.
content: Pitcher Connelly Early is coming to Washington. Kevin Ng/AP Photo In late March, the Nationals traded a young catcher named Boston Smith for an Australian infielder named Curtis Mead, who had been solidly below-average in career plate appearances — and was just designated for assignment by the White Sox, a team that lost games in . And then late Saturday night, the Nats flipped Mead to the Red Sox for left-handed pitcher Connelly Early, which was both their first trade deadline deal and a clear self-assessment for the new front office and coaching staff. They are feeling very, very good about the organization’s ability to develop hitting — and particularly power — in the majors and minors. They have every reason to, too, given that Mead went from floating in the ether to having a breakout year, including 17 home runs in less than four months. Players up and down the Nats’ major league roster are also tracking toward career highs in homers, if they aren’t there already. Which is all why it made perfect sense to trade from a position of strength (bats) to improve a glaring weakness (arms). ( ESPN first reported the Mead-Early trade .) Some more top-line details: Early is only 24 and will be under team control for another five years after this one (through ). Mead, 25, is controllable through . Early has been on the injured list since July 1 with left elbow inflammation, which underscores the inherent risk of swapping a hitter for a pitcher who’s never thrown more than innings at any level. But the Nats’ front office is intimately familiar with him, seeing that Paul Toboni, the team’s first-year president of baseball operations, was a key decision maker when Boston drafted Early in , as was Devin Pearson, now one of Toboni’s assistant general managers in Washington. (Toboni has now done two deals with his former club.) The deadline is Aug. 3, meaning the Nats could just be getting started. Shortstop CJ Abrams is generating real interest, according to multiple people familiar with his market, though it would take a massive return for the Nats to move him while hanging on the edge of the wild-race race. It wouldn’t require nearly as much for them to part with first baseman Luis García Jr. or starter Foster Griffin — though Griffin, an All Star with a 2.68 ERA, is in a higher tier than García, who would be a lefty platoon bat for a contender. And if the Nationals can improve on their 53-52 record over the next week, they could very well seek bullpen help while weighing offers for the players above. If the Mead-Early trade revealed anything about their broader deadline approach, it is that it’s not necessarily a binary choice between buying or selling. Early has allowed a ton of hard contact in 91⅔ innings this season. But he’s still managed a 3.44 ERA while mixing five to six pitches. Advanced metrics love his changeup. His extension, which measures the distance between the rubber and where a pitcher releases the ball, is well above average, a trait the Nats’ front office likes. And with the Red Sox, obvious needs lined up at the perfect time. The Red Sox just ripped off a 15-game winning streak and needed more offense for their playoff push. The Nats, confident they can replicate the process that revived Mead’s career, leaped at the chance to bring in a high-upside pitcher they know well. The Red Sox have the pitching prospects to backfill Early’s spot. The Nats have a handful of intriguing infield prospects, including Brady House, who will join the team Sunday to replace Mead on the active roster (which The Athletic first reported ). That’s the anatomy of a one-for-one trade of young big leaguers. House will be the next test of just how well the Nats can coach up power hitting in the majors, which they’ve done with multiple players now by emphasizing pulling the right pitches in the air. A first-round pick in , House started the year with the Nationals and struggled with contact and pitch selection. When he did connect, he hit the ball hard more often than not, resulting in seven homers in a limited sample. But he also struck out 50 times, nearly a third of this plate appearances, while working only 13 walks. Righties have chewed him up. That’s not to say that House’s next two months should color the assessment of trading Mead for Early. House’s promotion doesn’t mean the Nationals necessarily view him as their third baseman of the future, especially given how they pulled Mead from obscurity to effectively replace House for a few months. But House, who just turned 23, is coming off an encouraging stretch in AAA. And if the major league staff can keep turning him in the right direction, Saturday’s deal will make even more sense.

title: The LeBron James Sixers Really Could Win It All
author: Martenzie Johnson
summary: NBA superteams rarely work out. Here's why this one might be different.
content: LeBron James is headed to Philadelphia. Kyusung Gong/AP Superteams in the modern era of the NBA rarely work out. For a litany of reasons — chemistry, coaching, injury — a collection of stars on one team often doesn’t lead to championships. The Heat did it, sure. The Warriors did it, of course. But for every Heat and Warriors there are many more teamups that end up in failure and dirt being thrown around in the media. So there’s reason to be reluctant to … king the 76ers as next season’s champions simply because LeBron James decided on Friday his “last decision” was to sign with them. But sometimes in basketball the obvious is in front of you. Of course we all should have assumed the Knicks would win the Finals after they kept blowing out all of their Eastern Conference playoff opponents. Of course Victor Wembanyama was going to live up to the hype; he did this before even making it to the NBA. LeBron James — the LeBron James — just joined a team with former MVP Joel Embiid, former Finals MVP Jaylen Brown and two of the more promising young guards in the NBA in Tyrese Maxey and V. J. Edgecombe. What weaknesses does this collection of players have? All five of them are capable of regularly putting up 20 points. Four can regularly give you 30. Three can easily get you 40 or 50 if you absolutely need them to. Oh, and Embiid went for 70 just two years ago. The 76ers’ defense wasn’t great last season (16th in defensive efficiency) but adding Brown to play alongside Edgecombe on the wing and Embiid in the post makes that unit difficult to score on. James isn’t the all-defensive team player he used to be, but he’s who you fear like Michael Myers lurking on a fastbreak layup attempt. The bench lacked scoring (32.4 points per game ranked 27th) but the additions of Dean Wade (5.8 points per game) and Anfernee Simons (14.3) should be enough to hold the second unit afloat. Sure, there’s only one basketball: Brown (3rd) and Embiid (6th) were top 10 in the NBA in usage rate last season; Maxey ranked 27th and James 47th. But when these starting five are on the court you can’t double-team anyone, you can’t sag off of anyone, you can’t zone your way out of those problems. How many lineups in the league have five players who could reasonably take the last shot in a game? I’ll wait. The one thing that can trip these 76ers up is all the testosterone in that locker room. We know James brings a media circus wherever he sets up, not to mention his style of leadership has at times been described as passive-aggressive. Embiid has no problem throwing a teammate under the bus, as he infamously did to Ben Simmons after the playoffs. Brown has publicly bad-mouthed Embiid (“[He] flops. He know it.”) and James’ son (“I don't think Bronny is a pro.”) and overall isn’t afraid to say what’s on his mind. Maxey and Edgecomb may not say as much, but their collective demeanors read: Try me if you want to . Egos or toxicity ruined the -04 and -13 Lakers, the late 2000s Celtics, the -18 Cavaliers, the -22 Nets, and Kevin Durant’s recent stints with the Suns and Rockets. But if no issues arise in the Philadelphia locker room, and if — big if — Embiid is playing healthy ball in April and May next year, this very well could be the year the 76ers finally do it. (And the fact that they built this team not from intentionally losing games to get high draft picks, as they did in the Process era, is certainly not lost on most Philly fans.) We could be looking at the -27 NBA champions being formed in real time.

title: Bowser’s Final Lap
author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman
content: Children play in the streams of water in the M Street Water Park in the summer heat on July 20, in Washington, D.C. Samuel Corum/Sipa USA via AP Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: Mayor Bowser’s final priorities, a win for ranked-choice voting and a Reddit AMA. Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region . THE LATEST Pools are simple. Politics, less so. That’s the reality Mayor Muriel Bowser is likely to in her final five months in office, and one she indirectly seemed to embrace Thursday when she cut the ribbon on the $6.8 million renovation of the outdoor Rosedale Pool in Ward 7. No one has officially declared her a lame duck, but conversations inside and out of the Wilson Building have shifted from what Bowser is doing to what Janeese Lewis George , her presumptive successor, is promising to do and the challenges she’s likely to . Bowser — a political institution in her own right — just isn’t the center of the political conversation anymore. That’s not to say Bowser is phoning it in. She told NOTUS that she plans to keep hammering home the message that D.C. needs to focus on growing an economy that has been hit hard by sweeping cuts to the once-steady federal workforce. “We worked for 12 years on making sure our finances are robust,” she said. “So our No. 1 issue for the next months, and even for the next mayor, is how do we grow our city? Attract businesses, create jobs, keep D.C. residents, and attract more D.C. residents?” Housing is another priority: This month, Bowser introduced a package of bills touching on everything from eviction timelines to tenant rights in buildings that hit the market. None of this is to say the D.C. Council will heed her words, much less pass her bills. Bowser has had a prickly relationship for years with city lawmakers, many of whom are now looking to what’s next. But where politics may come up short, pools — and other public projects — will remain. D.C. officials tell NOTUS that there are at least 28 planned groundbreakings or ribbon-cuttings planned for the remainder of the year, everything from an expansion of the Southeast Tennis and Learning Center in Ward 8 to the reopening of a brand new Harriet Tubman Elementary School in Ward 1. FROM THE DISTRICT Most D.C. voters ranked two or more candidates in the June 16 Democratic primary, according to a new analysis by FairVote, an elections reform group. Why does that matter? FairVote, which supports the use of ranked-choice voting, says it shows that D.C. voters were able to navigate the system in its inaugural usage. The data also shows that while Lewis George won the Democratic nomination for mayor with 54% of the vote, 71% of voters ranked her in their top three. Want even more nerdy data on the election’s outcomes? Find it here . Understaffing at D.C.’s public safety agencies resulted in a “substantial” $ million spent on overtime last fiscal year, according to a new report from D.C.’s auditor. The family of a 6-year-old boy who nearly drowned at a D.C. summer camp on Monday told City Cast DC that he faces a “long and uncertain” road ahead. Some students who’d been accepted to Howard University say the school unexpectedly unenrolled them for unpaid tuition balances, weeks before move-in. The university acknowledged Thursday it had unenrolled some students, but said families had been notified multiple times about payment deadlines. D.C. homicides have fallen by 37% over the past year, according to preliminary crime data — one of the steepest declines in the country, WTOP reports . FROM MARYLAND The Board of Public Works approved a nearly $85 million contract for a new voting system ahead of the election, Maryland Matters reports . METRO MOMENTS On Fridays, this is your space. We want to feature your photos, your questions, your “only in D.C.” moments. Email us with any of the above: metro@notus.com . SPORTS The Mystics have reached the All-Star break , and there is no longer any doubt that they are contenders, writes NOTUS’ Dave Sheinin . With the trade deadline around the corner, should this young team go all in for a playoff push? Heads up, Nats fans: NOTUS sports reporter Jesse Dougherty will be doing an AMA over at r/nationals at noon today. title: The Mystics Are Officially a Problem for the Rest of the WNBA
author: Dave Sheinin
summary: Washington closed the first half of its season with a win over the powerhouse Aces, further proving it is a legitimate contender.
content: Forward Kiki Iriafen is one of several young players that stepped up for Washington in the first half of the season. Santiago Mejia/San Francisco Chronicle via AP The transcontinental stretch of games that closed out the first half of the Washington Mystics’ season could best be described as Odyssean: six contests across 11 days, half of them against the top tier of WNBA opponents, and requiring four flights and nearly 6, air miles to navigate before they finally reached home. Along the way, the league’s youngest team nearly everything short of cyclopses, cannibals and sirens. What to make, then, of head coach Sydney Johnson revealing late Wednesday that the top item on his All-Star break bucket list — apart from family time, a little film work and some couch-side viewing of Saturday night’s WNBA All-Star Game — is to take in the new epic remake of “The Odyssey” with his wife? “I just really want to see that movie,” Johnson shrugged, with something short of Homeric grandeur. Truth is, he doesn’t need to see it. He just lived it. By the time the Mystics had slain the last beast on their own odyssey — taking down the defending champion Las Vegas Aces, -99, at home Wednesday night to complete that grueling, six-game stretch with a 4-2 record — it was the rest of the WNBA that was collectively waking up to a realization: The Mystics are officially a problem. Despite having the second-youngest roster in league history, they arrive at the All-Star break, and on the cusp of the Aug. 2 trade deadline, with a 14-12 record, far above most preseason predictions and good for the eighth and final playoff spot if the season ended today. Even more impressive is the way they closed out the first half: with back-to-back wins at Golden State and at home against Las Vegas — the No. 2 and No. 3 teams in the W, respectively — in a 72-hour stretch, with a cross-country flight in between. “They’re very long. They're athletic. They're well-coached. I’m not surprised they're sitting where they're sitting,” Aces coach Becky Hammon said of the Mystics. “They don't go away. They hang around in games, which always gives you a chance to win. There is a skillset in winning together, and even though this team is young they're proving that they're developing [the ability] to win tough games down the stretch. “Their length and their physicality and athleticism are [elite]. I don't think too many teams in this league can deal with that.” On Wednesday night, the Mystics pummeled Hammon’s Aces inside and out. Washington’s three bigs — 6-foot-3 Kiki Iriafen, 6-foot-5 Shakira Austin and 6-foot-7 Lauren Betts — combined for 50 points and 19 rebounds, more than making up for the 38 and seven they conceded to Aces legend A’ja Wilson. Meantime, guard Sonia Citron poured in 20 points (along with eight assists), with 11 of them coming in the decisive fourth quarter, when Citron, who typically plays off the ball, shifted to point guard and the Mystics stormed back from nine points down in the final four minutes. The victory over the Aces made the Mystics the only team this season with wins over all three of the league’s top teams: Minnesota, Golden State and Las Vegas. Regardless of where they finish in the standings, they have become that team no one would want to in the playoffs. Lauren Betts Mystics AP - ( , AR: 1.50) “We don’t make it a secret: We want to make the playoffs. We want to make a push,” said point guard Georgia Amoore, who scored 10 on Wednesday. “We’re not that team that other teams can relax against, or take a night off against. We’ve proven that.” The next stop for Iriafen, Citron and Austin is Chicago, where Iriafen and Citron — the first WNBA teammates in 27 years to earn All-Star berths in each of their first two seasons — will be on opposite squads for the game itself, while Austin, a notable snub in All-Star selections, will participate in Friday night’s Shooting Stars competition. The Mystics’ sooner-than-expected arrival as a playoff threat and their enviable collection of young talent — the 25-year-old Austin and 26-year-old forward Michaela Onyenwere are the only players on the roster with more than one and a half years of WNBA experience — has both given them the appearance of a nascent juggernaut and also made them an intriguing factor ahead of next month’s trade deadline. Up to now, the Mystics have been pointed decidedly and aggressively in the direction of rebuilding, hoarding draft picks and emphasizing player development. A year ago at the trade deadline, sitting on a 13-15 record, they dealt away veteran guard and three-time All-Star Brittney Sykes, then finished the season on a 3-12 skid. Might Washington take the opposite approach this summer, and perhaps spend some of its remaining draft capital and young talent on a veteran or two — in effect stopping the rebuild and turning this into a go-for-it year? Among the team’s needs: a veteran point guard (the assortment of point guards on their roster have amassed -0.2 win shares this season) and/or a deadly three-point shooter (they rank next-to-last in the league in three-point attempts, makes and shooting percentage). Among the available targets: 35-year-old veteran and seven-time All-Star Skylar Diggins, whom the Chicago Sky may be shopping . But the likelier play for the Mystics would be to stand pat at the deadline, let the season play out and make their next push this offseason via free agency and/or the draft. They already own Chicago’s first-round pick in , which is likely to be high. That means the Mystics could have their choice of a game-changing talent like USC’s JuJu Watkins, Texas’ Madison Booker or Notre Dame’s Hannah Hidalgo. The Mystics have been operating without a general manager since parting ways with Jamila Wideman in April, meaning Johnson and Michael Winger, president of basketball operations for Monumental Basketball, will be making the big calls on the Mystics’ direction and philosophy. On Wednesday, Johnson deflected a question about the team’s trade deadline strategy. “Every player on our roster has gotten better. Every single one of them. And that has allowed us as a team to get better. And we’ll lift our heads up in August and just kind of see where we are,” Johnson said. “What we talked about at the start of the season, in terms of having a young group that was eager to get better, to grow individually and as a team — so far, so good. We’re on track in terms of taking a step forward. But the [ ] journey is only a little more than halfway through.” Once they return from the All-Star break, the Mystics a gauntlet of a schedule in the first half of August, including back-to-backs against both Dallas (currently fourth in the standings) and Las Vegas (currently third). There is also another stretch of six games in 11 days featuring another pair of cross-country flights. Which means before Johnson and the Mystics can look too far down the road, he still has one Odyssey to at the cinema and another on the basketball court.

title: You Have Dining Questions. Tom Sietsema Has Answers.
author: Tom Sietsema
summary: In his NOTUS debut, our award-winning food correspondent fields questions on where to eat on the Mall, D.C.'s best sushi deal, and his go-to restaurants right now.
content: Tom Sietsema is joining NOTUS as its food correspondent. Courtesy of Deb Lindsey Photography When NOTUS reached out recently to ask me what I’d like to do, the first idea that came to mind was to host a regular Q&A with readers. During my 25 years as the food critic for The Washington Post, from which I took a buyout last summer, the most important hour of my work week was 11 a.m. Wednesdays, when I’d answer reader rants, raves and everything in between. Ask Tom was a place where I tried to help people find what they wanted, learn something new, solve a dining dilemma. The online exchange was so popular that it often trumped Trump news. The interactions also gave me an immediate sense of what readers were thinking about, which led to a number of my best-read critic’s notebooks. Besides, even after I left The Post, readers followed me with their questions. Why not create a dedicated forum for responding to them? Welcome, then, to my new advice column, Talk to Tom, where I’ll be addressing your dining questions — every Thursday. Got a gripe or concern? Something you’re curious about? Send me an email at TalkToTom@notus.com . Questions and comments may be edited for length. Why do so many American restaurants force us to eat in the dark? We are frequent travelers to Europe, where you can actually read the menu and see your food without using a flashlight. A dim interior accomplishes several things. For starters, it tends to relax people, which makes eating feel more pleasurable and may encourage lingering (say, to order more drinks, a win for the restaurant). Darkness also has a way of compressing even large rooms, creating cocoons of space, at least mentally. Dim lighting can hide flaws, too, in the decor as well as on diners. Don’t we all look better away from klieg lights? That said, a thoughtful restaurant provides sufficient illumination — and a menu with easy-to-read print — for diners to see what’s in front of them. I've long said, restaurateurs need to audition everything diners will touch or see — utensils, chairs, lights — before buying them. I’ve got family coming to D.C. Is there a restaurant on the Mall you prefer? For proximity to the museums and value, I’m partial to America’s Table Cafe inside the lower level of the National Museum of American History, which fuels between 6, and 8, visitors a week around this time of year. Leading the kitchen: executive chef Mollie Kaufmann , who previously served as the culinary operations manager for World Central Kitchen, and who offers food more personal than the crowd-size suggests. (Quick, what other local cafeteria offers shrimp and grits, flavored as if you were in the South?) A recent lunch also embraced a snappy bratwurst striped with brown mustard and topped with tangy sauerkraut; a salad bar that goes beyond the expected; and appealing side dishes to accompany the generous entrees. Fresh-tasting apple-fennel coleslaw, mustard-punched baked beans, and pickled okra outperformed a plate of slightly dry smoked chicken thighs. Nodding to the season was a fine trifle sweetened with blueberries and peaches. I get hungry just typing that. Lines tend to move fast, by the way, thanks to friendly cashiers. “You’re going to fall asleep, eating all that!” one of them teased two of us as we paid. Snare the right table, and you can enjoy your meal with the Washington Monument as a backdrop — a twofer attraction. Help settle a debate. I say it’s just as easy to open a $30 bottle of wine as a $ bottle. An oenophile in my group thinks otherwise — and says the tip should be higher on the more expensive wine. Much as I enjoy wine, which I tip on like the food it is — 20%, the industry standard — I seldom splurge on anything priced in the triple digits. Regarding dearer bottles, I turned to ace wine consultant and former restaurateur Janet Cam , who thinks an extra 10% or so gratuity should be applied to wines in the $ and up range. In those situations, she says, “expertise [is] expected.” Customers should receive proper stemware, “ideally finely made Riedel, Schott Zwiesel and Glassine,” she gives by way of example. “The thin lip of the glass affects the taste and perception of wine.” Cam says the wine should be presented and tasted before the food arrives, as “food aromas enter the glass, distorting the perception of wine.” Higher-priced wine typically involves the sommelier’s “attention, knowledge, time in sourcing the wine” and storing it properly — conditions the wine authority says “should be considered and compensated” with “cash in the hand of the sommelier.” In short, sourcing, storing and serving minor versus major wines requires different effort. Sushi seems to be on everyone’s mind in the District these days. Unfortunately, I find many non-omakase meals to be exceedingly “spendy,” as you say in Minnesota. Can you recommend a spot that doesn’t cost the fish’s weight in gold? Let me introduce you to the youthful Kiyomi from Masaaki “Uchi” Uchino , who made a splash in Washington when he helmed the top-notch Sushi Nakazawa at the back of the late Trump hotel (now the Waldorf Astoria). Since April, the chef can be found behind a handsome wooden door at L St. NW, in a small dining room set off with woven balloon lights overhead and a counter ringed with 16 seats. “Japanese style,” says Uchino, “with American feel.” Friendly, in other words. The lure: a parade of (seven) nigiri or hand rolls plus miso soup for a bargain $40. The pleasure might begin with pale pink tile fish, garnished with lime zest, on a pillow of warm rice, and continue with raw yellowtail, Spanish mackerel, -colored tuna streaked with veins of fat, and porgy splashed with lemon juice and a touch of sea salt. The last gets hit with a blow torch before Uchino places the morsel on a small slate plate in front of you. IMG_0572.jpg ( , AR: 0.75)My neighbors on a recent weekday murmured in unison as they bit into salmon smoked in hay, a technique that elevates the flavor of the fish without masking it. Even if you go the sushi route, the drill includes a hand roll. (Make mine yellowtail ignited with citrusy yuzu, please.) At present, the venue is walk-in only for lunch. Omakase, served on Friday night for $ a person, is by reservation for two seatings and includes grilled and fried dishes while featuring mostly fish from Japan, says Uchino. Kiyomi, the chef’s sister’s name, translates to “pure beauty” — an apt way to describe a deal of a meal in the city. Now that you no longer have an expense account, have your restaurant habits changed? For sure — but not necessarily for budgetary reasons. After decades of eating out, sometimes as many as 10 meals a week for work, I’m rekindling my love for cooking at home. (Meatloaf, roast chicken, composed salads, BLTs and eggs for dinner are my current jam.) While I remain curious about the restaurant scene, locally and beyond, I’m also free to eat wherever I want, not where I feel obliged to visit. There are a handful of places I return to frequently, both because they’re easy to get to (close to home) and their menus are to my taste: Bombay Club and Casa Teresa downtown, Perry’s , Reveler’s Hour and Rye Bunny in Adams Morgan, Donsak Thai Restaurant in Woodley Park, and Buck’s Fishing & Camping near the senior Politics and Prose are where you might find me most often. Finally, I’m probably drinking less than when I was out every night, too; a cocktail followed by a glass of wine. No more bottles of grape juice unless I’m with a group. My liver thanks me. Two food lovers are heading to Iceland for several days. What shouldn’t we miss? You’ll want to book in advance for the top draws, which include Dill, the first Icelandic restaurant to get a nod from Michelin; Ox , which offers the feel of a speakeasy; Moss at the Blue Lagoon, whose seasonal tasting menu focuses on New Nordic flavors and whose view embraces lava fields; and, for something different and more relaxed, Sumac Grill + Drinks . The last is a lively brasserie with a charcoal grill and twists on Middle Eastern accents. Suddenly, I’m hungry for Reykjavik again. I have a hankering for Burmese food. Point me in the right direction. Arlington — specifically Padaek , the largest of the area Thai and Laotian restaurants owned by chef Seng Luangrath . Her partner in the kitchen is Nyi Nyi Myint , a native of Yangon (formerly Rangoon) who recently several flavors from his homeland to the menu. “There aren’t a lot of Burmese restaurants” in the area, Myint says of the decision to broaden the script. Spring for the fermented tea leaf salad — a crunchy-tangy toss that includes shredded cabbage, tomatoes, nuts, lime juice and chiles — and the fish soup mohinga that’s considered Burma’s national dish. Once you start spooning into the steaming, turmeric-tinted mohinga — thick with thin rice noodles, a whole egg, shredded blue catfish, and crisp Lao squash fritters — it’s hard to stop. Fresh ginger, garlic and fish sauce weigh in with their charms, too. Myint says he has more Burmese dishes to add after vacation. September can’t come fast enough for some of his fans.

title: Five Players to Watch at Commanders Training Camp
author: Martenzie Johnson
summary: Washington opens camp next week, and these players have plenty to prove ahead of a new season.
content: Rookie wide receiver Antonio Williams will aim to cement himself as a top pass-catching option during training camp. (Nick Wass/AP Photo) Let’s get this out of the way: You’re not here to read about Jayden Daniels or Terry McLaurin or Laremy Tunsil or Sonny Styles. We all know they’re vital to the Commanders’ success this season. But there’s about 70 other guys reporting to Ashburn for training camp next week, and they could very well dictate whether Washington makes a deep playoff run like it did in or goes 5-12 like last season. Before the pads come out next week, here are five (fine, technically six) key players to watch in the home stretch of the offseason. Nick Allegretti, center The Commanders are set to return 80% of the starters on their offensive line: tackles Tunsil and Josh Conerly and guards Chris Paul and Samuel Cosmi. The only change will be at center, where Allegretti is expected to replace Tyler Biadasz, who was released back in March. Allegretti has spent most of his eight-year NFL career at guard, including five seasons with the Chiefs. But he’s played center since childhood and was a top center prospect coming out of high school, according to 247Sports. He spent time at both center and guard over four seasons at Illinois. While the offensive line has continuity on its side, it wasn’t exactly the best unit in the NFL last season: ESPN placed the group in the bottom half of the league in its run- and pass-block rankings. Allegretti started last season at guard while Cosmi recovered from injury, but he was removed from the starting unit after just two games. Allegretti has said he’s sat in on center-quarterback meetings since signing in , and he put that experience into practice by starting the last two games of the season at center. There’s reason to believe the Commanders feel optimistic about Allegretti. They signed him to a multi-year contract extension in March after letting Biadasz go, waited until the sixth round of April’s draft to take a center (Michigan State’s Matt Gulbin) and didn’t add any veteran competition in free agency. Trey Amos, defensive back They say the best ability is availability. Another popular idiom: You have to see it to believe it. Both of those apply to Amos. The second-year cornerback didn’t participate in organized team activities (OTAs) or minicamp in June after fracturing his fibula during a Week 10 loss to the Lions. Amos proved last season he’s one of, if not the best one-on-one defender in Washington. He allowed just one touchdown in coverage last season, and his six pass deflections ranked third on the team despite the fact that he appeared in just nine and a half games. He played particularly well against the Packers in Week 2. The Commanders need Amos’ speed and physicality. Last season’s pass defense was more accommodating than an AirBnB host, allowing the second-most pass plays of 40 yards or more. It’s not clear how Washington feels about Amos’ recovery, but it’s apparent the team is focused on the secondary: Earlier this month, they signed veteran Rasul Douglas to a one-year contract. Douglas started 13 games for the Dolphins last season and was one of the better lockdown defenders in football last season with 13 pass deflections and a 54% completion percentage allowed in coverage. For what it’s worth, Amos said on a Twitch stream last week that he’s healthy and ready for training camp, according to the Full Command Youtube channel . Croskey-Merritt Commanders AP - ( , AR: 1.50) Bill Croskey-Merritt, running back On paper, Croskey-Merritt had as good of a season as could be expected of a seventh-round draft pick who played one game in his final season of college ball. He finished with a team-high rushing yards and eight touchdowns. But look closer and you can see areas Croskey-Merritt will need to improve. He lacked the pass-catching skills and explosive runs that make an offense dangerous: Of players with or more rushing yards last season, he ranked last in receptions (9) and receiving yards (68) and tied for last in rushes of 20 yards or more (3). Croskey-Merritt also tied for the third-most fumbles (3) by a running back. If the second-year back, who has visibly bulked up this offseason, wants to be more of a bell cow than a member of a committee, he’ll have to prove it in these coming weeks. And that’s not me talking, that is his head coach: After minicamp, coach Dan Quinn said he wanted to see improvement from Croskey-Merritt in pass-catching and explosiveness, and foresees him splitting reps with the other backs, including free agent signee Rachaad White ( receptions, 1, receiving yards and 11 receiving touchdowns in four seasons with Tampa Bay). “I do like the competition in the group,” Quinn said. “I think we'll for sure be more than just one [running back].” Leo Chenal, linebacker Seeing as most Americans choose the Super Bowl as the one NFL game they watch each season, Chenal’s name should sound familiar. In the Chiefs’ championship wins in and , he totaled 12 tackles, two tackles for loss, a forced fumble and one quarterback hit. The linebacker, who signed a three-year deal with the Commanders this offseason, stuffed All-Pro 49ers running back Christian McCaffrey at the line of scrimmage on a third-and-2 in the fourth quarter of Super Bowl LVIII. That nose for the football is desperately needed in Washington. The Commanders missed the second-most tackles ( ) in the NFL last season, according to Pro Football Reference. Chenal’s 5.2% missed-tackle rate is the lowest among linebackers since , per Next Gen Stats . Chenal will be battling for first-string camp reps with first-round draft pick Styles and returning starter Frankie Luvu, but his ability to pursue, cover tight ends in coverage and fight through offensive linemen should go a long way towards improving a defensive unit that has struggled the past three seasons. Antonio Williams and Treylon Burks, wide receivers To paraphrase the immortal words of Rick Pitino: “ Brandon Aiyuk ain’t walking through that door.” For all the chatter about the Commanders needing another receiver ahead of training camp, it seems pretty clear they’re rolling with what they currently have. Which means someone has to line up opposite McLaurin, and it would appear Williams, a third-round pick, and Burks, a first-rounder in Tennessee, have the upper hand. During 7-on-7 and 11-on-11 drills at OTAs and minicamp, Williams and Burks got a lot of time working with quarterbacks Daniels and Marcus Mariota. Williams was primarily used out of the slot at Clemson last season, and his production didn’t exactly scream modern NFL starter (55 receptions, yards, 11.0 yards per reception). But he is versatile and slippery, often used in jet sweeps and screens that take advantage of his speed. Much like most of the rest of the receiving corps, Williams is not a deep threat, but he can feast on defenses in intermediate routes. Injuries have derailed Burks’ career, limiting him to just 35 games played in the last four years. But he’s shown big-play ability , albeit in spurts. If Williams can find gaps in coverage and Burks can stay healthy, there’s a good chance one of them will earn a starting spot by the end of camp.

title: Smithsonian Showdown
author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman
content: Anthea Hartig, director of the Smithsonian Institute's National Museum of American History, is sworn in to the House Oversight and Government Reform Delivering on Government Efficiency Subcommittee hearing titled "Rewriting American History: Examining the Smithsonian's Efforts to Reshape the Past," in Rayburn building on Tuesday, July 21, . Tom Williams/AP Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: The Smithsonian under scrutiny, Carter Barron’s (temporary) return and a fresh look at the Commanders’ stadium plans. Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region . THE LATEST Republican lawmakers grilled the director of the Smithsonian’s U.S. history museum yesterday over concerns the institution is too “woke.” The two-hour hearing was the latest installment in President Donald Trump ’s “ ongoing review ” of the Smithsonian and his continued effort to remake Washington and its cultural institutions. Representatives took aim at several exhibits, including ones on slavery, the American entertainment industry and girls going through puberty, NOTUS’ Eric Katz reports . “History is incredibly challenging and … if we tell it in its richness, we absolutely, I think, have objects that can make people uncomfortable,” director Anthea Hartig fired back. There are signs of life in Rock Creek Park, despite the cultural climate. Carter Barron Amphitheater, the park’s 76-year-old outdoor venue that has been shuttered and in disrepair for a , will host a three-night concert series in August featuring jazz, gospel and go-go. But this isn’t a permanent reopening. Carter Barron still needs significant work, and a local effort to upgrade the iconic site is ongoing. FROM THE DISTRICT Trump’s plans to renovate the golf links at East Potomac Park could affect the park’s other public spaces, worrying everyone from cyclists to fishers, NOTUS’ Shamira Muhammad reports . Metro wants automated doors on Red Line platforms to be installed as part of a $ million modernization project, ABC7 reports . D.C. firefighters will get higher wages after their union reached a new collective bargaining agreement with the District yesterday, following nearly two years of contentious negotiations. They’ll receive a 3.5% increase next fiscal year and retroactive 2% and 3.5% increases for the and fiscal years, too. “Like everybody else, we're all struggling with higher utility bills, elevated grocery prices, you name it,” the union’s president, David Hoagland, told NOTUS. “It's a much-needed increase at a time when affordability is [at] the top of everybody's mind.” FROM VIRGINIA A new Virginia law extending the grace period for paying rent to 14 days is just one of the tenant protection policies being rolled out by the state, the Virginia Mercury reports . FROM MARYLAND Marylanders are fighting back against data centers and getting results, WAMU reports . Montgomery and Prince George’s counties have paused the development of new data centers, and one state senator told WAMU they may propose a statewide moratorium this summer. PLAN YOUR WEEKEND For the Swiftie: Rock the Dock: A Taylor Swift tribute at The Wharf, Friday. For the Potterhead: Harry Potter Day at Nationals Park, Saturday. For the history buff: District Vibes at Martin Luther King Jr. Memorial Library, ongoing. For more info on this weekend’s events, read our weekly culture calendar here . SPORTS Commanders stadium updated rendering ( , AR: 1.90) Check out this fresh rendering of the new Commanders stadium. Buried in a recent presentation to the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts is one of the first comprehensive views of what the new stadium will look like for most fans approaching from the west, including what’s being called Festival Plaza and the residential and retail development that will frame one side of it. There’s lots more to dig through here . Congratulate AJ Dybantsa on a new position. More young athletes are opting for LinkedIn as their social media of choice, The Banner reports , using the buttoned-up, business-centric platform as a way to connect with fans without sharing too much. The Wizards rookie has gotten in on the trend, posting last month that he was starting a new full-time role as “Professional Basketball Player.” What to Watch Today MLB: Nationals at Rockies, 3:10 p.m. ( MLB.TV ) WNBA: Mystics vs. Aces, 7:30 p.m. ( Monumental ) Thank you for reading! If you liked this newsletter, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com . The newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Michael Errigo and Nikie Johnson. Photo from the U.S. Commission of Fine Arts. One last thing: that three-bedroom house with a pool we showed you yesterday is located in Virginia, and 36% of you guessed that right. The most common guess was Maryland.

title: From Cycling to Fishing, Concerns About East Potomac’s Future Go Beyond Golf
author: Shamira Muhammad
summary: President Donald Trump’s plan to renovate the island park’s golf course has created an uncertain future for the area’s other public spaces.
content: Will Edwards and his family are regulars at East Potomac Park. (Shamira Muhammad/NOTUS) Will Edwards, born and raised in southwest D.C., has been coming to East Potomac Park his entire life. On a warm Monday evening, he and his family set up camp near Hains Point, the island park’s southern tip. They had a portable table, some chairs and some toys for Edwards’ son. A dinner of chicken and biscuits was spread out in front of them. Fishing rods hung on the fence. “This has been a landmark for years,” Edwards said. “Years.” Before he was married, Edwards said he used to come down here looking to meet women at social events. His wife, Carla, has different but also fond memories: as a child, she used to crawl on The Awakening, a large sculpture that was once located at Hains Point but has since moved to Maryland. The lines from Edwards’ rods were being gently tugged by the water as he discussed the many types of fish he hoped to catch. “Catfish, maybe a cod. Alligator gar,” he said. Not far from the family sat a discarded container of chicken gizzards, popular bait for blue crabs. To Carla, the park creates a sense of community. “Most people see you fishing, they offer their bait,” she said. But the future of these Edwards family trips to East Potomac is uncertain. The park has served as a political football in the months since President Donald Trump announced his intention to renovate the golf links at its center — an extensive project that would likely impact the entire island. Much of the discussion in the months since has been centered on golf and golfers, but the park has a long history of recreation beyond the links. East Potomac also features tennis courts, a playground and abundant green space. Hains Point is a popular destination for picnics and weekend gatherings. In nice weather, the wide road that encircles the park is often filled with runners and bicyclists. Hains Point recreation family ( , AR: 1.50) Early renderings of Trump’s plan seemed to spare Hains Point and other adjoining areas. But recently, Trump has been seen with new blueprints that suggest otherwise, creating a panic regarding the future of the park. On Saturday, the Washington Area Bicyclist Association hosted a rally called “Hains Point Hoopla” to raise awareness about the public amenities that could be at stake. Trump has said he would like construction to begin in September, but his plan is certain to red tape. In the meantime, the park continues to serve its regulars. On Monday night, plane after plane landed at Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport, located directly across the water from the Edwards family. Will said any large-scale changes to the park would be “devastating.” “This is somewhere people need to come, just to relax, despite a day,” he said. “Anybody could have a bad day, but they come here, they sit in the car, you know. Just relax.” Earlier this month, four senators sent a letter to the Department of the Interior and the National Park Service seeking clarification on final plans for the park. The agencies are defendants in an ongoing lawsuit brought by the D.C. Preservation League and local residents, aimed at halting any proposed overhaul. Neither the National Park Service or the Department of the Interior could be reached for comment. This past winter, the Trump administration terminated a 50-year lease with the National Links Trust, the nonprofit tasked with managing the course. The Department of the Interior has since allowed the trust to operate the course until a “historic renovation” begins. Torrence, who declined to give his last name because of privacy concerns, is also a District native who’s been coming to the park most of his life. Although he wasn’t aware of the proposed changes to the golf course, he has sensed more tension in the area. “I've never had anybody ask for a fishing license down here, but now all of a sudden you have to have a fishing license, and they try to give you a citation or a ticket,” he told NOTUS. “This place was very peaceful at one point.” Torrence said he comes to the park to “breathe life” and escape the reality of his densely populated city. “We live in an inner city surrounded by concrete,” he said. “It's not too much wildlife out here, outdoors things you can do. So this is one of the places that a lot of inner city people come to just release.” Many regulars admit that the park needs upgrades. Some bathrooms are out and there is overgrowth on the waterfront. The park is not perfect, but it is where they choose to spend their time. “If anything, give it a facelift,” Torrence said. “Pick up some of these broken-down trees and stuff around there. Invest money into this place.”

title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend (July 24)
author: Torrie Herrington, Rebecca Ritzel
summary: A Taylor Swift tribute band, Harry Potter Day at Nats Park, and performances across the DMV.
content: Brayden Bambino (Pippin) with Hank von Kolnitz, Calvin L’mont Cooper, and Ben Bogen in Pippin at Signature Theatre. Daniel Rader Thursday ¡Puro Ritmo! The Musical Journey of Salsa at the American History Museum Constitution Ave. NW, D.C., 10:30 a.m., free Located in the Molina Family Latino Gallery. Explore the rhythm, history and energy of salsa music through a guided tour. This is a bilingual multimedia exhibition presented by the Smithsonian’s National Museum of the American Latino. Summer Culture Hub: Textile Techniques at Montpelier Historic Site and Museum Muirkirk Road, Laurel, MD, 10 a.m. to 4 p.m., free. Through Sunday, July 26. Laurel’s Georgian plantation house hosts a weekend of family-friendly, hands-on crafting workshops. Learn about historic textile arts that would have been practiced by both enslaved artisans and wealthy landowners at this event run by the Maryland National-Capital Park and Planning Commission. Girl Scouts block party at Franklin Park I St. NW, D.C., 6:30 p.m., free Enjoy sweet treats and dance the night away to Be'la Dona, an all-women group performing live go-go music. There will also be food vendors, paintings, glitter tattoos, nail art and other interactive activities for all ages. More to explore: Analog Dinner Nights: Mahjong! at Flor Coffee + Books Board Game Speed Dating at Dacha Beer Garden (Shaw) Friday Rock the Dock: A Taylor Swift tribute at The Wharf Wharf St. SW, D.C., 7 p.m., free Every Friday night at the Transit Pier, enjoy free live music next to the water. This Friday, The Fearless Eras, a Taylor Swift tribute band, will be playing all the hits. All ages are welcome, as are dogs on leashes, and enjoying food from the Wharf’s many restaurants is encouraged. Pianist Joyce Yang with the Baltimore Symphony at the Music Center at Strathmore Tuckerman Lane, North Bethesda, MD, 7:30 p.m., $35 to $ (second show Saturday) In early 1800s Italy, rumor had it that violinist Niccolò Paganini sold his soul to the devil in exchange for virtuosic talents. A century later, Russian composer Sergei Rachmaninoff arranged one of Paginini’s signature motifs into his fiendishly difficult “Rhapsody on a Theme of Paganini.” Pianist Joyce Yang takes the devil down to Strathmore, with Lidiya Yankovskaya in the conductor’s seat. Candlelight: ’90s Hip-Hop on Strings at National City Christian Church 5 Thomas Circle NW, 6:45 p.m., $63.50 to $ Prefer your Snoop Dogg played by a string quartet? Fever, the national event presenter that curates romantic musical evenings outside of traditional concert halls, has arranged a memory-lane playlist including Lauryn Hill, the Notorious B.I.G. and the Wu Tang Clan, to be performed by the Listeso String Quartet. Rooted in Resistance dinner at the Festival Center Columbia Road NW, D.C., 7 p.m., $50 to $ Enjoy Palestinian food, art and performance at the dinner that kicks off the Rooted in Resistance: Here Eternally festival weekend, organized by the Museum of the Palestinian People. Alongside dinner, guests can experience live music, spoken word, dance, art and a moderated panel, with proceeds supporting the museum. More to explore: Jazz in the Garden at the National Gallery of Art Sculpture Garden D.C’s Best comedy showcase at Hotbed Saturday Poet Life Fest at Gateway DC pavilion Martin Luther King Jr. Ave. SE, D.C., Noon, free Part of a weeklong lineup of events, Poet Life Fest is a family-friendly, daylong experience for attendees to enjoy performances of poetry and music, plus vendors, food trucks and community. Harry Potter Day at Nationals Park South Capitol St. SE, D.C., 4:05 p.m. As the Washington Nationals play the Arizona Diamondbacks, Nationals Park will transform into Hogwarts for Harry Potter Day. There will be a themed photo booth, painters, balloon artists, caricaturists and a potion-making station. “Pippin” at Signature Theatre Campbell Ave., Arlington, VA, 8 p.m. Signature Theatre will stage its final showings of “Pippin,” a coming-of-age musical with music and lyrics by Stephen Schwartz. A traveling troupe of performers takes the audience through the story of Pippin, the restless heir of Charlemagne, on his quest for purpose. Changed American Culture.” The exhibit focuses on the contributions of D.C. to America, from the football hurdle to the modern blood bank.
