title: Suspicion and Doubt at the National Civics Contest
author: Sam Fortier
summary: America’s finest young scholars competed to mark their country's birthday. It led to a disputed finish in the age of mistrust.
content: Aangad Singh, 15, competes in the Presidential Award competition. Jalani Morgan for NOTUS The morning after the competition, Aangad Singh's family was trying to figure out what went wrong. They were walking through the National Museum of Natural History, going over answers, doing the math. “It doesn’t make sense,” said his mother, Ramandeep. Ramandeep was good at numbers. But she couldn’t make them explain how her 15-year-old son had missed the top three in the Presidential Award competition, the civics contest for high schoolers that President Donald Trump’s party planners had created to celebrate America’s 250th birthday. She had watched the first round, when the field was whittled from 20 to eight, and the second round, when it went from eight to three. There was celebrity host Mario Lopez, an exclusive broadcast deal with CBS and a Kennedy Center stage that mixed game show spectacle with civic pageantry. The only thing missing was a scoreboard. She told herself not to complain. She didn’t want to be that mom, a sore loser whose kid could never fail. On their way out, though, other parents kept stopping them. “Shocked,” said more than one. Later, a boy stopped her and said a group of contestants had kept score themselves. “We thought he won,” the boy said. She approached an official from the Department of Education, which had helped run the contest, and asked for the final scores. “Proprietary,” the official said. In the museum, Ramandeep furrowed her brow. “How did they count the numbers?” she said. “That’s something we need to understand.” “We can only find out when they telecast it,” said her husband, Bhalindar. Ramandeep pursed her lips. The broadcast was three weeks away. -S3410642- - ©Doug Coulter (1).jpg ( , AR: 1.78)It wasn’t like them to feel skeptical. She and Bhalindar were Indian immigrants whose trust in the American system had led to degrees, careers and citizenship. They bought a four-bedroom Colonial in a quiet Connecticut city and sent their kids to public school. They passed their faith in the United States down to Aangad, who won awards for his speeches about the country’s founding ideals. But now they, like so many others, were wondering whether the game was rigged. It was a reluctant half-step into the age of suspicion. The U.S. was just one of many democratic nations riding the same wave of paranoia, with polls showing trust in major institutions at or near all-time lows. In America, the president questioned whether the elections were free and fair as citizens sank deeper into the embrace of their tribes. The world’s leading deepfake expert told The New York Times that he no longer trusted his own eyes, that our whole visual system was on the verge of collapse. And just as the Singhs were walking the halls of the museum, senators and Trump judicial appointees on Capitol Hill were sparring over the results of a presidential election that happened six years ago. Aangad’s parents didn’t want to accuse anyone of fixing the competition. But they felt compelled to ask questions because their son never would. When his mother had dropped him off for his first day of kindergarten, he did not cry, even though she could tell he wanted to. For years the story served as a tidy summation of her son, a rule follower who hid his emotions, an intellectual who didn’t mind having more books than friends. But at some point she had figured out how to tell he was upset: He would take little sips of water over and over again. Shortly after noon, the Singhs left the museum and went to a café. When Aangad opened the door, he ran into the blond girl from Wyoming, Miriam Washut, who he was pretty sure had won the whole thing. She must be headed to the White House for the special tour of the Oval Office, he thought. Her father, wearing a black cowboy hat, stuck out his hand. “You did extremely well,” he said. “Thank you,” Aangad said. P20260610MR- (1) copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.78)Aangad turned to Miriam, whose eyes dropped to the floor. Her voice pitched up. She waved her hands at her sides. “That was insane,” she said. “You clearly knew everything.” Aangad nodded, blank, and Miriam’s family went on their way. Aangad walked over to his parents’ table. “What did she say?” his father asked. “That I should have won,” Aangad said. No one said anything for a long time. Aangad took a small sip of water. * * * Three weeks later, Aangad’s family took positions in the living room. His dad was on one couch, laptop open to a spreadsheet titled “1776_Broadcast_Audit.” His mother was on the edge of the other couch, drumming her right foot like a kick pedal. Aangad was between them, lying on a recliner with his feet up, talking quietly to his little sister. On the side table was a black metal water bottle. He had just filled it. They were at his uncle’s house in suburban Toronto, where they vacationed every year. Ramandeep and her brother had grown up on a farm in India. They didn't go back much; they liked how little their kids knew about homesteading. Now, the siblings were competing to see who could own the biggest house in North America, and her brother, a hardware engineer, was winning. Ramandeep had done everything to help her kids get ahead, too, including giving them names that started with two As in part so they'd always be first in alphabetical lists at school. SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM017 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM055 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)“It began online with the Impossible Civics Test,” Mario Lopez said on TV, and everyone in the room stopped talking. CBS didn’t show the round of 20. And it cut the opening speech from Education Secretary Linda McMahon. “There is hope for the next 50 years that the flame of liberty still burns bright in the next generation,” she had said. "The great American story is still being written by you.” They’d hoped the broadcast would include a live scoreboard, so they could see where things went wrong. But the first segment sped by without one. “Why aren’t they showing scores?” his uncle asked. Then the second segment sped by too. “What’s the score?” Aangad said, looking at his dad. “I don’t know,” his dad said. The show was going too fast and the commentary in the living room was too loud for him to keep up. Aangad knew he’d been behind at this point. He’d won the buzzer race only once in eight questions. But the final two segments were far more valuable, and he knew he’d done well. On TV, Mario Lopez introduced the third segment: Each contestant would stand alone at the lectern to answer a multipart question about the U.S. Constitution. Then each of the five judges would grade it. SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM086 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)Aangad watched the contestants. The boy from Michigan got a full 20 points. The girl from Washington did too. So did the girl from Wyoming. “According to Article 3 of the U.S. Constitution, in which cases do the federal courts have jurisdiction?” the proctor said to Aangad on TV. “List at least four for full credit.” As he answered, little summary boxes popped up on screen. “Maritime jurisdiction.” Green. “Parties of state and citizens of another state.” Red. “What?” Aangad said on the couch, his voice sharp. He got two more green boxes, then another red: “Case with state and foreign nation.” “What?” he said again. He handed his dad his phone. He’d pulled up the Constitution and highlighted a paragraph with the phrases “between a State and Citizens of another State” and “between a State, or the Citizens thereof, and foreign States, Citizens or Subjects.” “Read this, read this, read this, read this right now,” Aangad said. His dad read it. “It’s within the Constitution,” he said. SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM038 copy.jpg ( , AR: 2.02)At the end of the segment, a scoreboard flashed onscreen. Michigan was first with 23 points. Aangad was sixth with 16. He took a sip from his water bottle. “They just made this whole thing for show,” his uncle said. “They know who they want to win.” The final challenge was a lightning round. Each contestant had 30 seconds to answer as many questions as possible, and each correct answer was worth two points. Michigan got 10 right. Washington, 10. Wyoming, 10. Then Aangad came to the stage. The first question flashed on the monitor: “Which amendment ended slavery?” Aangad answered. Incorrect. “Thirteenth!” Aangad cried on the couch. “I said Thirteenth!” After that, TV Aangad started flying. All the nights he and his dad had practiced the lightning round were paying off. He processed questions nearly instantly and answered almost without thinking. The screen said +2, +2, +2. SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM097 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)Aangad got one more wrong. But watching from the couch, he didn’t protest. He saw now the judges had wanted a more technical answer. In the end, the judges marked 12 answers correct. Aangad concluded they must have thought he pronounced thirteenth like fourteenth. “I say that TH irteenth like an ‘F’ sound.” Later, he’d feel validated when he realized the auto-generated subtitles said “thirteenth.” Before Mario Lopez revealed the top three, he walked around the stage and interviewed every contestant. Aangad gave a polished answer about being proud to share his knowledge of the nation’s founding principles. The girl from Washington was brought to tears again. A boy from Arizona said winning would mean everything: “I’ve always wanted to meet the man, the myth, the legend — Donald Trump!” After the finalists were announced, Aangad watched Michigan, Washington and Wyoming take center stage. On TV, he calmly applauded. On the couch, he picked up his water bottle and took a big gulp. SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM068 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50) * * * Aangad’s family watched the rest of the program in relative quiet. Miriam from Wyoming won, just as Aangad had suspected, and then the finalists took a trip to the White House. They stood by the Resolute Desk, a snapshot of Trump’s education agenda. Miriam was homeschooled. The boy from Michigan attended a private Catholic school. The girl from Washington, who went to public school, had told CNN that she supported Trump and believed the most important thing was “everyone walking away from the competition knowing this is the greatest country of the world.” In the Oval Office, she told the president she wanted to go to Hillsdale College. “Hillsdale?” Aangad’s father said. “Republican college,” Aangad reminded him. They’d been on campus in Michigan last month for the American Legion’s National Oratorical Contest. The school had donated $10 million to the president’s Freedom committee and helped develop its history programs. “I can give you a recommendation,” the president said to the girl. “I think we should get you in.” SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM104 (1) copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.00)The finalists left with two commemorative coins, one of which said “THE FINAL MISSION,” a reference to the education secretary’s promise to “sunset a 46-year-old, $3 trillion failed federal education bureaucracy in Washington, D.C.” Then the broadcast ended. “You could have been there,” Aangad’s father said. Everyone let his words hang in the air. * * * Over a late dinner of curry chicken, two factions began to form. Aangad and his father thought the judges must just be incompetent or mistaken. Aangad’s mother and uncle suspected a conspiracy: Someone had not wanted the brown kid in the turban to represent the youth of America in the Oval Office. His uncle advised them to go directly to the Education Department. “The whole point is to initiate the investigation,” he said. “They may have some kind of intention that these people shouldn’t be there,” his mother said. “You don’t know that,” Aangad replied. “You’re just assuming.” Aangad spooned out more chicken and rice. “I personally think that they just had faulty sources,” he said. Discussion turned to the five judges. They were all teachers from across the country who were past recipients of the prestigious James Madison Memorial Fellowship to study the Constitution. At least three of them must have mistakenly graded the constitutional answers as incorrect, Aangad said, and it seemed likely to him that they hadn’t memorized Article 3 as well as he had. Or maybe his answers didn’t match the phrasing on their rubrics. “That shows ineptness,” he said. After tiramisu, Ramandeep made an impassioned case for justice. She didn’t care about the share of $ , in scholarship money, she said. She wanted recognition for Aangad’s hard work. And if the system really was biased, they had to fight on behalf of every kid who could be hurt by it. SINGH_FAMILY_NOTUS_JM107 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)“But we don’t know if it’s systemic,” Bhalindar replied. He defended trusting the system, trusting the nation’s founding documents, which he had devoted hours to helping their son study. A few bad judges don’t undermine an entire system. Aangad’s uncle had gone to bed. Aangad was on the couch, eyes closed. If they made a strong case, Bhalindar said, maybe the Education Department would admit its mistake. Ramandeep doubted they’d even get a response. She was equally pessimistic that they could get anywhere by filing a lawsuit. “We will not be able to afford to fight against the system.” On that point, Bhalindar had to agree. The best strategy, Ramandeep said, was media attention. They could present their findings and let the public decide. "That's your power," she said, turning to me. This was uncomfortable. Weeks earlier, as I looked for a way to write about America’s 250th, the Education Department had recommended I reach out to the Singhs. I then followed Aangad through the competition, not knowing if he would even advance. Now, their predicament felt like a window into something bigger: If the government or the courts couldn’t bring them justice, then maybe, they thought, the media could. All I could do was write what happened. But the Fourth Estate was another institution at low ebbs in trust and influence, and Bhalindar knew it. He doubted the government would bow to media pressure. “At least our story is in front of the public,” Ramandeep said. “That’s our closure.” “‘Closure’ is the right word,” Bhalindar said, and just before midnight, all out of words, he reassured his wife that they would figure this out together. She gave him a tired smile and went upstairs. Bhalindar sat on the couch for a while and looked at the dark TV. * * * The only way to know whether the system was fair was to test it. So, back home in Connecticut, Bhalindar used a chatbot to find lawyers with experience in federal education, federal agencies and administrative law. “Dear Counsel,” he wrote to them, “I am seeking a confidential initial consultation regarding a potential dispute.” He attached a packet of evidence that included their calculation of the final scores. Michigan, 43. Wyoming, 42. Washington, 41. Aangad, 40. If either of Aangad’s “incorrect” answers had been scored correctly, his father argued, he would’ve finished in the top three. “I am looking for counsel who can objectively evaluate the facts, advise on preservation of evidence and procedure, and determine whether there is a viable legal or administrative path forward,” Bhalindar wrote. Aangad moved on. He followed the U.S. in the World Cup and enjoyed fireworks on the Fourth of July. He didn’t see Miriam, the girl from Wyoming, tell her local newspaper that she was surprised by who made the top three. He didn’t see the Education Department use Miriam’s homeschooling as a cudgel in the culture war. His dad would email the Department of Education to ask for a review, and then ask again, and hear nothing back. His belief in the system would remain steadfast, though he’d wish someone would acknowledge his requests. The Education Department would tell NOTUS that the competition questions were “developed, judged, and scored independently by the James Madison Memorial Fellowship Foundation.” The foundation would not respond to a detailed list of questions. Meanwhile, Aangad focused on the future. He made videos about public speaking and wrote a speech about Sikhism and looked into the U.S. Senate Youth Program. He geared up for junior year and tried to figure out what to study in college. Law, maybe? Anything but medicine, for sure; blood made him queasy. But first, he would accept an award from the Connecticut American Legion. His winning speech had focused on the dangers of civic ignorance. As long as people have the power to make choices, he said, democracies are a series of infinite crossroads. The Constitution, the Bill of Rights, the Federalist Papers — they embody these crossroads. And on the nation's 250th anniversary, Aangad urged his fellow Americans to choose to learn their history before a tyrant defined their rights for them. He stood in a suit at a lectern at the front of a ballroom. The audience was mostly old, white men, but the traditional American Legion caps they wore were shaped like Aangad’s red turban. 20260517_Connecticut_Aangad Singh_JAB3324 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)Aangad told the crowd his favorite article in the Constitution was Article 3, Section 3, which in three sentences established a high bar for what could be considered treason against the United States. “It truly is extraordinary how our founders had incredible foresight, and the various methods to which our Constitution attempts to integrate its people into government,” he said. The people applauded. Aangad stepped back and nodded. He hadn’t brought any water with him. He didn’t need it now.

title: Smithsonian Director Defends U.S. History Museum Against Republican Attacks
author: Eric Katz
summary: Lawmakers say the museum should not focus on the negatives of American history.
content: Anthea Hartig, Director of the National Museum of American History, rebutted Republicans' accusations that the Smithsonian Institution is an “ideological” political organization. Jacquelyn Martin/AP “History is incredibly challenging,” the director of the Smithsonian Institution’s National Museum of American History testified in the House, rebutting the Republican-led effort to reshape what the nation’s government-sponsored museums say about America. For two hours Tuesday, Anthea Hartig a hostile panel of Republican lawmakers who cast the Smithsonian Institution as an “ideological” political organization and aired what they saw as perceived slights against the founding fathers, cultural icons and conservative ideas contained in the museum’s galleries. Hartig pushed back, saying the museum "tries to reflect the richness of our history" without advancing any political agenda. “If we tell it in its richness, we absolutely, I think, have objects that can make people uncomfortable,” Hartig said. She continued, “It’s not for me to determine what’s problematic, it’s for me to determine what’s accurate.” Republicans during the hearing largely focused on specific exhibits and merchandise within the museum they found controversial, including a display centered on the U.S. entertainment industry and another on girls going through puberty. They grew increasingly frustrated throughout the hearing after accusing Hartig of deflecting from their most pointed questions. “You have pictures of bondage,” Rep. Tim Burchett (R-Tennessee), who chaired Tuesday’s Delivering on Government Efficiency subcommittee hearing, said before a poster board displaying some items and photographs featured in the museum. “You have some overtly sexual things up there. You have transgender folks, I assume that’s what they are.” Rep. Nancy Mace, (R-South Carolina), focused her questions more explicitly. “My staff tells me this little trinket around the penis, this is BDSM in a setting where children are walking through,” she said. “That's disgusting. Like, what kind of message are you trying to send to kids with BDSM imagery?” Hartig said the puberty exhibit was not designed for children and contained a warning about its contents. After the hearing, Burchett told NOTUS that Congress should withhold funds from the Smithsonian but speculated leadership is not “going to do a dadgum thing.” He he would talk to the Smithsonian Board of Regents, composed of Vice President JD Vance, lawmakers from both parties and others, to voice his concerns. Shortly after taking office last year, President Donald Trump signed an executive order aimed at “restoring truth and sanity to American history” that prohibited Smithsonian exhibits that "divide Americans based on race.” In subsequent letters to the institution, the White House requested all descriptions and plans for current and upcoming exhibits to ensure compliance with new policies. While the agency is only partially government funded, Office of Management and Budget Director Russ Vought noted he could withhold funds if the Smithsonian did not comply with Trump’s order and document production requests. On July 4, the White House issued a report finding the American history museum strayed from its mission and has become a “political instrument to divide, dispirit, and discourage our citizens.” It accused the museum of demonstrating activism toward “illegal aliens,” transgender individuals and against white Americans. The Trump administration has also directed the National Park Service to remove signage and displays it deemed as promoting diversity, equity and inclusion, though those efforts have been held up in ongoing legal disputes. Hartig, who is set to testify again on Wednesday before the House Administration Committee, rejected the White House’s findings, arguing they contained several inaccuracies. She said she takes the White House’s concerns seriously, but noted the report erroneously suggested that several pieces of U.S. history were not on display, including passages from the Declaration of Independence, a uniform and writing desk belonging to George Washington and celebrations of the country’s 250th anniversary. “We unwaveringly attest that it does not fairly or accurately characterize the full body of work at the museum,” Hartig said. “There is always room for improvement, but I also know the beauty and the inspiration and the expertise that lies in our collections, our exhibits and our programming.” David Blight, a history professor at Yale University who also testified at the hearing, similarly castigated the White House for its report. “The recent report by the White House Domestic Policy Council is nothing less than a declaration of political war on the historian's profession, as well as on the freedom and curiosity of anyone who reads,” Blight said. “In other words, President Trump has declared war on free minds and free education.” Republicans, meanwhile, repeatedly criticized the museum for its exhibits on slavery, saying it should focus on efforts to abolish the practice rather than its horrors. Democrats chided Republicans for holding the hearing, saying they were looking to erase key parts of U.S. history. Rep. Jasmine Crockett (D-Texas) called it a “white pride rally disguised as a congressional hearing.” Other Democrats questioned the majority’s intentions. “I think what’s actually happening is not that you don't want ideology in the museum,” said Rep. Suhas Subramanyam (D-Virginia). “You want your ideology in the museum.”

title: What $1 Million Gets You in D.C., Maryland and Virginia (With a Pool!)
author: Rebecca Ritzel
summary: Our weekly column compares home listings across the metro area.
content: Courtesy of Garland Gay It’s summer, D.C. is steamier than a crab pot, and even casual Zillow browsers might be thinking: If only I could step straight out my door and into a pool. For NOTUS’ inaugural D/M/V real estate column, we found listings in the District, Maryland and Virginia that, for a million dollars, will make that dream a backyard reality. One caveat: Getting a pool of your own in the District isn’t easy for a cool million. (Although, for $15 million, this seven-bedroom compound in Georgetown comes with a courtyard pool.) So, we found what we think is the closest thing. Here are three homes we found priced at a million dollars and ideal for anyone prioritizing pool access as they house-hunt. (Which one would you choose? Or, have a comparison you’d like to see in an upcoming column? Let us know at metro@notus.com.) D.C. The listing: Sutton Place NW, Unit D The price: $ , Untitled The specifics: A two-bedroom, two-story, three-bathroom townhome with a private courtyard. Built in but recently renovated with fresh paint and white trim throughout. The pool: Shared between just 42 homes, the Sutton Place pool is perfect for splashing, lap-swimming or relaxing. Be sure to budget for $ a month in condo fees. Sell us on it: “Private community pools are a rarity in Northwest, D.C., especially for homes around the $1 million price point,” said Northgate real estate agent Ilse Padron, who also noted the location is “just minutes from Cathedral Commons, Georgetown, downtown D.C. and some of the city's top public and private schools.” Maryland The listing: Putters Ct, Upper Marlboro, Md. The price: $1, , Untitled The specifics: The former third home for a family of jet-setters, this property functions like a year-round resort, with an outdoor pool to enjoy in the summer. Prefer the après-ski lifestyle? You’ll enjoy the patio jacuzzi, indoor sauna and multiple fireplaces. The walk-out finished basement currently houses a gym, perfect for a pre-swim workout. There’s no HOA fees, but the Marlton Golf Club is just on the other side of the woods for anyone who wants to hit the greens. (Hence the road name, Putter’s Court.) The pool: Surrounded by a wrought-iron fence, and with woods rimming the nearly four-acre lot, the pool feels extra private. There’s a lengthy shelf perfect for splashing toddlers, and on the opposite side, built-in bar stools for adult swim. Sell us on it: “I can’t believe this home is still on the market,” said broker Tina Marie Marshall, adding: “The owners kept it immaculate. We barely had to stage it, this is how they lived.” Virginia The listing: Annandale Road, Falls Church, Va. The price: $1, , Untitled The specifics: Who needs a large house when you have a pool house? This modest, three-bedroom, brick Cape Cod is all business in the front yard and party in the back. A stone patio connects the main house with a pool house, creating additional year-round space for noisy kids or a quiet work-from-home office, depending on your family’s needs. The pool: Surrounded by willow trees and other lush landscaping, this in-ground pool has a new companion salt-water spa in . Sell us on it: “You're not just buying a house; you're buying an excuse to cancel your vacation plans,” said Compass listing agent Ana Maria Menendez. “You're going to be … wondering why you ever paid resort prices when your own backyard feels better.”

title: What $1 Million Gets You in D.C., Maryland and Virginia (With a Pool!)
author: Rebecca Ritzel
summary: Our weekly column compares home listings across the metro area.
content: Garland Gay It’s summer, D.C. is steamier than a crab pot, and even casual Zillow browsers might be thinking: If only I could step straight out my door and into a pool. For NOTUS’ inaugural DMV real estate column, we found listings in the District, Maryland and Virginia that, for a million dollars, will make that dream a backyard reality. One caveat: Getting a pool of your own in the District isn’t easy for a cool million. (Although, for $15 million, this seven-bedroom compound in Georgetown comes with a courtyard pool.) So, we found what we think is the closest thing. Here are three homes we found priced at a million dollars and ideal for anyone prioritizing pool access as they house-hunt. (Which one would you choose? Or, have a comparison you’d like to see in an upcoming column? Let us know at metro@notus.com.) D.C. The listing: Sutton Place NW, Unit D The price: $ , Untitled The specifics: A two-bedroom, two-story, three-bathroom townhome with a private courtyard. Built in but recently renovated with fresh paint and white trim throughout. The pool: Shared between just 42 homes, the Sutton Place pool is perfect for splashing, lap-swimming or relaxing. Be sure to budget for $ a month in condo fees. Sell us on it: “Private community pools are a rarity in Northwest, D.C., especially for homes around the $1 million price point,” said Northgate real estate agent Ilse Padron, who also noted the location is “just minutes from Cathedral Commons, Georgetown, downtown D.C. and some of the city's top public and private schools.” Maryland The listing: Putters Ct, Upper Marlboro, Md. The price: $1, , Untitled The specifics: The former third home for a family of jet-setters, this property functions like a year-round resort, with an outdoor pool to enjoy in the summer. Prefer the après-ski lifestyle? You’ll enjoy the patio jacuzzi, indoor sauna and multiple fireplaces. The walk-out finished basement currently houses a gym, perfect for a pre-swim workout. There’s no HOA fees, but the Marlton Golf Club is just on the other side of the woods for anyone who wants to hit the greens. (Hence the road name, Putter’s Court.) The pool: Surrounded by a wrought-iron fence, and with woods rimming the nearly four-acre lot, the pool feels extra private. There’s a lengthy shelf perfect for splashing toddlers, and on the opposite side, built-in bar stools for adult swim. Sell us on it: “I can’t believe this home is still on the market,” said broker Tina Marie Marshall, adding: “The owners kept it immaculate. We barely had to stage it, this is how they lived.” Virginia The listing: Annandale Road, Falls Church, Va. The price: $1, , Untitled The specifics: Who needs a large house when you have a pool house? This modest, three-bedroom, brick Cape Cod is all business in the front yard and party in the back. A stone patio connects the main house with a pool house, creating additional year-round space for noisy kids or a quiet work-from-home office, depending on your family’s needs. The pool: Surrounded by willow trees and other lush landscaping, this in-ground pool has a new companion salt-water spa in . Sell us on it: “You're not just buying a house; you're buying an excuse to cancel your vacation plans,” said Compass listing agent Ana Maria Menendez. “You're going to be … wondering why you ever paid resort prices when your own backyard feels better.” Sign up for the NOTUS Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region .

title: Welcome to NOTUS Metro
author: Martin Austermuhle, Zara Norman
content: A view of the U.S. Capitol building in Washington DC. (Mark Alfred/NOTUS) Mark Alfred/NOTUS Good morning, D.C. In today’s newsletter: A welcome, a scathing audit, free buses (maybe) and the AJ Dybantsa hype train. HELLO! Welcome to NOTUS’ daily newsletter focused on all things D.C. We’re building Washington’s next great newsroom, and over the past two months, we’ve formed a team of local reporters to cover news, sports, food and all the quirks and curiosities that make our region tick. Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman will keep you in the know and set the tone for your day. We’d love to hear from you! Send us an email or ping us on social media — let us know what you’re interested in, what you’d like to see us cover and what we might be missing. THE LATEST Add a scathing audit to the mountain of problems plaguing D.C.’s housing authority, which has also struggled to address poor housing conditions, leadership turnover and a recent cyberattack . Auditors from the D.C. inspector general’s office, who released their findings last week, couldn't verify how much money the agency had, or where it was, to the tune of hundreds of millions of dollars, according to NOTUS’ Jenny Gathright. The housing authority also didn’t adequately protect millions of dollars in bank deposits, and there were signs that money designated for certain federal programs may have been used for other purposes, the audit found. The mistakes could have serious implications. The housing authority, which receives a significant amount of its funding from the U.S. Department of Housing and Urban Development, submitted “material misstatements” to the federal government, the report said. The agency did not dispute the findings. It is working to remedy the issues, many of which were repeated from last year, and noted that a transition to new accounting software exacerbated some of them. DEEP DIVE Where are D.C.’s free buses? District leaders, including Mayor Muriel Bowser and council member Charles Allen , have tried for years to make it happen. It’s never stuck. Janeese Lewis George (who’s all but certain to be D.C.’s next mayor) wants to make the Metrobus free for SNAP recipients, who already get a 50% discount. She’s not ruling out eventually making it free for all, her campaign told Zara. Will it happen? It’s not just a District decision, since WMATA is a multistate agency, and JLG would need to find the revenue. WMATA relies on bus fares for 10% of its passenger revenue, but only 1 in 4 riders paid to board this May. In May , it was 3 in 4. Rather than writing that off, WMATA is cracking down. The agency asked bus operators to start quoting the fare again as riders board — something drivers say can lead to violence. Expect a debate next year once a new mayor is sworn in, Allen told NOTUS. FROM THE DISTRICT D.C.’s cyclist community gathered at East Potomac Park over the weekend to protest President Donald Trump’s planned renovations there, NBC4 reports . Protestors also rallied outside an old hospital campus in Southeast D.C., worried it will be redeveloped into an ICE facility, WTOP reports . Three people were arrested after a car crash near D.C.’s World War II Memorial, including two people who stopped to help the driver but were later picked up on drug charges, ABC7 reports . FROM VIRGINIA Vice President JD Vance is reportedly moving into a second home in Middleburg. The affluent Loudoun County town has mixed feelings about its newest resident, The Washington Post finds . FROM MARYLAND Ten people were hospitalized , and a Tesla Cybertruck was cut in half, in a Silver Spring collision Saturday that involved at least 11 vehicles, WTOP reports . D.C. TRIVIA Which president was famous for skinny-dipping in the Potomac River? James Madison John Quincy Adams Teddy Roosevelt Email us the answer — the first reader who gets it right gets a shout-out. The answer will be at the end of tomorrow’s newsletter. SPORTS The AJ Dybantsa hype is real, with Wizards owner Ted Leonsis going so far as to compare the NBA’s No. 1 overall pick to an all-time great. "What I was impressed with was when we introduce him to people, he makes eye contact, he asks, 'What's his name?' Shakes his hand. He's a very magnanimous personality," Leonsis told ESPN . "It reminded me, I hate to say this, of Alex Ovechkin , where he just lights up the room.” Josiah Gray may have been forgotten by many Nationals fans, but he’s still fighting to get back on the mound. NOTUS’ Jesse Dougherty has the exclusive interview. What to Watch Today Nationals at Rockies, 8:40 p.m., MLB.TV Mystics at Valkyries, 10 p.m. Thank you for reading! Today’s newsletter was produced by Jaden Amos, Jeff Dooley and Nikie Johnson. If you liked it, please forward it to a friend. If someone shared it with you, please sign up — it’s free! Got a tip or comments to share? Email us at metro@notus.com .

title: Will Free Buses Ever Arrive in D.C.?
author: Zara Norman
summary: Janeese Lewis George wants to make the metrobus free for residents on SNAP, but that "doesn’t need to be where we end."
content: The Alexandria Transit Company (DASH) has figured out how to make buses free for all residents. Kainaz Amaria/NOTUS Janeese Lewis George, who is all but sure to become the D.C.’s next mayor , wants to make the Metrobus free for recipients of the Supplemental Nutrition Assistance Program. “A bus system that’s free for people on SNAP would mean residents in all eight wards, no matter their economic status or background, would be able to get to jobs, grocery stores, medical appointments, community gatherings, and social events,” her campaign told NOTUS in a statement. If that comes to pass, Lewis George won’t rule out eventually expanding “the universe of people receiving free transit” if and when revenue is available. “I see SNAP recipients as a good place to start but it doesn’t need to be where we end,” her campaign wrote. It’s not the first time the District has floated free bus access for residents, more than 70% of whom already evade the fare, a Metro board member said during a May meeting . Mayor Muriel Bowser once made the Circulator service free, but that didn’t stick . The city already offers kids free rides and gives discounts to government employees and those receiving SNAP . Neighboring cities like Baltimore and Alexandria , Virginia, have figured out how to make buses free for all residents — so, why not D.C.? For starters, Alexandria and Baltimore receive state money to operate their buses, while the Washington Metropolitan Area Transit Authority is a multistate agency without a dedicated revenue stream. When D.C. Council member Charles Allen, chair of the District’s transportation committee, proposed a monthly $ credit on every D.C. resident’s Metro card in to fund city transit, Maryland and Virginia nixed the idea. Allen’s bill passed without the credit, but did implement 24-hour bus service. He told NOTUS that he had hoped the credit could remedy D.C.’s “upside down” transit-benefit system. “The overwhelming majority of people with transit benefits have high-paying jobs,” he said. “The majority of low-wage workers do not have a transit subsidy.” That’s the demographic Lewis George is targeting with her proposal, which her campaign told NOTUS does not yet have a revenue source. Still, Allen called the idea “incredibly achievable” given that SNAP recipients already get a 50% discount. Some transportation advocates argue that free buses should not be the focus of transportation reform. Alex Baca, the D.C. policy director at Greater Greater Washington, said increasing bus frequency and reliability are better targets. “It doesn’t really matter if the bus is free if it doesn’t show up,” she told NOTUS. Though bus fares accounted for 10% of WMATA’s total passenger revenue in the first quarter of fiscal year , the agency says fares are a key part of its ability to deliver services. Fare evasion leads to around $50 million in lost revenue annually, Metro estimates . While Metrobus ridership has largely recovered since the COVID-19 pandemic, fare payment has not. The bus saw 10.4 million boardings in May, but only one in four of those trips were paid for. Compare that with May : 10.9 million boardings, but three in four trips paid for. boost revenue, WMATA introduced a policy in May requiring bus drivers to quote the fare as riders board. Operators aren’t happy . “Chasing down fare evaders isn't going to solve the systemic budget shortfalls that WMATA or other systems in the country ,” said Ben Lynn, a spokesperson for the local union representing more than 15, regional transit workers. Quoting the fare can lead to disputes, which sometimes end in violence, Lynn said. D.C. recorded assaults on bus operators this past fiscal year and the year prior, according to data a WMATA spokesperson shared with NOTUS. Al Clements, an operator who lives in southeast D.C. but drives Alexandria’s DASH bus, almost quit his job after one such confrontation. It was , and he’d just quoted a rider the fare. “He talked to me real crazy, he called me all kinds,” Clements said. “We was going down the road, and he just kept verbally abusing me. Sitting right there in that first seat.” Since DASH went fare-free in , Clements said he doesn’t have to worry about riders getting embarrassed or agitated and confronting him. “It went from ‘F you,’ and ‘you an A-hole’ to ‘I appreciate you,’ ‘thank you,’” Clements said. “It makes the job a lot more tolerable.” _C0A4629 copy.jpg ( , AR: 1.50)DASH ridership has increased from 3.77 million boardings in to 5.67 million last year. Assaults on bus operators have fallen “dramatically” in that time, said Raymond Mui, DASH’s chief infrastructure and development officer. There were two incidents recorded last year, as compared to nine in . “We made public transit as easy to use and as carefree to use as a public sidewalk, or as an elevator, or as a park, or as a library,” Mui told NOTUS. But going fare-free didn’t come at the expense of frequency or reliability, Mui said. The city has been able to get people on and off the bus much faster, meaning the bus travels faster, too. “We were able to speed our buses up, increase our services and get more bang for the buck for the community,” Mui said. Alexandria is a fraction of D.C.’s size and serves a fraction of its population, but leaders in the District think there’s a way to eventually roll out free access citywide. The route to that reality will begin if and when Lewis George is sworn in and makes her push to bring free transit to SNAP recipients. “It’s absolutely a goal that she and I share,” Allen said. “It’s something I want to do. It’s something we’ve been working on different ways to get at.”

title: Josiah Gray Still Wants to Help the Nats. Maybe Even This Year.
author: Jesse Dougherty
summary: Once the of the Nationals’ rebuild, the 28-year-old pitcher is nearing a comeback after two years of injury rehab.
content: Nationals pitcher Josiah Gray hasn't played in a major league game since April of . (AP Photo/John McDonnell) John McDonnell/AP For a while there, all Nationals fans had to get excited about were debuts. Or, to parrot the social media hype machine, all they had to get excited about were DEBUTS. There was Keibert Ruiz and CJ Abrams, MacKenzie Gore and Cade Cavalli, Jackson Rutledge and Brady House, James Wood and Dylan Crews, DJ Herz and Robert Hassell III, Daylen Lile and Jake Irvin. For the darkest days, there was Blake Rutherford. For the waiver nerds, Alex Call. For the sickest of sickos, Jake Alu. But before all of them was Josiah Gray, who debuted for the Nats on Aug. 2, — when, maybe more than ever, fans needed a sign that things might eventually be OK again (heavy emphasis on might). Three days earlier, he had arrived in the Max Scherzer-Trea Turner trade, which had capped a deadline fire sale that saw eight veterans go out and 12 unproven players come in. Gray was, in turn, the roster’s first public of the rebuild. And because of that, he would answer so many questions about patience, about sticking with a broken club, about what it would take for an odd collection of dreamers and has-beens to eventually play respectable baseball. Sign up for our Metro Newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region. And he pitched, of course, at one point so well that he was an All Star in . And then he basically disappeared. “Man, where to even begin …” Gray said to me over the phone last week. He picked up the call from South Florida, where he’s spent the better part of the last two years and three months, stretching and throwing and eating quiet breakfasts at the Nationals’ team facility, marooned. Because for that entire time, he’s been trying to get back from injury, first with a long recovery from Tommy John surgery, now after a devastating setback at the end of spring training. He last pitched in the majors on April 4, , when some of the fielders behind him were Joey Gallo, Jesse Winker, Trey Lipscomb and Ildemaro Vargas. But after throwing off a bullpen mound in West Palm Beach on July 10 , Gray, 28, feels closer to a return than he has in a good while. “When it’s been this long, it can be hard not to feel like you’re forgotten about,” Gray said. “But that’s one of the things that you just try to not let build up in your head. I’m trying to have a fresh mindset and put all the work in behind the scenes, so that when my name is called I’m ready. I mean, it’s been time to make new baseball memories.” One big question, should Gray keep progressing, is if he can still fit into the Nats’ future, especially with a whole new front office and coaching staff. And another is how different a pitcher he might be if he gets back to a major league mound. After missing the first half of with elbow and forearm strains, Gray underwent Tommy John surgery that July. He rehabbed for the rest of that season, then all of , finishing that year with three short appearances in the minors. The goal was to compete to reclaim his rotation spot this spring, which resulted in the team telling him he needed some more time. He was optioned to Triple-A Rochester in late March. The plan was for him to start during the Red Wings’ opening series in Jacksonville. But then, during a final tune-up in West Palm Beach, his elbow didn’t feel right. Tests revealed another flexor strain, the same issue that first slowed him down two years before. It was straight back to the injured list. “I was so close to escaping that rehab mindset,” Gray said. “You know, that was a tough one.” No cliché is off limits when you’ve spent more than two years rehabbing your arm, far away from your teammates, worlds away from your major league life. And so Gray uses a lot of them. He is just stacking one good day on top of another. He has learned a lot about himself. He is enjoying the process, at least as best he can, and appreciating how many people are invested in getting him back to the show. That’s no small thing, he says. It is its own kind of blessing. But none of that means there isn’t a real, aching itch to help the Nats however he can. They have been short on arms all year, cycling through options in a tortured effort to find the 27 outs needed to win. And Gray is also eager to work more with the new staff, which is much more data-minded than his previous coaches in D.C. Gray has always pored over his metrics, the kind of guy who throws a pitch in the bullpen and immediately turns to an iPad to look at how it spun and moved. At his best, he’s ridden his plus slider as much as possible, working it off four-seam fastballs at the top of the zone. At his worst, those high fastballs have been way too friendly to power hitters, which is why he led the league in homers allowed in and part of why underlying numbers have never considered him a top-of-the-rotation arm. But in , his All-Star year, he performed above average across six months, showing that, before the injuries, he could have contributed to a winning club. When he talks about doing that now, Gray says it could be as a starter, as a reliever, whatever is needed for a Nationals team that’s still overachieving at 50-50. He expects to have a better idea of how he’s changed — or, ideally, how he hasn’t — once he pitches in minor league games in the near future, which would be the next step in his comeback. But until then, he’ll stay in the same routine for at least a bit longer. He’ll show up at the facility between 8 and 9 a.m. He’ll eat his breakfast, warm his arm with plyo balls and then work off the mound. Then, back at home, he’ll hang with his wife and their dog, Cowboy, an Australian shepherd. He might fire up the grill. And then they’ll probably turn on the Nationals game. “I wish I was a bigger part of it,” Gray said. “But with time left in the year, I think I could still make an impact.”

title: A D.C. newsletter from D.C. experts
author: Martin Austermuhle
summary: Introducing the NOTUS Metro Newsletter with Martin Austermuhle and Zara Norman.
content: We’re building Washington’s next great newsroom, and today, we’re proud to launch NOTUS’ new daily newsletter focused on all things D.C. Sign up here. We’ve formed a team of local reporters to cover news, sports, food, and all the quirks and curiosities that make our region tick. You’ll soon be seeing more of NOTUS’ local team and reporting on social media, we’ll be hosting events, and our reporters will continue digging up stories that hold the powerful to account, explain how our city and region work (and sometimes don’t), and highlight the people and personalities driving conversations and drawing interest. title: In an Age of ‘Takeovers,’ D.C. Gives Teens Another Place to Party
author: Shamira Muhammad
summary: The District’s Parks and Rec department has been hosting teen parties since . This summer, they're as popular as ever.
content: The line to enter the June 26 Late Night Hype party stretched down the block. (Marcus Hopkins/DCPR) A threatening sky shows signs of a storm, but the teenagers don't seem to notice. Thirty minutes before the party is supposed to begin, there is a line of them snaking down North Capitol Street. They’re waiting outside Reservoir Park on this Friday night in late June for some city-sanctioned fun, a weekly summertime party thrown by D.C.’s Parks and Recreation department called Late Night Hype . The parties started in as a way to keep 13- to 18-year-olds busy and safe during the COVID-19 pandemic. But in the years since, the increasingly popular events have become an antidote to another issue: “teen takeovers.” The term seems to be ubiquitous in the District, sparking heated debates on social media , countless segments on the local news and even talking points in this year’s mayoral race . In reality, a teen takeover is an impromptu social gathering of young people in a public space. Often taking place in nice weather, they are most associated with the Navy Yard neighborhood of Southeast D.C. The crowded, sometimes chaotic gatherings have led to fights, robberies, assault and gunshots. In May, four teens were arrested after a viral video showed a wild, chair-throwing brawl inside the Navy Yard Chipotle — an incident that seemed to push the hot topic to its boiling point. On Thursday, the city put new curfew laws into effect. For the rest of the summer, any resident under 18 will have to be home by 12:01 a.m. each day. The Metropolitan Police Department also has the authority to designate “extended curfew zones” where that rule could go into effect as early as 8 p.m. One item on the short list of exemptions: attending a recreational activity sponsored by the city. "Teens want somewhere safe to go in their city,” Parks and Rec Director Thennie Freeman said. “D.C. doesn't have malls. So where can young people go to hang out, to walk? “How can we still make them feel welcome and safe?” But safety and fun don't always coexist, especially when there are hundreds of kids involved. Even the best parties can get out of hand. Late Night Hype DC basketball ( , AR: 1.25) In full swing On this warm June evening, the theme for Late Night Hype is sports jerseys. In line, girls chat in small groups sporting carefully swooped edges and Fulani braids. Boys have their hair in twists, locs and braids. Almost every young person in line is Black or brown. Attendees had to register for the event with proof of their age and residency. They cycle through metal detectors and bag checks at the front entrance. They pose for pictures from professional photographers. They are greeted by music courtesy of DJ Ranger, a full-time park ranger who often gets on the decks at these events. He grabs the mic for a little housekeeping. “This little group right here, I see y'all made a mess,” he says. “Y'all gotta clean it up. Look right underneath your feet. Pick your trash up, take your hoodie off.” There’s a tent serving free Rita’s. Another for popcorn. One tent is a lounge, with comfortable chairs and video games. Next door there are henna tattoos. Nearby tables provide information on internships and community volunteer opportunities. Around 8 p.m., a team of beauticians offers free services — retwisting locs, cornrowing hair and preparing extensions for braids. Freeman said that, in March, an advisory committee of local teens made a list of what they wanted to see in the parties this summer. “I don't think it's really that difficult to create events for teens,” she told NOTUS. “I think if you listen to them, they'll tell you exactly what they want.” Event organizers said they try to “pack the schedule” for these parties, aiming to keep the kids occupied. A few small fights have occurred, they said, but nothing major. As the party gets going, curious neighbors stand on nearby rooftops with drinks, watching. One boy steps away from the action and calls a friend on FaceTime, encouraging him to come to the next event. He says the food has been good, there are plenty of girls and lots of dancing. Lauryn, who is being referred to by her middle name because she’s a minor, says this is not her first Late Night Hype. She also enjoys the free food and the dancing. She is still buzzing as she makes her way to the exit around 9:30, unaware that the vibe outside the party has started to turn. Late Night Hype crowd ( , AR: 1.26) Losing control Night has fallen and it’s dark now. There are still several dozen teens lined up outside the entrance, waiting to get into the party. They inch forward, the heavy bass of DJ Ranger’s music pulsating in the air. Suddenly, there’s an explosion. Kids begin screaming and running. There’s another loud noise and smoke rises in the area of the line. Teens stampede the line’s barricade, looking to get out of harm’s way. Police officers begin yelling at them to move out the way, shoring up the park’s outside wall of metal barricades. Word spreads that the noise is from fireworks, set off by a small group near the entrance. Police do not immediately find a culprit, but work to get control of the crowd. As they do so, most of the teens inside the party remain unaware of the disruption. Each week, Parks and Rec officials try to be deliberate about how they send teens home from these events, providing shuttles to Metro stations or holding kids inside until their parent or guardian arrives. But, as the fireworks continue, there is no such order. The police shut down North Capitol Street and parents are forced to do pick-ups at least a block or two away. Some walk from their cars to the entrance, searching for their children. Freeman tries to make her voice heard over the melee, checking in with attendees. One boy cries as volunteers try to console him. He had gotten separated from his sister in the chaos. When she shows up, tears are streaming down her , too, and she holds his hand. Days later, when the Parks and Rec Department posts to social media about the night, the fireworks color the comments. One commenter chastises Parks and Rec for not addressing the incident enough, writing that organizers “ain’t reached out to a parent yet.” One woman, who identifies herself as a resident of the area, says the event “went terribly wrong,” with teens “terrorizing the neighborhood.” “It’s sad to see a well intentioned event go horribly awry,” she writes. For a majority of attendees, that is not the story of the night. Most teenagers in the comments section are only concerned with where they might find more pictures of themselves. So the parties continue. On Friday, Parks and Rec will host its largest Late Night Hype of the summer, an “all-white party” held at the Mystics arena in Southeast D.C. “We have an obligation to have teens feel safe in their city,” Freeman said. “We know that anywhere you want to go, this is your city. You just have to behave responsibly."

title: The Mystics’ Sonia Citron Is an Unmistakable Star
author: Dave Sheinin
summary: Handed the keys to Washington’s offense, the second-year guard has quickly emerged as an elite playmaker.
content: Mystics guard Sonia Citron has emerged from the shadows into WNBA stardom. Erica Denhoff/Icon Sportswire/AP She saw the guy heading her way and knew what was coming next, with the sort of sixth sense a star athlete develops when they’re out in public and can feel all the eyeballs pointed at them. Sonia Citron, at the time an all-conference guard at Notre Dame, was at a restaurant with friends in South Bend, Indiana. She was still mulling how best to respond to an unwanted request for an autograph and a photo when he arrived at their table. “Excuse me,” the man said. “Are you Caitlin Clark?” Citron, now a second-year pro and two-time All-Star for the Washington Mystics, chuckles at the memory. It was neither the first nor the last time someone had noted her resemblance — same dark hair, same dark eyes, same build, same No. 22 jersey, even the same middle name (Elizabeth) — to Clark, the former Iowa Hawkeyes and now Indiana Fever superstar. But these days, at least around the WNBA, it is Citron’s court vision, efficiency and playmaking ability, more than her physical appearance, that are drawing comparisons to Clark and some of the other top guards in the league. And as the season careens towards the All-Star break, she is the number one reason the Mystics, despite carrying the second-youngest roster in the history of the league, are hanging onto playoff hopes with a 12-10 record. “She’s an amazing basketball player,” said Mystics forward Kiki Iriafen, who will be joining Citron at the All-Star Game on July 25 in Chicago, as they became the first WNBA teammates in 27 years to make the All-Star roster in each of their first two seasons. “You can already see a huge jump from Year 1 to Year 2, and [she] had an incredible Year 1.” Entering this week, only four players in the WNBA were averaging at least 18 points, four rebounds and three assists per game: rookie of the year Clark, rookie of the year Paige Bueckers, rookie of the year favorite Olivia Miles and Citron. And when you sort that quartet by true shooting percentage — an advanced metric that measures overall shooting efficiency from two-point and three-point range, plus free throws — Citron’s . mark tops them all. “Her normal,” Mystics coach Sydney Johnson said, “is a lot of other people’s great.” “She’s a silent killer,” teammate Shakira Austin marveled. Citron may not be as nationally famous as the other players on that list — which is perfectly fine with the self-described introvert — but WNBA coaches, by necessity, have become quite attuned to the threat she presents on the court. This is perhaps best evidenced by another advanced metric: “player gravity,” which measures how much attention a player commands from opposing defenses compared to what the spacing on the floor would predict. (During the -26 NBA season, for example, the league leaders were Shai Gilgeous-Alexander and Anthony Edwards.) This season, Citron ranks behind only Toronto’s Marina Mabrey as the top focus of opposing defenses. Sonia Citron Shakira Austin AP - ( , AR: 1.49) “If you take one thing away, she gets to the next action. She’s like [Bueckers] in that way, in that they just flow through the game,” said Fever coach Stephanie White. “They don’t get rushed. They don’t get sped up. [Citron] is a tough matchup because you have to play her honest. You have to play her straight-up. And when you do, she reads it and reacts to it quickly.” It is typical for collegiate stars entering the WNBA to see their numbers fall as a professional — and that is true for Bueckers, Miles and Clark. But Citron, selected by the Mystics with the No. 3 overall pick in the draft, is outperforming her Notre Dame production to a significant degree. In part, that’s a function of who she played with in South Bend: three seasons with Miles, a pure point guard who led the ACC in assists in each of those seasons, and two alongside Hannah Hidalgo, a dynamic scorer who has averaged 23.9 points per game through her first three collegiate seasons. Meantime, Citron, who has three inches on Miles and seven inches on Hidalgo, functioned more as a traditional wing, playing mostly off the ball, setting screens and leveraging her size to post up smaller guards. It was a similar story in when Citron first arrived in Washington, where All-Star point guard Brittney Sykes ran the Mystics’ offense, and Citron settled into her usual off-ball role. But a process that began when she first arrived in D.C. — Citron taking on a bigger role in the offense than she was used to at Notre Dame — sped up following the August trade that sent Sykes to the Seattle Storm. The Mystics’ coaching staff sat Citron down and told her, in so many words, the team’s offense from that point on was going to be run through her. “We saw a player who was highly, highly efficient, with a very low-level usage,” said Mystics assistant coach and director of player development Clinton Crouch. “I wouldn't say she was in shock, but she was kind of like, ‘Are you sure you're talking to me?’ But while she may have been shocked we’re having this conversation, all the numbers back it up. We basically said, ‘Get used to wearing this hat.’ “If she can do this now, and we’ve got a long way to go, imagine what kind of player she can become. And now the whole world is seeing that.” Sonia Citron Mystics guard AP - ( , AR: 1.50) The process has continued through . Despite the presence of three point guards on the Mystics’ roster — including first-round pick Georgia Amoore — it is a rare offensive possession when the ball doesn’t wind up in the hands of Citron, whose stats this season are marks she hasn’t hit since she was a McDonald’s All-American at Ursuline High in New Rochelle, New York. “At Notre Dame, she didn’t play as the featured player, if you will,” said Johnson. “We asked her to do that in D.C., and that takes some growth. But at the same time, we’ve never asked her to do anything she can’t do … The more touches you get, and you’re still able to produce at a high level — that’s the mark of a great player.” When Citron decides to take over a game (or more accurately, when she is told to take it over), the results can be breathtaking — as when she scored a career-high 32 points in the Mystics’ four-overtime win over the Portland Fire on June 28. With six minutes left in regulation, Citron had just seven points, but she scored 25 across the game’s final 26 minutes to lift the Mystics to a win. The 52 minutes 33 seconds she played in that game, including no breaks after the third quarter, were more than anyone else on the floor and the sixth-most minutes in a single game in WNBA history. “It’s a super-big adjustment doing what I’m doing now,” Citron acknowledged. “A lot of times I’m uncomfortable doing something I’ve never done before. They want me to take more shots, or they want me to be more involved [in the offense]. All of that is an adjustment for me. … There’ve been some bumps in the road, but I’m learning through experience.” The only downside to Citron’s emergence is the fact it has become more difficult for her to remain under the radar. She may never reach Clark’s stratosphere as a marketing sensation and cultural lightning rod — not that she wants to — but even her lesser level of WNBA stardom has forced her out of her comfort zone. “I’m definitely more introverted. I don’t love all the hoopla,” she said. “But at the same time, knowing what comes with being an athlete in the WNBA — I know I can’t avoid this.” It may be just a matter of time, in other words, until some selfie-seeking autograph hound approaches Caitlin Clark in a restaurant and, before she can even reach for her Sharpie, asks her: “Excuse me, are you Sonia Citron?”

title: What to Do in the D.C. Area This Weekend
author: Rebecca Ritzel
summary: Trombone Shorty, a Beyonce dance party, and a classic movie screening at the National Gallery.
content: Trombone Shorty is coming to Wolf Trap. Carolin Harvey Thursday District Fringe at the Phoenix Theater Van Ness St. NW D.C., 6 p.m., $15 (Through July 26) District Fringe returns for the second weekend of its second season with three shows in the Phoenix Theater (otherwise known as the UDC Auditorium.) But wait, you say, hasn’t Fringe been around DC much longer than two years? That’s correct. District Fringe is a new festival arising from the ashes of the Capital Fringe, which closed for good in . (The peripatetic festival could not sustain the pandemic, a failed building acquisition and years of developer dodging.) Sign up for our Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region. But D.C.’s DIY theatermakers are a resilient bunch. Thursday’s lineup includes a pirate cabaret, a profanely titled puppet show and a play about the cutthroat world of high school volleyball. Other weekend highlights include the debut of “Well,” a one-man musical by local impresario Rex Daugherty. The Ubiquity of Jazz at IA&A at Hillyer 9 Hillyer Ct. NW D.C., 6 p.m.; Free Tucked away in the shadow of the Phillips Collection, IA&A Hillyer gallery consistently displays the best work of local artists, plus international work and cool ancillary programming. July’s “Third Thursday” event is a free jazz concert inspired by “Ubiquitous Ghosts,” an installation by Taiwanese artist Tao Ya-Lun. The trio features Noble Jolly Jr. on piano, Blake Meister on bass and Integriti Reeves on vocals. A free panel on art and generative AI is also scheduled for Saturday. More to explore: Summer Movies on the Lawn: “Rocky” at the Library of Congress Friday “Adrift” at Round House Theatre East-West Hwy., Bethesda, $20 to $40 (Through Aug. 2) Nothing signifies the DMV’s supportive theater community better than one company hosting another’s birthday party. Props to Round House Theatre for celebrating the 20th anniversary of Happenstance, a collective of multi-hyphenate performers who specialize in historically informing clowning (i.e. no red noses). The summer show is “Adrift: A Medieval Wayward Folly,” featuring puppetry, sets and costumes inspired by the bonkers -year-old paintings of Heironymos Bosch. Tickets for Friday’s opening night include a pre-show birthday party. Beyonce vs. Beyonce Dance Party at The Atlantis 9th St. NW D.C., 8 p.m., $26 It’s a big night for the Beyhive, with Cowboy Carter’s crew facing off against Sasha Fierce stans at a dance party at the Atlantis. Cash prizes for the best dancer and best dressed fan. More to explore: Smithsonian Dreams Art Installation at the Smithsonian Castle Garden Party at the Embassy of France Saturday “Crafternoon” workshops at the ALX Zen Center Duke St. # , Alexandria, 12 p.m., $39 Tie dye may be past its peak resurgence, but traditional Japanese Shibori textile art never goes out of style. ALX Zen Center is hosting a series of Saturday “Crafternoon” workshops, starting with a class that sends participants (ages 14 and up) home with a Shibora silk scarf. Trombone Shorty at Wolf Trap Trap Road, Vienna, 7 p.m., $62 to $ New Orleans neo-soul celebrates an old soul Saturday when Trombone Shorty and Baltimore-founded duo The War and Treaty share the Filene Center stage with Mavis Staples. The Americana gospel legend turned 87 last week, and has only a handful of U.S. dates on her summer schedule. Attending is an act of patriotism. More to explore: Lotus and Lily Festival, Kenilworth Park and Aquatic Gardens LibraryFest, Arlington Central Library Sunday “High Society” screening at The National Gallery of Art 4th Street and Constitution Avenue NW D.C., 2 p.m., Free Can’t afford to vacation in Newport, R.I., but craving a scenic break from the D.C. heat? The National Gallery of Art continues its “Lyrics in Motion: Great American Musicals” series with a screening of “High Society,” a film that stars Golden Age A-lister’s Louis Armstrong, Bing Crosby, Grace Kelly and Frank Sinatra, all singing the music of Cole Porter. (Kelly is also hoofing it on Saturday, when the museum screens “American in Paris.”) Carlise Floyd’s “Susannah” at Shakespeare Opera Theatre Brook Road, McLean, Va., 2:30 p.m., $39 to $59 Washington may not be home to destination summer music festivals, but we do have Shakespeare Opera Theatre, a small professional company focused on the intersection of music and literature. Floyd’s “Susannah,” a classic American opera about the dangers of valuing outward religion more than personal truth, closes out the season. More to explore: World Cup Final watch parties at FIFA Fan Zone (National Mall), The Wharf and Starr Hill Biergarten in Tysons

title: D.C. Council Approves Bill Capping Prices on Resale Tickets
author: Shamira Muhammad
summary: Resale tickets for live events such as concerts in D.C. can’t be priced more than 10% above original value.
content: In the lead-up to Tuesday’s vote, left-leaning advocacy group New Democracy sponsored ads that urged constituents to oppose the bill due to potential threats to a “free and transparent marketplace” that could empower Ticketmaster, which is owned by Live Nation Entertainment. Phelan M. Ebenhack/AP The D.C. Council on Tuesday unanimously approved an act aimed at reining in the increasingly expensive and unruly resale ticket market around concerts and other live entertainment events in the District. The Restricting Egregious Scalping Against Live Entertainment (RESALE) Amendment Act caps the price of resold tickets at 10% more than their original value. Tickets to sporting events are not subject to the law. The act also bans speculative ticketing, when resellers list tickets they don’t actually have, and surveillance pricing, when costs are determined by a user’s personal information. The latter amendment does not apply to senior or student discounts. The bill also requires anyone selling 50 or more tickets a year to get a license. If it receives the mayor's approval and passes a congressional review, the law is expected to go into effect in January. The bill received support from local venues including the 9:30 Club and the Anthem. Advocates argued that resellers on sites such as StubHub have hurt independent venues and artists. “I've been tracking the [resale prices] on our shows, and it's infuriating, it's horrifying, it's grotesque, and it does not need to happen,” Audrey Fix Schaefer, president of the board of the National Independent Venue Association, told NOTUS. Schaefer — who is also the communications director for IMP Entertainment, which represents 9:30 and others — first wrote to Ward 6 council member Charles Allen about creating the bill last year. She said she believes the city’s indie venues are having a hard time nurturing local talent and maintaining their autonomy because skyrocketing resale costs lead to less engagement and a loss of revenue. Critics of the act argued that it could give too much power to primary market operators such as Ticketmaster and could drive the resale market underground, where it would be less regulated. The act passed the first of two necessary votes late last month. Allen, who authored the bill and the amendment banning surveillance pricing, told NOTUS he wanted to help protect independent venues’ sustainability . On Tuesday, Ward 2 council member Brooke Pinto introduced an amendment that stripped the mayor’s authority over the regulation of fees in the primary ticket market, which she believes would make local venues less desirable for artists and promoters. “First and foremost, we would be the only jurisdiction in the nation that regulated the primary market in this way,” she said ahead of Tuesday’s legislative meeting. “I don't think that's good for consumers. I don't think that's good for our competitive market.” In the lead-up to Tuesday’s vote, left-leaning advocacy group New Democracy sponsored ads that urged constituents to oppose the bill due to potential threats to a “free and transparent marketplace” that could empower Ticketmaster, which is owned by Live Nation Entertainment. Ads say the act would not stop Ticketmaster from raising prices, but would punish fans looking to sell tickets they already own. In April, Live Nation was ordered to pay nearly $10 million to District residents for using “deceptive ticketing practices.” Ticket Policy Forum Executive Director Brian Berry, whose organization represents vendors including Stubhub and SeatGeek, was one of several signatories of a letter sent to Allen seeking to exclude venues with a capacity of 3, seats and higher. That amendment was not included in the bill. “The question has never been whether consumers deserve strong protections — they do. The question is how to achieve them,” Berry wrote in a statement after the vote. “The answer is greater transparency, stronger competition and consistent rules that apply across the entire ticket ecosystem, not bills like the RESALE Act that reduce choice, increase fraud, and ultimately keep control of ticket prices in the hands of the very monopoly Washington, D.C.’s own AG is working to dismantle.” John Breyault, vice president of public policy at the National Consumer League, said he believes the RESALE Act could push legitimate ticket exchanges to unregulated markets like Facebook Marketplace or Craigslist. “You're going to increase the risk of fraud, and so consumers are right not to like to pay above value,” Breyault told NOTUS. “But they're really going to hate it if they start paying for tickets and then never actually getting them because there are ticket scams out there.”

title: Five Things We Learned About Jayden Daniels in Netflix’s ‘Quarterback’
author: Martenzie Johnson
summary: The docuseries, which came out Tuesday, follows Washington’s star quarterback through the ups and downs of his sophomore season.
content: The new season of Netflix's 'Quarterback' follows Jayden Daniels through a tumultuous sophomore season. Abbie Parr/AP Minicamps are in the rearview mirror, training camp (and the requisite “Hard Knocks” season) is still weeks away, but the NFL knows how to satisfy the appetite for football content at any point in the calendar. On Tuesday, Netflix debuted the latest season of its “Quarterback” docuseries, which follows four NFL quarterbacks for an entire season as they navigate all that can entail: wins, losses, benchings, cuts, firings, injuries, fatherhood, etc. This summer’s installment, capturing the season, features the Buccaneers' Baker Mayfield, the Titans’ Cam Ward, the Browns’ (and Bengals’) Joe Flacco and, of course, the Commanders’ Jayden Daniels. Daniels, who took Washington to the NFC championship game and won rookie of the year in , high expectations in his sophomore season. But mounting injuries to Daniels and others torpedoed the Commanders’ momentum, leading to a disappointing 5-12 record and an overhaul of the coaching staff. After watching the entire seven-episode season, here’s what we learned about Washington’s young star: He has more personality than we think. Daniels is famously apprehensive about showing emotion to the public. His Instagram appears to be run by a marketing professional, and he hasn’t tweeted since September . In interviews, he often gives the media a whole lot of nothing. But “Quarterback” shows that Daniels does have personality. In Week 1 against the Giants, Daniels has this exchange with defensive lineman and fellow Campbell’s soup pitchman Dexter Lawrence after Lawrence hits him late: Daniels: “I thought me and you was like family.” Lawrence: “You on the other team today.” Daniels: “Look, Campbell’s, you know?” In Week 6 against the Bears, Daniels yells “don’t overplay that shit” at a defender after rushing for a key first down in the fourth quarter. Five games later, Daniels is sitting at home with an injury while the team is in Madrid playing the Dolphins. With the staff in Spain, Daniels can’t get his typical breakfast, so instead he settles for Panera. “Chick-fil-A not open, so this is the backup,” Daniels says, not trying to be funny but nonetheless getting a laugh out of this viewer. He did not agree with sitting out 10 games last season. Daniels suffered three injuries last season, not including the reaggravation of one that kept him out of the season’s final weeks. But other than the gruesome dislocated left elbow he sustained Week 9 against the Seattle Seahawks, Daniels says none of those injuries would have kept him out if it were up to him. After spraining the outside ligament in his left knee in Week 2 against the Green Bay Packers, Daniels missed two weeks. While he tells backup quarterback Sam Hartman that he couldn’t move following the game, Daniels doesn’t agree with the team’s decision to sit him. “I was not happy about getting the news that I was sitting out again week four,” he says. When asked if he felt better about the decision to sit out Week 3 after Washington beat the Raiders without him, Daniels demurs. “I don't know,” he says with a nervous smile. “No. No.” Daniels missed the Week 8 game versus the Chiefs after suffering a low-grade right hamstring strain the previous week against the Cowboys. At the time, Daniels knew the injury was bad, but “was praying it wasn’t too severe.” Regardless, while sitting on the bench against Kansas City, he tells teammates: “I wanted to play super bad. If it was up to me, I'd have played in every game.” After the elbow injury in the Seahawks game (more on that below), Daniels missed a month. He returned in Week 14 against the Vikings after he and coach Dan Quinn decided it was best for him to get the reps, even in a lost season. “The biggest thing for me is protecting the team, and that comes with protecting myself and being available on the field,” Daniels says. But it’s all for naught: In the third quarter, Daniels, wearing an arm brace, throws an interception to linebacker Andrew Van Ginkel. As Daniels chases down Van Ginkel, he gets rocked by a Viking defender, ending his game and his season. “And thats what I was fucking worried about,” Daniels’ mother, Regina Jackson, says afterward. He chose to stay in the Seahawks game. Quinn took the blame for leaving Daniels in the Seattle game while down 38-7, telling reporters afterward, “I missed it.” Quinn and the medical staff had final say, but Daniels makes clear he had no desire to wave the white flag that night. A Commanders coach is seen telling Daniels to not “do anything spectacular” and to just throw the ball away if he gets in trouble. Obviously that didn’t happen, but even in hindsight, Daniels says he wouldn’t have asked out of the game before the injury. “Hell no,” he says when asked if he thought about subbing out. “Not at all. I was always taught to finish what you start, and we still got to put our best foot forward even though we played like shit the whole game. Yeah, the game might be out of reach, but finish the game.” His mom sets the record straight. When people hear Daniels’ name, the first thing they might think of is his ever-present mother, Regina Jackson. Wherever Daniels is — the Heisman Trophy ceremony, the NFL draft, an NCAA men’s basketball game — Jackson is often by his side. While she may very well be a helicopter parent, Jackson has legitimate reasons for always being in the mix. She’s not only Daniels’ mother, but also his business manager and agent. Jackson says she helps her son so much because that’s what a mother does. But the former electric vehicle and solar energy manager makes clear she’s not using Daniels, as some have insinuated. “I don't need Jayden’s money,” she says. “I have my own money, I do my own thing.” His uncle steals the show. If Mahershala Ali can win an Academy Award for just 20 minutes of screentime, then Mark Greenhouse, Jayden’s uncle, should get his props for barely 20 seconds. In Week 5 the Commanders travel to Daniels’ native Southern California to play the Los Angeles Chargers. While in town, Jackson visits with family, including Greenhouse, her sister’s husband.
